Trans-Pacific Partnership—Leave to Move Motion Without Notice

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. I seek leave to move a motion w ithout notice that the House call on the New
Zealand Government to publish the text of the Trans-Pacific Partnership agreement—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! I now just need to put the leave. Leave
is sought for the member to move that mo tion. Is there is any objection? There is
objection.
Trans-Pacific Partnership—Release of Information and Ratification Process
1. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First)  to the Prime Minister: Does
he stand by his statement that “personally I’ve  been of the view that transparency is a
good thing. As Prime Minister I’ve tried to lead that charge…”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, I stand by that statement, which was
made in the context of discussing reform of  MPs’ remuneration and travel privileges
and transparency around expenses.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Could he explain to the count ry and the House how he is
leading the charge on transparency in respect of the Trans-Pacific Partnership
negotiations when, in his words—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: It’s the same as China.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: —exactly; that’s a communist  country, a one-party State,
thank you very much—“we do not know what is actually on the table and what is off.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: We are following the same process that has been followed for
all other free-trade agreements, including the China free-trade agreement.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Why is he trying to keep  the New Zealand public in
ignorance of Trans-Pacific Partnership negotiating terms and details when the European
Commission, in a similar deal with the Un ited States, the Tran satlantic Trade and
15744 Questions for Oral Answer 11 Feb 2014
Investment Partnership, is releasing bot h the proposed investment chapter and a
layperson’s explanation for public consultation?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: For a start-off, all members of the Trans-Pacific Partnership—
all 12 countries—have agreed to keep ne gotiating text confidential. Secondly, our
negotiators are negoti ating in the best in terests of New Zeala nd. You would not think,
actually, that we would go out  there and want to give an advantage to the other
countries we are negotiating with.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Is the Prime Minister aware of the likely date of the text being
tabled in the United States C ongress, and can he confirm that  that will be before the
mid-term elections and well before it has the opportunity for ratification?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No one knows that date, because the Trans-Pacific Partnership
itself has not been concluded yet.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Why is the Prime Minist er arguing for secrecy in
negotiations when it is co mmon practice in the World Tr ade Organization to release
negotiating texts?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It is not common practice wi th the way that free-trade
agreements have been negotiated in this c ountry. The member is quite aware, actually,
that we have a very thorough parliamentary pr ocess. At the point at which a text has
been agreed, then it will go through the full process, including going off to the Foreign
Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee, for input from the public.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Does ratification by Parliament represent transparency
when by that time the public would have had,  and will continue to  have, no say in the
negotiations; and what is in the negotiations and the discussions—[ Interruption] Struck
a nerve, obviously. What is in the negotiati ons and the discussions that is of such—
[Interruption] Mr Speaker, I would like to try to get this question out. It is rather
serious.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member has already got the fi rst question out. He is actually
asking a second supplementary question within it, but it would assist the order of the
House if the member could complete his question without interjections.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Does ratification by Parliament
represent transparency when by that time th e public would have had, and will continue
to have, no say in the negotia tions; and what is in the ne gotiations and the discussions
that is of such concern to him and his Government that they presently want to keep it all
secret from the New Zealand people?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: A few things. Firstly, my advice is that the Trans-Pacific
Partnership will require legislation, so, ul timately, once it has gone through the select
committee and the public have had their chance to have input, and it has gone through
all of those various stages, the Government of the day will require a parliamentary
mandate, so by definition people would have ha d a lot of input. The second thing is that
the consultation process undert aken by the Trans-Pacific Partnership is amongst the
most extensive that a New Zealand G overnment has undertaken for any trade
negotiations. Public comment on the Trans-Pacific Partnership was first sought in 2008,
and has been invited since. Negotiators have conducted a proactive consultation process
that has included regular meetings with business groups, local c ouncils, the health
sector and other representatives, unions  and other NGOs, and ot her individuals and
academics. Opposition parties have also been  briefed on the negotiations as we go
along. I think we all know that Mr Peters is opp osed to free trade. This is the man who
voted against the China free-trade agreement. Well, good luck, but they happen to be
our second-largest trading partner and almost certainly will one day be our largest.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Would the Prime Minister think th ere would be transparency in an
entity submitting multiple Official Information Act requests in a made-up name, such
11 Feb 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 15745
as, for example, Bruce Bayliss, and does he think such a practice would be transparent
enough for a political party research unit?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I have no evidence to support th at Mr Bayliss is putting in
Official Information Act requests under a pseudonym or false name, but I am aware that
Mr Bayliss is associated with, and works for, New Zealand First. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! A point of order has been called.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. There is emerging of
late a tendency to get up and ask a supplem entary question that has nothing to do with
the primary question or any supplementary question or any answ er that the Prime
Minister might give that would give that member liberty to exte nd his question. I have
got no idea who Mr Bayliss is.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The essence of the question was around transparency and
related to the original primary question.
Prime Minister—Statements
2. Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Lea der of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister:
Does he stand by all his statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Does he stand by his 2007 stat ement in relation to trans-
Tasman regulatory harmonisation, that “We al ways have to make sure what we are
doing is in the best interests of New Zeal and.”; if so, why did he come home empty-
handed from Australia in relation to the supermarket boycott of New Zealand products?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Far from coming home empt y-handed from Australia, we
came home with a trans-Tasman visa for the Cricket World Cup; we came home with an
invitation for New Zealand businesses to be part of the G20 and be part of 400 global
chief executive officers; we came home unpicking the terrible deal that Helen Clark and
Phil Goff and David Cunliffe signed New Zealanders up to, by making sure that student
loans actually will be accessible to New Zealanders who are special class visa holders—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That answer is quite long enough, thank you.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Has the Prime Minister sought any advice as to how many
Kiwi jobs will be lost as a result of this boyc ott; if so, what was the number, and, if not,
why has he not asked?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not have that number but I do have the number of people
who have lost their job in the Labour Pa rty today. It is one—the Leader of the
Opposition’s chief of staff has quit.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am trying to assist the member who is raising a point of
order.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: The question was a simple and straightforward one: “Has he
asked for any advice?”. He has not turned himself to that question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! There were two parts to the supplementary question. The
Prime Minister addressed one part in saying how many—he said “None.”

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: He said he didn’t have the number.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is true. He said he didn’t have the number, which answers the
question.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Does the Prime Minister agree w ith his soul mate that the only
appeal available to New Zealand exporters, who could be facing a loss of up to $700
million per annum, is an appeal to the Australian Competition and Consumer
Commission; if so, why?
15746 Questions for Oral Answer 11 Feb 2014

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: First, and quite fundamentall y, I think the Le ader of the
Opposition is probably inven ting numbers from somewhere. They are not from a
reliable source. More important—

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I apologise to the Prime Mi nister but we have a point of
order.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: The Prime Minister has called my veracity into question. The
number came from the National Business Review, a renowned—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Order! That is not a point of order. That is a matter of debate
within the answer, and the—[Interruption] Order! The member has the opportunity with
further supplementary questions, if he wishes  to tease out that information. Does the
Prime Minister wish to complete his answer?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: What is clear is that this is a commercial matter, and that in
fact the Government does not support a buy Australian-made campaign, any more that it
actually supports the supermarkets in New Zealand that actually run buy New Zealand -
made campaigns. What is clear is that the Australian Government is actually running a
full investigation into competition policy in Australia. There is an opportunity for New
Zealand companies to submit to that. But these are actions by a commercial company,
so if the member is telling us that he is going to intervene with them, that is a very
interesting thing to hear.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Does the Prime Minister consider cups of tea and shady deals
with extreme minor parties to be gerrymandering the MMP electoral system?

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: How does that relate to the Prime Minister?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The Prime Minister is quite capable of answering it.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think if the member wants to talk about some of those issues,
he should go and look in the mirror and also talk to Dr Norman.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Does the Prime Minister stand by his statement that “People
want greater transparency.”; if so, why will his Government not release the text of the
Trans-Pacific Partnership agreement before any final agreement is signed?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: As I said earlier, firstly, th e Government has been involving
all of the interested stakeholders. My understa nding is that the trade Minister has been
talking to both Mr Goff and Mr Shearer. If they feel they want more information and
they are prepared potentially even to answer  confidentiality arrangements, I am sure we
could go another step forward. We are following—

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Point of order, Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, no, sit down, sunshine, I have not finished.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Both members—[Interruption] Order! I am on my feet. Both
members will resume their seats. Is there a point of order?

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. As the question went to
the matter of the text of the Trans-Pacifi c Partnership agreement, I thought it might
assist the Prime Minister to clarify—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Again—[ Interruption] Order! That is not a valid point of
order. The question related to transparency, and the Prime Minister was addressing that.
Does the Prime Minister wish to add further to his answer?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do, Mr Speaker. The process that is being followed here is
the identical process that was followed with  the China free-trade agreement. We are
more than happy to try to keep parties up to date once texts are complete and we are in a
position to be able to do that through a proper process. This is the same process that was
followed for China.
11 Feb 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 15747

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Quite clearly the question
concerned the Trans-Pacific Partnership ag reement. The Prime Minister is obviously
new to foreign policy—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Again, for the third occasion, that is not a valid point of
order. What the member is attempting to do is to use the point of order process to debate
an answer that has been given. The process would be better accomplished by using
further supplementary questions.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Given that the Prime Minister routinely refuses to comment on
intelligence and security matters, why did he make statements in relation to operational
intelligence regarding New Zealanders in Syria?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: From time to time I do offer answers where I believe it is the
right thing to do. I have done that on othe r occasions in the past. Actually, the
interesting thing yesterday was that it wa s a great example of how the Government
Communications Security Bureau actually assi sts the Security Intelligence Service to
protect New Zealanders. Interestingly enough, I remember in this House about 6 months
ago the strongest opposition coming from the Labour Party, yet last night David
Cunliffe was once again on TV telling New Z ealanders he wanted to go further than
that. He wanted more information and more  laws. Fortunately, Mr Goff straightened
him up on the radio this morning.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Point of order—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is a point of order and it will be heard in silence.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I seek leave to table an arti cle on Australian supermarkets
locking out New Zealand exports—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The source—

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: —tabled in the National Business Review—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am not prepared even to put the leave. I am not tabling the
National Business Review.
Question No. 1 to Minister

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I seek to table a list of the New
Zealand First parliamentary staff showing no Mr Bayliss.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The easiest way is for the House to determine this. Leave is sought
to table a list of New Zealand First staff. Is there any objection to that being tabled?
There appears to be no objection. It can be so tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
Job Creation and Unemployment—Statistics
3. Hon KATE WILKINSON (National—Waimakariri)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Finance
items.text: How is the stronger New Zealand econ omy supporting more jobs and higher
incomes?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associat e Minister of Finance) on behalf of the Minister
of Finance: There are a number of indicators c onfirming that the stronger economy is
translating into more jobs and higher inco mes. They range from business confidence
and employment intentions running at the highest levels for ar ound 20 years, and the
number of job ads on the SEEK website increasing 13 percent to almost 24,000 in
January. Just last week Statistics New Z ealand issued the labour market data, which
confirmed further growth in job numbers and real wages, and a decline in the
unemployment rate from 6.2 percent to 6 per cent in the December qua rter. They are all
further signs that the Government’s ec onomic programme, including the Business
15748 Questions for Oral Answer 11 Feb 2014
Growth Agenda to help businesses invest, grow, and employ more people, is working
successfully as we recover from the global financial crisis.

items.speaker: Hon Kate Wilkinson
items.text: What did the official labour ma rket statistics say last week
about the growth in jobs during the period to December 2013?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The household labour force survey confirmed that
employment increased by 1.1 percent in the December quarter. That means 24,000 more
New Zealanders were in jobs in that quarter alone. For the year to December the news
was also positive. Between the December quarters of 2012 and 2013 employment
increased 3 percent, meaning another 66,000 Ne w Zealanders were in work compared
with a year earlier. That is the stronge st annual increase since June 2006, again
confirming that the Government’s economic programme is heading in the right direction
for the benefit of New Zealand families.

items.speaker: Hon Kate Wilkinson
items.text: What other indicators in the labour market statistics issued
last week provided further evidence that th e improving labour market is helping more
New Zealanders to get ahead?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Apart from the lower unemployment rate and the strong
increase in new jobs, another positive indica tor is the continuing growth in wages. The
quarterly employment survey is the best sour ce of wage movements, and that is why it
has been used by successive Governments as the basis for setting, for example, paid
parental leave and New Zealand superannuatio n. Using this measure, average weekly
earnings rose by 2.8 percent over the year to December, while inflation was only 1.6
percent. So, on average, wages ar e continuing to rise faster than inflation. The gains are
even more significant when measured on an  after-tax basis. The average weekly
earnings after tax—[Interruption]; they do not want to hear it—have gone up 25 percent
since September 2008, compared with inflation of just 10 percent over the same period.

items.speaker: Hon Kate Wilkinson
items.text: How has the growth in new jobs over the past 4 years, as
reported by Statistics New Zealand, compared w ith Treasury forecasts issued as part of
Budget 2010?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: In Budget 2010, Treasury fore cast that there would be
174,000 more jobs in the economy over the 4½ years to June 2014.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: That’s not what you promised, though—170,000 extra jobs over
3 years, not 4.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am pleased to report we a tracking pretty close to that
forecast, which I remember Opposition partie s dismissing at the time as being way too
optimistic for New Zealand. Actual employment growth in the 4 years to December
2013 was 139,000 jobs, Mr Parker. To meet that full 4½-year Treasury forecast, another
35,000 jobs need to be created over the next 6 months, which is not unrealistic, given
that 52,000 new jobs were created in the 6 months to December. This is further
evidence that the Government’s economic programme is working.
Wage Growth—Measurement and Comparison with Inflation
4. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Minister for Tertiary
Education, Skills and Employment : By how much did wages and salaries increase
between December 2008 and December 2013 acco rding to the Labour Cost Index and
how does this compare to inflation accordi ng to the Consumer Price Index over the
same period?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for T ertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): I will give the member the informa tion he has asked for, but the House
also needs to know that the labour cost inde x he refers to is not a measure of actual
wage and salary increases in the workforce. Wage and salary increases in the workforce
are captured by the quarterly employment su rvey and, in particular, the measure of
11 Feb 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 15749
average weekly earnings. That has increased 16.1 percent since December 2008. The
labour cost index, on the other hand, is a st atistical construct de signed to measure
inflation in the labour market. It ignores pay increases that are due to increased
performance or productivity, for promotion, fo r taking on extra responsibilities, or for
changing jobs. The labour cost index increased 9.3 percent since December 2008,
which, not surprisingly, is similar to the othe r measure we have of inflation, which is
the CPI, which increased 10.8 over the same period.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Can the Minister confirm that th e labour cost index went up by
9.3 percent under the National Government over this period, while inflation increased
by 10.5 percent over the same period, meaning that people’ s pay packets have gotten
smaller in real terms under the current Government?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No. With the greatest respect to the member, he is being a
bit tricky here, because the labour cost i ndex does not measure changes in wages,
salaries, and earnings over the period. It mentions the pure inflation in the labour market
for somebody who does not get any pay in creases from improved productivity or
anything like that. The quarterly  employment survey is actually the method via which
changes in employment, total weekly gross earnings, total weekly paid hours, and
average hourly and average weekly earnings are reflected. I th ink the member does
know that because he has asked questions  on the quarterly employment survey
previously. Today, interestingly, he is asking only about the labour cost index.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the Minister aware of Statistics New Zealand’s User guide
for Statistics New Zealand’ s wage and income measures , the third edition, which says
that “if you are interested in changes in earnings acro ss time, the Labour Cost Index
(LCI) is a better measure than the QES.”?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I have not got that particular  example in front  of me, but I
can tell the member that on page 15 of the quarterly employment survey, which has just
been released last week—helpfully, on the same day as the labour cost index, which
may be why the member has confused it— it says: “The unadjusted LCI measures
changes in salary and ordinary-time wage rates for a fixed quantity of labour.”—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Arrogant man.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —no, just correct, Mr Robertson, in this case—“It fixes the
relative importance of industries and occupati ons,” but does not fix the market rates,
and so on, in terms of the quarterly  employment survey. Again, successive
Governments have used the quarterly employme nt survey for calculating things such as
superannuation and paid parental leave because  that measures the change in actual
earnings of New Zealanders, and if the member  was not being tricky,  that is what he
would use.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does the Minister not understa nd what Statistics New Zealand
is saying in the quote from its own documents wh ere it says that the labour cost index is
the official measure of the change in earni ngs over time, not the quarterly employment
survey—which is why it puts it in its documents—because the quarterly employment
survey will produce misleading results, such as showing an increase in the average
wage when lots of low-wage jobs are lost, as has happened under this Government?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I disagree with the member on a couple of points here.
Firstly, if he has noticed in the previous ques tion, we were able to show the increase in
jobs over the period that this Government ha s been in office—certainly, in recent times
and since Budget 2010. But, again, I think the member is, I am sorry, being deliberately
disingenuous here, because the labour cost inde x is about a measure of pure inflation in
the labour market for a fixed and equal quan tity of labour that does not change. In
reality, people’s income goes up because th ey are more productive, it goes up because
they have been given a promotion, it goes up because they have changed jobs. That is
15750 Questions for Oral Answer 11 Feb 2014
captured in the quarterly empl oyment survey, and that is the actual measure of wages
for New Zealanders and of how they have changed over time.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Who is right: Statistics New Zealand, which produces both the
labour cost index and the quarterly employment  survey, and says, as I quote again, that
if you are interested in change s in earnings over time, the labour cost index is a better
measure than the quarterly employment surv ey—is Statistics New Zealand right about
the right measure, or is the Minister ri ght, because he seems to know more than
Statistics New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, the member and I can exchange these phrases as
often as we like. The unadjusted labour cost index, according to Statistics New Zealand,
measures changes in salary and ordinary time wage rates for a fixed quantity of labour.
It does not fix the quality of labour within occupations. As that ch anges, that actually
changes with the quarterly employment survey. So perhaps to try to resolve this we
could make a suggestion. If the member believes that the labour cost index is the correct
way that we should calculate the increase in wages of New Zealanders, then perhaps he
would like to commit to using that calcula tion for the calculation of New Zealand
superannuation, which would mean that we would all have to reduce New Zealand
superannuation to go back to th e labour cost index level, a nd perhaps he would like to
commit to that for paid parental leave. I think, regardless of how the Greens spin this,
the reality is that when in Government , Labour and the Greens use the quarterly
employment survey because that is what measures New Zealanders’ wages.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: In light of the previous member’s questions, can the Minister clarify
for us what in legislation has been used as  the definitive measure of wage and salary
growth, and what, in particular, that measure tells us about average weekly earnings?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income
Act passed under the previous Government uses  a measure of wage growth to set the
floor for New Zealand superannuation paymen ts. That measure is average weekly
earnings from a thing known as the quarterly  employment survey. Also, the Parental
Leave and Employment Protection Act, which was amended by the previous
Government, uses a measure of wage growth  to increase the payment rate for paid
parental leave. That measure is average weekly earnings from the quarterly employment
survey. Average weekly earnings have gone up by 2.8 percent in the last year, compared
with inflation of 1.6 percent. Once again, if the Greens and th eir friends are going to be
consistent, they should go out and tell supera nnuitants that they would intend to give
them less superannuation from a Labour-Green  Government because they are changing
the way they measure wage growth in the New Zealand economy.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Well, then, could the Minister tell the House how Statistics
New Zealand has got it wrong when it says in its User guide for Statistics New
Zealand’s wage and income measures , third edition—the most recent edition—if you
are interested in changes in  earnings across time, the la bour cost index is a better
measure than the quarterly employment surv ey? Can the Minister explain exactly how

Emissions Trading Scheme—Effect of Carbon Price on Forestry
8. Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM (Green) to the Minister for Climate Change Issues:
Is his Government’s emissions trading scheme working, given hundreds of thousands of
seedlings are being destroyed across the country due to the collapsed carbon price?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: Yes. Forestry is a
cyclical business. In the 4-year period from the start of this Government, the sales of
tree stocks in this country increased relent lessly from 41 million tree seedlings to 72.5
million tree seedlings in 2012. We are expecting the figures, when they come out for the
calendar year 2013, to show a correction on that . So the market has turned, and people
who overstocked may have been  caught out by it. Le t us hope that they made excellent
money during the 4 good years preceding it. Markets go up; markets come down.

items.speaker: Dr Kennedy Graham
items.text: How can you say the emissions trading scheme is working
when Graeme Dodds of Leithfield Nursery in  Southland has been forced to destroy
700,000 pine tree seedlings as part  of this so-calle d cyclical industry, losing tens of
thousands of dollars in the process, b ecause of a carbon price collapse—going up and
down?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: Well, I am very sorry for the company concerned and I just
hope that he gets his projecti ons right in the future and th at he does not overstock. The
same has happened to many other people stocking many other pr oducts—looking at a
rising trend and just making the wrong assump tion: it is going to go up; it will never
come down.

items.speaker: Dr Kennedy Graham
items.text: Will he also say sorry to, and is he equally concerned about,
Robin Appleton of Appleton’s  Nursery in Nelson, who ha d to kill off 300,000 Douglas
fir seedlings, which were grown in anticipation of not an up and down emissions trading
scheme but a stable and efficient emissions trading scheme?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: I would make exactly the same comment about that company
too. But there is an assumption underlying th is whole range of questions that is
fundamentally wrong, and that is that peop le plant trees only fo r carbon. People have
planted trees in our country  for generations before a nyone had heard of Kyoto and
carbon prices. And log prices, which I think th at people should take into account when
making decisions with a 27-year horizon in front of them, increased by a phenomenal
20 or 30 percent. I think it went from something like $140 to $180 per cubic metre in
December 2011 to around $180 to $206 per cubic metre a year later. So people should
look at the two reasons you plan t trees, not just car bon prices. I think it is extremely
unlikely that in 27 years, car bon prices—which have got no thing to do with the New
11 Feb 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 15755
Zealand emissions trading scheme; they are all influenced by the international price—
will be sitting around the current extraordinarily low levels.

items.text: Yes. I took the opportunity to raise with

that have specific concerns should make submissions to Australia’s competition
watchdog, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, and those with
wider concerns should engage with the Au stralian competition policy review. I also
raised with Prime Minister Abbott the issue of New Zealanders livi ng in Australia. We

items.text: What’s your problem now?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If the member wants to stay in th e House to raise a point of order, I
expect him to sit down when I rise to my feet . I will hear a fresh point of order from the
member but I want to be absolutely clear to  the member that if he is attempting to
relitigate in any way a decision I have made in  ruling that question out of order, I will
take that as leading this House to disorder. Does the member wish to raise a fresh point
of order?

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Yes. I raise a point of orde r, Mr Speaker. There would not
be one self-respecting West ern democracy where fitness for appointment was not the
issue. In countless cases in the UK, Australia, and elsewhere—Canada, the United
States, and here in this Parliament, one of only nine that has had unbroken elections for
155 years—you are saying that suitability and fitness for appointment, on a past record,
is not a present consideration?

Police Resourcing—Front-line Foot Patrols and Mobile Technology
12. MIKE SABIN (National—Northland)  to the Minister of Police : What recent
announcements has she made on the number of foot patrols undertaken by Police?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Today—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Nothing in Kaitāia.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Has he finished? Have you finished?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have called the Hon Anne Tolley to answer a question.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Today I announced that there has
been a 155 percent increase in foot patrols unde rtaken by the police in the last 2 years.
They have increased from 40,918 in 2011 to  104,321 in 2013, while recorded crimes
have dropped by 17.4 percent over the last 3 years. Front-line foot patrols help cut crime
because officers are out and about and are visi ble in the community. They walk the beat
in known trouble spots, and at the times when crime is most likely to occur. This acts as
a strong deterrent to criminals, helps our co mmunities feel safer, and leads to fewer
victims.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: What steps has the Government taken to ensure our front-line police are
able to be so visible in the community?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Last year, visibility—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Last year this Government supported the roll-out of mobility
technology to all front-line police officers. Smartphones and tablets allow the police to
have access to the information that they ne ed while they are out in the community, and
reduce the amount of time that they need to spend behind a desk completing paperwork.
This technology allows each officer to spend an extra 30 minutes a shift—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How come the numbers are falling?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: —30 minutes extra a shift, Mr Peters—out in the community
preventing crime, which is about half a milli on extra hours, and is  equivalent to an
additional 354 front-line police officers every single year.

DEBATE ON PRIME MINISTER’S STATEMENT
Debate resumed from 30 January.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: It is great to be back for
what will doubtless be another action-packed year, especially in the area of Treaty
settlements. Just last Friday I signed a d eed of settlement in the far north with Ng āti
Kurī, and I want to acknowledge the support an d presence of Mrs Turia, Shane Jones,
Hone Harawira, Claudette Hauiti, and Mike Sabin at that very important ceremony, and
I ask Mr Harawira to pass on to the troops up north that the Te Hiku Claims Settlement
Bill is going to be introduced to the House within the next couple of weeks.
Over the break a number of my colleagues indicated they were intending to retire
from Parliament, and I want to wish them all the very best. They are fantastic colleagues
and friends, and I am sure they are going to do very well in a post-parliamentary life.
Before the year gets too partisan, Mr A ssistant Speaker Robertson, I also want to
acknowledge your contribution. You are, beyond doubt, an outstanding member of
Parliament, have been a great Assistant Spea ker, and I want to wish you all the very
best for the future. There are a number of others whose retirements are being reported
about at the present time, and so, in a dvance, may I wish Dave Clendon, Steffan
Browning, and Rajen Prasad all the very best for the future.
I hope honourable members are pleased with the progress on the National War
Memorial Park—I certainly am. The concretin g of the floor has st arted and it should be
covered by August, and the tunne l will be open by September. In fact, it is hard to
believe that Helen Clark was going to have a highway going through the park right next
to a school—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Always nasty!

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: Oh, the unpleasant member for Wellington
Central cannot contain himself. Every statemen t he makes is unpleasan t. I do think it is
most unfortunate.
We had a very busy end to 2013. Just be fore Christmas the Prime Minister, the
Minister for Economic Development, and I an nounced new film incentives and that the
next three Avatar sequels will be filmed in New Zealand. It seems that the Leader of the
Opposition was apparently opposed to this  wonderful announcement, though Jacinda
Ardern, at least, appeared to be pleased. I ha ve heard it said that Labour supporters in
Rongotai are saying that Annette King had a role in getting the Avatar sequels here.
Well, that is, of course, a complete falsehood. The self-styled “MP for Weta Workshop”
had nothing to do with that announcement, just as she did nothing in 2011 when trade
union thugs were trying to destroy the film industry.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: What a lie. Your nose is growing, Chris, and I’ll beat you a third
time.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: I hear the honourable member interjecting. I
think she is saying that she knows someth ing about James Cameron’s films. She
remembers the film The Abyss . I think she thinks it was a documentary about what
happened to the Labour Party when she was deputy leader and Phil Goff was the leader,
but I am afraid that is not correct.
On the subject of these two venerable member s now in their fourth decade here, it is
worth noting something about their careers. In the 1980s they were zealous Rogernomes
in a neo-liberal Government. In the 1990s-2000s  they reinvented themselves as social
democratic spendthrifts. Now in their four th decade here, they are tribunes of the
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15761
working class in a far-left Labour Party. In f act, it has been quite a journey. It does not
matter whether they are administering liberal po licies, or social democratic policies, or
far-left policies—so long as they are the ones administering. They stand for nothing
except for self-interest. They are the worst form of careerists.
But looking at the Opposition today, as I do, one is left with one conclusion: Labour
members are heading for an extinction event when they sell out their party’s great
heritage to a coalition with the Green Party. One has only to look at the experience of
Tasmania. Having entered a coalition with the Green Party in Tasmania, the Labor Party
in that state is morris dancing its way to  oblivion. Listen to these words from the
national secretary of the Aust ralian Workers’ Union. He sa id: “There’s no advantage in
Labor and the labour movement being aligne d with the Greens. The Greens’ … views
and ideologies are contrary to the views and ideology of the labour movement. … I can
understand why Tasmanian workers would be  concerned about th e destructive and
negative role the Greens have  played in destro ying parts of the Tasmanian economy
when they go to the ballot box,” because that is the ex perience in Australia of a
coalition with the Greens.
The current stewards of the Labour Party are betraying their party. I think of some of
the greats from the Labour past—people I grea tly respect: Peter Fraser, Norman Kirk,
Michael Bassett, Roger Douglas, Fran W ilde, Paul Swain, and that wonderful,
wonderful friend of mine Winnie Laban. One could never imagine those people walking
out on the traditions of the Labour Party and doing a deal with the Greens. The Greens
are out to destroy them and the Greens regard them, as Lenin would have said about the
kulaks, as nothing more than “useful idiots”. That is going to be the fate of the Labour
Party as it turns away from its traditions and betrays its traditions.
In the last couple of weeks there have b een a few articles in the press about my
outstanding style guide. The styl e guide is actually very helpful. It is modelled on,
actually—in fact, someone sent to me—Tom Shand’s style guide from 1967, which was
very, very similar. The key points about sp eech writing are these: use plain English,
avoid waffle at all costs, get to the point qui ckly, state the point, and move on. That, as
you can see from this speech, is exactly what  a style guide should be—where there is a
need for clarity.
Of course, elections are about choice an d elections are about  clarity. The people
deserve to know where the parties stand on va rious issues. Waffle is of no use, as Mr
Cunliffe found out last week when he tried to be tricky over the “baby bonus”
announcement. Among the policies dumped by Mr Cunliffe has been his policy of
letting Dr Norman have a podium next to his at announcements. But do not be fooled;
everything is not as it seems Members opposite are listening very carefully because they
are worried. What we see now is a Labour Party that is selling out on every single
policy.
So we need clarity on some of these points, for example. The Greens support internet
freedom whereas Labour wants to shut dow n Facebook. The Greens want to legalise
cannabis but Labour is opposed. The Greens wa nt to print money;  Labour does it the
old-fashioned way through borrowing and raising taxes. Russel Norman wants to be
Minister of Finance; David C unliffe says no, but there could but a role for him in some
of the broader economic portfolios. We are entitled to know what the true position is on
these and other issues.
My advice to the Labour Party—friendl y, constructive advice —is that as we
approach the election season, use plain language, get to th e point quickly, state the
point, and then move on. That is certainly the approach that I am going to be adopting in
the great seat of Rongotai later in the year, when the venerable Annette King and I front
up for another fight. She just about lost the party vote in 2011—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: But she thrashed you, Chris—11,000 votes.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: She did thrash me in the electorate vote, but
so what? As the great Judy Kirk said, it is the party vote that ma tters. I say to Annette
King—fond of her as I am on a personal leve l—that she is hopeless. I am very much
looking forward to a good scrap in Rongotai  in 2014 as she stands there for the 40 th

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: I was worried there that the previous
speaker, Christopher Finlayson, was slipping into a catatoni c slumber as he began to
speak more and more slowly as the minut es dragged on. The House is mercifully
released from that last contribution.
I want to talk about National’s housing crisis . The entire country is talking about it,
so it is right that this H ouse talks about it too. The reason that everybody is talking
about the housing crisis is that it is corrodi ng away things that we  care deeply about in
New Zealand. Under the Nationa l Government, first-home buyers are shut out of the
housing market and homeownership is dropping  more quickly than ever before. Our
children are being hospitalised because that Minister of Housing, Nick Smith, refuses to
regulate the private rental market and require a decent roof over people’s heads—at
least insulation and efficient heating.
Housing costs are not only squeezing middl e-class families across New Zealand,
they are wiping out household budgets. Interest  rates are about to go up. They are going
to add hundreds of dollars to the mortgage repayments of families in the mortgage belt.
As the Child Poverty Monitor told us a few weeks ago, it is rising housing costs that are
keeping child poverty high in this country. At  the sharp end of the housing crisis, the
most vulnerable families are living in tent s, in sleepouts, a nd in garages, and
Government agencies are even referring people to live on camping grounds.
Well, it is a mess. It has been brewing fo r several years—almost the entire time that
National has been in office. National has failed to act for 4 long years. It has failed to do
anything about the housing cris is. I guess that when you repr esent the big end of town
and about half your caucus are major landlor ds, the concerns of young, struggling first-
home buyers, of families who are livi ng in substandard and overcrowded
accommodation, and of State house tenants are not at the top of your lis t of priorities. I
suppose, given this and given that member s of the National Party caucus are major
property owners in their own rights, it is no t surprising, for instance, that they oppose a
capital gains tax. To wait 4 l ong years before doing anything about the housing crisis is
unforgivable.
Then what do we get? Last year we got Nick “Calamity” Smith running around like a
mad thing, turning up at the unveiling of a new door handle, pretending to be Michael
Joseph Savage carrying the furniture of Stat e house tenants into their new house. There
was an endless stream of photo opportunitie s and little schemes like flogging off
broken-down old State houses to first-home buyers at a heavy discount in provincial
New Zealand where there is no t a housing crisis. That is what passes for a housing
policy under this Government.
But it is too little too late. Not even the fu ll force of the Reserve Bank, with its loan-
to-value ratio lending limits, appears to be able to dampen the Auckland housing
market. If you look at the front page of today’s New Zealand Herald, you will see that
house price escalation is as rampant as ever  under this Government. Not even loan-to-
value ratios seem like they can put a dent in  it. The latest data from Quotable Value
shows that first-home buyers have been squ eezed out of the market, but that has not
stopped prices rising, because the speculators, both forei gn and domestic, have stepped
into the space. They are snapping up the hous es and that Minister will not do anything
about it.
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15763
The crazy thing about the housing crisis is  that the National Government had the
perfect opportunity to do some thing about it back in 2011  as the housing crisis was
beginning to bite. We had low interest rates,  an army of builders with nothing to do, a
city that needed rebuilding after the Cant erbury earthquakes, and an economy that
desperately needed the stimulus. It would ha ve been the perfect time for a Government-
backed building programme to build houses for first-home buyers and to add to the
State housing stock—instead of flogging it o ff, as this Minister is doing—but the
Government did not want to know. It wasted  the perfect opportunity to head off the
housing crisis as it began to bite.
Why is the housing crisis such a problem ? Why do the opinion polls show that New
Zealanders are desperately conc erned about it and so disappoi nted in the failure of the
National Government to act? Well, I think the first reason is that the housing crisis and
escalating house prices, particularly in Auck land and Christchurch at the moment, are a
major cause of the yawning gap between rich and poor in Ne w Zealand. Under the
National Government there are basically two classes of people. There are those with
assets, who are the property owners who are raking it in from tax-free capital gains.
Most of the National Party caucus are in th at category. Then there are the rest: the
people who contribute to the prosperity of this nation from the sweat of their brow.
They pay tax but are struggling to get ah ead because this National Government is
content to run an economy that rewards the speculators.
And because National has allowed Auckla nd house prices to get away on it and
because it mismanaged the roll- out of loan-to-value ratios, it  has failed to protect first-
home buyers. The Prime Minister in the middle of last year was cr ying crocodile tears
for first-home buyers, saying that he was going to sort it out with the Reserve Bank. He
said he would organise a carve-out for firs t-home buyers so that  they would not be
affected by loan-to-value ratio lending limits, which have imposed a 20 percent
minimum deposit on first-home buyers in this  country. The National Government said
that it would do something about it, but it did nothing.
In fact, under the Official Information Act, what we know is that Bill English did not
ask for advice from Treasury about the eff ect of those lending limits on first-home
buyers until after he had negotiated an ag reement with the Reserve Bank to roll out
those limits. What we know is that he di d not even ask Nick Smith, the Minister of
Housing, for advice in writing on the imp act on first-home buyers. They simply
discussed it at one of their regular catch- ups. That is how much National cares about
first-home buyers. It has allowed these loan-t o-value ratio lending li mits to shut first-
home buyers out of the market and, as a result, Generation X and Generation Y are
becoming a nation of renters under National.
But perhaps just as bad, just as depressing, is that the housing crisis and Nick Smith’s
inept, chaotic mismanagement of housing policy is blighting the life chances of
hundreds of thousands of Kiwi children. When a youngster in Te Atatū, in my electorate
in west Auckland, is living with her family a nd her four siblings in an uninsulated, one-
room garage, as was reported in the Western Leader recently, it is inevitable that that
youngster will get sick in the winter. She is  not going to be able to do her homework
properly when she is sharing a one-room Sky line garage with the rest of her family.
When that family moves from place to plac e, as it inevitably will—to relatives,
crammed into a spare room or into a slee pout, or to emergency accommodation, if they
are lucky—that young girl is going to be move d from pillar to post, from one school to
another, and that is why in  west Auckland there are a num ber of primary schools that
report a wildly fluctuating roll. It is because  of housing insecurity. It is because of the
housing crisis and this Government’s failure to do anything meaningful about it.
15764 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 11 Feb 2014
The Bay of Plenty Times reported today that a desperate family were forced to live in
a tent for 5 weeks as they waited for th e Housing New Zealand Corporation to find
them a house. Housing New Zealand has apolog ised for that. It has apologised for the
fact that it took a story in the Bay of Plenty Times  before it even visited the family.
Housing New Zealand statistics themselves te ll us that there are 77 vacant properties in
the Bay of Plenty at the moment, but Housi ng New Zealand staff c ould not even visit a
family living in a tent in a park by a river because a house was not available to that
family.
So even though National’s hous ing crisis is widening the gap between the rich and
the poor and even though it is driving families into poverty and making our children
sick, that Minister, Nick Smith, refuses to regulate the standard of housing in the private
rental market. National is denying ordinary New Zealanders a decent start in life for
their children. It refuses to tackle the fundamentals of the housing crisis. It refuses to tax
speculators, even though Auck land has become a speculators’ paradise. Speculators
both foreign and domestic are driving prices higher and higher and out of the reach of
ordinary New Zealanders. National refuses to  build affordable starter homes for first-
home buyers. It refuses to set minimum standa rds for private rental properties. All we
get are photo opportunities, tinkering with the Resource Management Act, and the
running down of Housing New Ze aland, the last part of th e housing safety net for New
Zealanders in need. It is a disgrace.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Mr Assistant Speaker Robertson, a
happy New Year to you and to th e House. It is, in fact, with great pride that I speak in
this debate, because I am also privileged to be the Minister of Justice, the Minister for
ACC, and the Minister for Ethnic Affairs.  I would like to take  the opportunity to
acknowledge my colleagues in the justi ce sector, the Hon Anne Tolley, the Hon
Christopher Finlayson, the Hon Chester Borrow s, and our chief executives, for the very
hard work and concerted work of working t ogether that they have done over the last 2
years. Can I also acknowledge in the ACC area the Hon Craig Foss, who is the
Associate Minister for ACC. Craig and I work very well together, and he has done
sterling work, particularly over the last 2 year s. In the ethnic affairs area I would like to
acknowledge Melissa Lee, the Parliamentary Private Secret ary to the Minister for
Ethnic Affairs, and all of our ethnic affairs team in National,  which, I have to say, is a
fantastic team, working together for the people of New Zealand.
The member who has just resumed his seat, Phil Twyford, made some very
interesting comments about what he had lear nt in his local newspaper about what was
happening in his local electorate. Let me gi ve him a piece of advice. As an electorate
MP, he should not be getting his stories out of  his local newspaper. He should be giving
the stories to the local newspaper. He shoul d be getting up off his chuff, getting around
to the garage, getting the story, helping th ese people to get their home through the
Housing New Zealand Corporation or some othe r provider. That is what electorate MPs
do. They do not sit around waiting for the newspaper to give them the stories.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: That’s Simon Bridges’ job in the Bay of Plenty.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I understand that there are a couple of list MPs over on
the other side of the House who do not agree wi th me. Well, let me just tell them that
that is how it works in the real world when  you are an electorate MP and you want to
stay one.
Today is the first day that I have been able to speak in the House this year, because I
have been representing New Zealand at th e United Nations Human Rights Council at
Geneva. I have to say that it was a ve ry proud experience for me because New
Zealand’s record on human rights is, frankly, second to none. I would like to say that
the good thing is that the Labour  Party was still on holiday, so  it could not actually put
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15765
out a press release attacking New Zealand or  our record on human rights. However, the
Greens were not. So Jan Logie from the Green s put out a press release and made many
other comments, and you woul d have thought, if you had list ened to them, that New
Zealand was one of the worst countries in th e world for human rights. Actually, we are
pretty much the best.
The response that we got from other nations to our report, where we acknowledged,
for instance, that we want to do so much better as a country when it comes to things like
domestic violence, and where we acknowledg ed that children stil l live in relative
poverty—but, having said that, look at our immunisation rates. L ook at our rates of
early childhood education. Look at the way in  which people are given a chance to get
ahead. We acknowledged those as well. We are never goi ng to be perfect, because
nobody ever can be in the real world, but we are always going to keep trying to be.
Instead, what did we get from the Green s, these people w ho want to be in
Government with the Labour Party and howev er many other parties that they would
need to put together? Well, we got that the next day, after that. This week, what did we
get? We got them bullying Nauru—Nauru—a nd refusing to apologise for bullying
Nauru on its record. For goodness’ sake! Why do these people not just get to work and
do a decent living, instead of attacking every country in the world except those that they
think are going to do whatever they want? So  Nauru. Nauru has its challenges; so do all
countries. But we should applaud where peopl e get ahead, applaud where they improve
their human rights record, and applaud where there is democracy. These are the things
that we want to applaud.
One of the things that we need in the country is a lack of corruption. This country has
been recorded by Transparency  International as being the least corrupt country in the
world, by the perception of the public of our Pu blic Service, for the last 8 years in a
row—either first or first equal. This is a fantastic record, and what it does is it says to
New Zealanders that when you want to ge t a passport in New Ze aland, you do not have
to pay a bribe. What you do is you go through  the normal process and, in New Zealand,
that is something we should value.
Crime generally—5 years after we came into Government, recorded crime is down to
the lowest level it has been in 33 years. Wh en I came in as the Minister of Police in
2008, I was told that we c ould do nothing about the crim e in the Counties Manukau
Police District in South Auckland, where my el ectorate of Papakura was. I was told that
this was all demographics. That was utte r rubbish—utter rubbish. What it needed was
policing. It needed smart policing, it need ed preventive policing, it needed strong
morale, and it needed a Government that backed  the police, and that is exactly what we
did. All these years later what have we got? Five years later crime is down to its lowest
level in 33 years. We have set Better Public Services targets and results. Our targets are
to reduce by 2017 overall crime rates by 15 per cent, violent crime by 20 percent, and
youth crime by 25 percent. Where are we at  the moment? Total crime is down by 12
percent, violent crime is down by 8 percent, and youth crime is down by 19 percent, and
we have still got 3 years to go on these targets.
So what we are seeing is that things  are changing. We got the alcohol reform
legislation through. We changed the law on alcohol. In fact, just before Christmas, what
did I get from the Green Mayor of Wellingt on? I got condemned by her because we did
not think it was all right for people to be out drinking on the streets until 6 o’clock in the
morning. She wrote to me and said that was dreadful; it was stopping business. These
are the same people who rail da y in, day out at alcohol—appa rently, all other drugs are
all right—except, of course, when they are running for local government or to be
members of Parliament.
15766 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 11 Feb 2014
What else did we do? Well, we brought in maximum jail sentences with no parole for
the worst serious violent offenders under th e three-strikes law. One of the other
previous Labour spokespeople on law and order and on justice said Labour was going to
get rid of that. That was about  four people back, so I am no t quite sure whether that is
still its position. It certainly is the Greens’ position. We brought in tougher sentences for
crimes against children. Now it is a crime to  stay silent if you know that a child or a
vulnerable person is at risk. We brought in t ougher sentences for involvement in gangs,
and we have brought in 24-hour GPS mon itoring for highest-r isk and child sex
offenders out on release in the community. We have toughened up and strengthened the
bail laws. We have done this w ith the support of other partie s in the House that believe
that this is important. We have also made 17 to 19-year-olds subject to adult tests for
bail if they have served time.
What we have done is make it a lot easie r for the police to do their job. We know
there are 600 extra police on the front line.  We also know, and we heard again today
from the Hon Anne Tolley, that the technol ogy that police are now  using means they
can spend more time on the front line and less time back at the office. We had 70
percent more police foot patrols in 2012. Th e police now have Tasers, lock boxes in
their cars, DNA testing of offenders, smartphone s, and tablets. What we now have is a
much safer New Zealand.
The police are not just getting tough on th ings; they are getting smart on things. We
have got pre-charge warnings: 41,000 of them  in the 24 months up to May last year.
That means actually dealing with issues straight away rather than waiting 6 or 7 months
for a court case. We have rolled out the smartphones. Illegal st reet-racing offences—
remember them? Remember how the Labour Pa rty said our law would not help? Well,
by the way, they are down 35 percent. There are huge changes: a clamp-down on gangs,
organised crime, and methamphetamine.
The big thing that is different from all the years that Labour was in office is we have
put our victims first. We have put victims first. We have brought them back into the
system and we have said that we will not cen sor them when they want to say what they
want to say in their victim impact statemen ts. We are bringing in the Harmful Digital
Communications Bill, the Public Safety (P ublic Protection Orders) Bill, the Parole
Amendment Bill, the Objecti onable Publications and Inde cency Legislation Bill, the
Victims’ Orders Against Violent Offenders Bill, and the Victims of Crime Reform Bill.
This is a Government that works very seri ously and works very well on justice and
on law and order issues. I would like to say thankyou to my colleagues for the support
and the backing you have given us, and th ank you to the people of New Zealand for
giving us the privilege of continuing to do this work.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: Could I take this opportunity, as well,
to wish you, Mr Assistant Speaker Robert son, and the House a happy New Year. In a
few months the Minister of Finance, Bill English, is likely to present his first Budget
surplus—his first Budget surplus in 6 years. It will be the last Budget that he presents to
this House and—good for him—it will be in surplu s. It must be galling that after nine
surpluses under Labour it has taken 6 years in order for him to be able to deliver one
Budget surplus to this House. He is obvious ly getting the hang of it. Nine years of
surplus and 5 years of deficit, and finally we get a Budget surplus, or that is what we are
led to believe. A Budget surplus, to the La bour Party, is a given. That is what we do
when we are in Government: we produce Budget surpluses. That is what we do.
Here is another statistic. Ever since the first National Government  came into office,
the average GDP growth under all National Governments right back through history has
been 2.9 percent—the average GDP growth. The average GDP growth under all Labour
Governments throughout history has been 3.7 percent—3.7 percen t. Every Labour
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15767
Government has been able to produce better growth than any National Government. So,
despite what this Government says about Labour Governments, they are the most
economically prosperous Governments, and they have been able to deliver what New
Zealanders want. We have been sound financ ial managers and we have been able to do
that every time we have been in Government.
Our economy has gone through the global financ ial crisis, as has the rest of the
world. We have had the rebuild of Christchurch, which has helped with half of the GDP
growth that we are seeing at the moment. Our commodity prices are doing very well,
and that has obviously cont ributed much of the rest . But although our economy is
starting to move again, along with the rest of the world, the question is whether New
Zealanders are any better off. Are New Zeal anders any better off? Are they doing as
well as the New Zealand economy is said to be doing? I know that many of those people
out there who might be watching this now w ill say no, because 50 percent of them will
not have had a pay increase. Fifty percent w ill not have had a pay increase in the last
year.
House prices are unaffordable. I ran into a couple the othe r day and we were talking
about their particular plight. They lived in a rented house, saving hard for a house. They
made improvements to their rented house because, to be quite honest, the couple wanted
to live in good accommodation. So they painted it, they put in a sandpit for their kids,
and they even put in a barbecu e. As soon as they did that , the landlord moved them on.
They are now in more expensive accommodati on, renting, and still trying hard to save
for that house, but finding it more and more di fficult to be able to do that because this
Government completely ignored the cost of  housing and the pric e of houses in the
economy.
As a result, young couples who have spoken to me say they go along every week to
yet another auction and they ar e always outbid. They just cannot  seem to be able to get
to that price. A father of a young woman I know said to me that it makes him angry that
his daughter, his son-in-law, and their three kids cannot do what he  did when he was
young—move into their own house and be able to afford that. That is the opportunity
those people had back then and young people today simply do not have. The
opportunities for young New Zealanders are simp ly not there and have slipped away
under this Government.
In fact, you were telling me today, Mr Assi stant Speaker Robertson, that a house in a
street that I grew up in, in your  electorate in Papatoetoe, the other day sold for a million
dollars—a million dollars. That is a house for hard-working New Zealanders, middle of
the road, middle class—it went for a million dollars. To buy that house, because this
Government has brought in the loan-t o-value ratios, you would need a $200,000
deposit. What sort of family can afford a $200,000 deposit? Absolutely nobody. Not a
young couple—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: You can.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: Maybe you, Mr Bridges, but certainly not a young couple who
are aspiring to own their own home. Who has that sort of money?
And, while we are on the subject, power prices have continued to climb. House
prices and electricity prices have continued to climb. I will not forget a woman who has
come to see me and said to me that she gets so sick in her stomach every time that she
goes out to her letterbox, just in case her electricity bill has arrived—just in case her
electricity bill has arrived. Ye t she reads in the paper co mments from Mr Bridges and
from everybody else and all his friends that we have one of the most competitive
electricity markets in the world. It is just that  it does not bring lowe r prices—that is all.
Everybody is changing companies, but it does not bring the price down. Last year the
inflation rate was 1 percent and the electricity rise was 5 percent. You tell that to
15768 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 11 Feb 2014
Kiwis—that somehow their competitive mark et is making them better off—and they
will laugh in your face, because they are turning their driers off, their heaters off,
because they cannot afford to pay their bills, and this Government will do nothing about
it.
That is why people want a Labour Governme nt—because we want a fair society. We
do want to see opportunities. We want New Zealanders to have opportunities—the same
opportunities that I had when I grew up, the sa me opportunities that I want for my kids
as they are growing up, as well—where New Z ealanders can afford a house, where they
can afford to pay their power bills. That is the sort of country that I want to live in; not a
country where this Government is so out of touch and so arrogant that it does not
actually understand what real New Zealanders  actually want. The Government believes
that somehow the house prices can be cured by Mr Nick Smith’s pixie dust that he
sprinkles around all over the place or Mr Bridge’s plaintive cries that we have somehow
got a very competitive energy market. It is absolute nonsense and people out there know
that.
Yet Government members are not listening to ordinary New Zealanders. They are so
arrogant and they are so out of touch that they do not actually understand what it is that
New Zealanders want. They are not listening. They are not list ening to the fact that this
Government is about to sell off yet another power company. Genesis Energy is soon
going to be on the block—Genesis Energy, whic h no mums and dads wi ll invest in. Let
us face it. When was the last time that you heard about mums and dads investing in
power companies? They do not. Only 1.5 percen t of New Zealanders actually invest in
these power companies, and I can tell you what. They are not ordinary mums and
dads—not the people whom I speak of. That is  how out of touch this Government is.
Does it really think that mums and dads are buying them? No, the corporates are buying
them. The financial companies are buying them. The overseas companies are buying
them and shipping the proceeds and the profits off to other places outside of here.
This Government is out of touch. It is out of  touch, it is arrogant, it has lost the plot,
and that is the reason it will lose this year . I congratulate Mr English on his last Budget
being in surplus. I am so sorry that the other fi ve were in deficit, but at least his last one
is in surplus. His days are numbered and so are this Government’s.

items.speaker: Hon TODD McCLAY
items.text: I do not think that the last member
who spoke in this debate, David Shearer, belie ved anything that he said there, but at
least finally we have receiv ed an apology from the Labour Party for the atrocious mess
that New Zealand was left in when we took office, and it was a heartfelt apology to the
New Zealand people. In fact, as I looked across, it was almost like that was a speech
from the latest member of the former leaders’ club, and there are two of them sitting
there together. It used to be so very, very exclusive, but it is not that exclusive any
more—almost as exclusive as the membership of  former chiefs of staff of leaders of the
Labour Party—numbering around about five now.
But both of those men over there are better than their current leader, because they are
genuine men who believe in making a diffe rence for New Zealanders. They are not
tricky. They do not go to one audience and say one thing and then go to another
audience and say another thing. The one thing I would say that  I learnt in my 5 years in
this time about Phil Goff and David Shearer is that when they stood up in the hustings
and said something, they meant it. They mi ght have been wrong every single time, but
at least they meant it.
That cannot be said for the new leader of the Labour Party, “Mr Tricky Dickie”, who
actually likes to go to part s of Auckland and stand on t op of buses with a microphone,
putting on funny voices and telling people what  they should do and how they should
vote. I have got to tell you, on behalf of t hose people whom he was speaking about, that
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15769
that was an outrageous thing that he di d. He was condescending to them. He was
horrible to them, and I bet you that he then went to another audience, changed his voice,
was oh so very tricky, and gave them such a different idea of what the country would be
like.
I actually say that there needs to be anothe r member of the former leaders’ club, and
that is their current leader  on that side, “Mr Tricky”. He should go and join them. On
behalf of the Labour Party and New Zealande rs, I say that either of those last two
gentlemen, David Shearer or Phil Goff, who act ually did a great job on behalf of the
Labour Party and who were let down by the Labour Party, should come back and
actually fill the great void that sits over there.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Now who’s being tricky?

items.speaker: Hon TODD McCLAY
items.text: I am not being tricky at all;  I am being genuine. Anyway,
enough about them, because that is it. What I want to do is congratulate my friend and
colleague and our newest Minister, the Hon Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga. What a great thing it
is—and such a diverse party we have here  in the National Party—that he becomes a
Minister in our Government. Indeed, the gr eat thing about this Government, compared
with that party opposite that governed for 9 very long years when New Zealanders were
left in the cold, is that it is about what is best for New Zealanders going forward. I think
that having Sam Lotu-Iiga become a Minister says so very, very much.
Indeed, I read in a newspaper the other day that when we come to the election later
this year, there will be 13 people who were  members of this Parliament from the
National Party, as it stood at  the 2011 election, who will have resigned. Some have
already gone. Some are retiring and going ba ck to their lives—great service to New
Zealand—and they are going on. As I skimmed down that article and had a look, there
was only one person from the Labour Party who actually has done a great service to
Labour over many years, who has decided to re tire and who can be very proud of what
they have done. I think the reas on that that person has decided to retire is that they have
just had enough of the trickiness and they want to go back to their life—and some
members are nodding their heads—and they said that the Labour Party they are in
today, which they have served dutifully for all of those years, is  not the Labour Party
that they joined all those years ago, which actually seemed to care about New
Zealanders at the time but now will just say a nything to any audience to get any vote so
it can get over on this side and start ruining the country again.
Can I say I am grateful to our Prime Mini ster not only for the leadership he has
shown over the last 5 years but also for gi ving me the honour of doing a little bit of
extra work, as part of his Government, as a Minister.
I want to pay a tribute to another very ha rd-working member of this Parliament who,
I think, has many, many years of  good service ahead of him, and that is the Hon Peter
Dunne. Can I say that when I took on the re venue portfolio, I thought there were very
big shoes to fill, but I can say honestly, with my hand on my heart, that there is a man
who did a great job on behalf of New Zealand taxpayers to make our tax base fair so
that New Zealanders would comply and pay thei r taxes, and to make sure that we had a
broad base and low rates, compared with mo st countries of the world. I know that he
had to fight tooth and nail when he was part of a previous Government under the
Labour Party to try to get thos e tax rates down to be fairer  to New Zealanders. If you
work hard and earn income, we want you to actually be responsible for spending it
yourself, rather than taking it off you, spe nding it on your behalf, and expecting you to
be grateful. I think that Pe ter Dunne has done a great job and I look forward to working
closely with him in his new portfolio areas.
I can also say that in the 6 or 7 months th at I have been Minister of Revenue, I have
had a chance to get out and meet so very many people who work for the Inland Revenue
15770 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 11 Feb 2014
Department—our staff—and they are hard-wor king individuals who actually also come
to work every day to serve New Zealanders and to make their lives better.

items.speaker: Here is the great thing about tax
items.text: we all have to pay it, but we know that lots of
people do not want to. I hear d a story not so long ago, duri ng this term of Parliament,
about somebody who had a bank account in Ne w York who was keep ing money there.
That would not be so th at they did not pay tax on it at all. It must have been because
they wanted to save up that $200,000 deposit th at they are now saying they need to go
and buy a house on the old street  that they grew up in. But the thing about tax rates is
that when they are lower, when they are br oad, and when New Zealanders see that they
are fair, then they will pay them. As soon as you start tinkering with these things—if
you try to be tricky, if you tr y to move the rates around and put them up in some
areas—then people look for ways within the law to avoid those taxes.
The great thing that we have in New Zeala nd is that our tax base is broad, the tax
income that the Government is getting is going up, and we are doing so in an extremely
fair manner. New Zealanders expect to pay their fair share and they are happy to when
they see that their Government is using that  money well and using it to good effect to
better things in society. They do not want to  pay their taxes when the rates are far too
high, when they are unfair, or when the m oney is being used and squandered. Let us
say, for example, that you put the tax rate up  as far as you can and then you take that
money and you give it back to a c ouple who might—I do not know—earn $300,000 a
year. The wife decides to have a child and not work, and their income goes down to
$150,000 a year, and you give them 60 bucks a week for that child.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: They have a child and they stop work.

items.speaker: Hon TODD McCLAY
items.text: I guarantee you that there will be hard-working people—
hard-working plumbers and builders in Hamilton, the seat that that member opposite has
continued to fail to be elected in—w ho are earning $60,000 or $70,000 a year. They go
to work every day, and they do not have any kids. The Labour Party wants to be tricky
and take their hard-earned taxes and give them to somebody down the road—from the
really expensive houses like the Leader of the Opposition owns—who earns $150,000 a
year. Labour wants to give them $60 of the ha rd-earned taxes that that builder has paid.
I think that that is ridiculous. It is sad and it is disgraceful that members opposite will
say and do anything—by being quiet when thei r leader makes things up and is tricky—
to get any vote so that they can get on this side of the House and ruin the great record
that New Zealanders have worked hard on over the last 5 years.
Here it is as easy as it ge ts. Most other countries in the world have an unemployment
rate higher than ours and it is going up. Our rate went down. Labour does not like that
because it wants people to be dependent and miserable, and that is why the number of
