people in the country who are members of the Labour Party is at a record low.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: The unemployment rate was the lowest under Labour.

items.speaker: Hon TODD McCLAY
items.text: Here is the thing about the member opposite with the
loudest voice on that side. It sounds good when she is on TV but every 3 years, when it
comes time for people to vote for her, she is  too tricky and it never works out. Here is a
prediction: if she does not swap seats and go somewhere to help out another National
Party candidate to get a bigger majorit y, Tim Macindoe, up and down his electorate,
will tell people what is going on. The people of Hamilton are very, very intelligent
people. I give you an absolute heartfelt guarant ee that her result will be worse than that
of the member opposite who is really tricky, th e leader of their part y, who is trying to
convince people all over the c ountry. It will be. Tim Macindoe will continue to be the
hard-working MP for Hamilton, as David Be nnett is. The Prime Minister was right: if
those guys want to be tricky, I cannot wait for the election this year. Let us bring it on.
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15771

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: That was an extraordin ary contribution from Mr
Todd McClay. He spent the better part of hi s speech talking about himself and thanking
people. You were not winning an Academy Aw ard, Mr McClay. It was meant to be a
debate on the Prime Minister’s statement, but most of the first part  of the speech was
talking about himself and al l the people who have suppor ted him throughout his career
and thanking them.
The take-home messages from Mr McClay’s speech were these. One, I want to
justify tax cuts for the wealthy. His first message was that tax cuts for the wealthy,
which overwhelmingly go to people who do not need them and did not ask for them, are
good for this country. That was his first message. His second message was “Do not
support children.” He said it is a bad idea to ensure that every kid in this country gets
the best start in life. This is coming fr om the party that ta xed paper boys on their
income. We know that National does not want to support ch ildren—those little
bludgers—it just wants to tax them on their paper routes. National does not want to see
a Government that is going to take the tax cuts that were given to the wealthiest New
Zealanders and distribute them to the most important people in this country, who are our
future: the children of this country. Hi s final message was that, you know what,
everything is great. Everything is fine.
Well, you know what, Mr McClay ? Everything is not fine. Everything is not great in
New Zealand at the moment. The National Pa rty might think that just by saying the
Crosby/Textor playbook lines over and ove r again they are going to fool New
Zealanders into thinking that everything is great, but every time that Kiwi families open
the power bill, or go to the s upermarket, or have to pay their rent, they know that things
are not great. They know that th is Government is not listen ing—that it arrogantly just
wants to tell them that they are wrong. Do you know what? In th e big end of town
things probably are pretty good at the moment , but most New Zealanders are struggling
to keep their heads above water, and too many are going backwards.
I want to talk about a young single mum I me t who came to tell me her story in my
office. She said to me that she was on the DPB. She is trying to  do good by her kids so
her bills are paid automatically—they come out before she sees the money hitting her
account. But then one week that did not happen, so one week she ended up with a whole
lot of money in her account. And she got a rush of blood to the head—she is human—
and she spent it. She should not have. She rang the Budget Advisory Service because
she was so upset. She knew that she had to  pay it back. She did not know how she was
going to do it. She was scared that she was going to get into trouble.
The Budget Advisory Service staff went to  see her. When they went around there
they were expecting that she had spent th e money on alcohol or cigarettes. Do you
know what she had spent that money on? She had spent it on non-perishable food. She
had filled her pantry with that money. She sa id to me that she knew that she should not
have done it, but she said that she just wanted  that security—to feel  that security that
she had not felt for a long time of knowing wh ere the next couple of weeks’ meals were
going to come from. And she said that she wa nted to say to her kids: “Tonight you get
to eat until you are full.”
When did food become a luxury item in this country? Because, I tell you what, it is
under this Government.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Rubbish!

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: In New Zealand food should not be a luxury item and for too
many families it is. Nick Smith can say “R ubbish!”, but I was moved by that young
woman who came to see me, because it show s that New Zealand has changed. And it
has not changed for the better. Todd McClay and Simon Bridges can laugh, but the fact
is that that is the reality out there for too many of our families. That is the reality out
15772 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 11 Feb 2014
there for too many of our children, and you te ll me that $60 a week is not going to help.
I tell you that it will, and I am proud of that policy. I am proud of that policy.
I want to talk a little bit about power pric es—a little bit about power prices. Simon
Bridges and John Key constantly tell us that power prices are competitive; that power
prices are not too high. We know that that simply is not true. We have flattening
demand for electricity in this  country. We have an over-surplus of generation. We have
a collapsed carbon price.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: That’s right, and you want to ramp it up. You want to ramp it
up on poor Kiwis.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: If power prices are not going to go down now, Mr Bridges,
they are never going down. So this side of  the House is saying we are going to do
something about that. We are going to bring down power prices.
What is Simon Bridges’ response to this? That people can go on the website, if they
have a computer and access to the internet, and use the What’s My Number campaign to
change power retailers. That is your answ er, Mr Bridges. Well, you know what, Mr
Bridges? For a lot of families, they are lucky—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Why don’t you just ask me a question in the House?

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: You do not need to scream at  me. I know this is sensitive
because you know that you have failed in this area. But most families I deal with are
lucky if they can get one electricity retailer to pick them up. The idea that they have a
choice, Mr Bridges, is pure fa ntasyland, la-la stuff, and shows how arrogant and out of
touch this Minister of Energy and Resources  is—just how out of touch the Government
is. They are lucky if they can get one power retailer.
Most of the difference in power prices act ually comes from early payment discounts.
That is the big difference. Well, an ear ly payment discount does not matter if you
cannot pay the bill, Mr Bridges. You do not get the early payment discount if you
cannot afford to pay the power bill. Oh, a little light bulb goes on over his head. So the
What’s My Number campaign does nothing for the poorest families in this country. It
actually does nothing for many of the middle-cl ass families in this country. But that is
this Government’s solution to power prices. That is this Government’s solution.
So I want to come on to the issue of  housing, which my colleague Phil Twyford
talked about. I want to talk about social hous ing a little bit, becau se in the provinces
what we used to have is a waiting list of cat egories A, B, C, and D, in declining need.
And what this Government did is it said  “You know what? Anyone  who is category C
or D, we’re going to kick them off the wa iting list. That cate gory no longer exists,
because they’re not needed.”

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: That’s not true.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: That is absolutely true. In  the provinces—and I know in
Gisborne—80 percent of our waiting list was categories C and D. And it is not that
these people are wealthy; it is that the rent s, on which we base the income-related rents,
are lower than they are in the cities. So it is not that these people’s incomes are high; it
is that the average rent is low. But we do not have enough landlords in provincial New
Zealand to meet the need.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: You haven’t been in provincial New Zealand in years.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: That is where social housing fills an incredible—I live in
Gisborne.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: No you don’t.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Oh, for God’s sake! That is how pathetic it is. I do not live in
Gisborne when I live in Gisborne. That is what Simon Bridges is choosing to focus on.
This is a man who in his electorate had a family living in a tent for 5 weeks. For 5
weeks they were living in a tent. What did you do about that?
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15773

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: I didn’t know about it.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Nothing. Why do you not just ta lk about how I do not live in
Gisborne? That is how seriously this Government is taking the difficulties facing
families in this country.
So, if I go back to it, what happens is we have State houses sitting empty right across
New Zealand—3,500 houses sitting empty right across New Zealand—while families
are living in tents. How does that make sense? We have 4,500 people on the Housing
New Zealand waiting list, and that is ignor ing the 5,000 people it kicked off categories
C and D. This Government’s social housing plan  is to kick people off waiting lists, stop
putting people into houses so it can then pret end that there is no n eed, and then have an
excuse to flog the houses off. That is wh at National did the last time it was in
Government, so we should not be surprise d. We should not be surprised. It hocked off
nearly 13,000 State houses in the 1990s.
When we were in Government we manage d to rebuild nearly 8,000 houses, and that
was despite the fact that we were going th rough a building boom, and you could not get
a builder for love or money, because we ha d to rebuild that hous ing stock. We brought
income-related rents back. We started the maintenance programme that had stopped
under the National Government. You know what? In  9 years we did not get to repair all
the damage wreaked by 9 years of a Nati onal Government—we did not. And had we
won again in 2008 we would have continued to repair the damage done to social
housing by the 1990s National Government.
But, unfortunately, all we are seeing is hi story repeating itself. It is dressed up
differently. Crosby/Textor has put a different spin on it, bu t it is the same old Tory
policies—kick people out of social housing. They do not deserve to be there. Kick them
while they are down, rather than using soci al housing and seeing social housing as the
one opportunity that Governments have to provide security in a family’s life. We do not
get to do it with any other intervention that  we have as Governments. But with housing
we do. We can give people a home. We can give them a community. When there is
social housing, we can connect them to the support that they nee d. Because, let us be
honest, Housing New Zealand is often the landlord of last re sort—it is. But if we just
keep kicking people out of social housing, where do they go? They do not disappear.
They do not suddenly vanish and not be a problem any more. They just become
someone else’s problem and we never ever get to the root of that problem.
You see this with what you saw in Gisbor ne with an 80-year-old man who had a
stroke. He was living in a Housing Ne w Zealand house. Housing New Zealand
approved his nephew moving in to look after the hous e, do the maintenance, and look
after the gardens while he was in hospital.  Well, the nephew planted some dope on the
property. The police came in. There was an  investigation. The 80-year-old man was
completely incapacitated after his stroke. He got evicted from his Housing New Zealand
house because this lot are so inflexible when it comes to housing that they could not see
that it was not that elderly gentleman’s fault.  He had been in that home for 50 years. It
was his home. Housing New Zeal and staff locally were distraught that they had to evict
him, but they said that there was no wri ggle room. They were no longer allowed to
take—thank you, Mr Heatley, for that, by the way—the personal circumstances of those
tenants into consideration wh en making these decisions. Th at is the New Zealand we
now live in. That is going to change this year when we elect a Labour Government.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Fancy living in a Housing New Zealand home for
50-odd years. Fancy not going and buying your own house. Fancy not asking the
Government for assistance to buy your own hous e but rather staying there for 50 years.
It is a State house. It belongs to the State. It is there to help those in need, for goodness’
sake. That is the reason for a State house.
15774 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 11 Feb 2014

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: He was in need.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: And while we are talking about State houses, Ms Mackey—
before she goes—cast your minds back to 1936 and Michael Joseph Savage. Phil Goff
was there, but I was not. Cast your mind back  to that day when Michael Joseph Savage
was given a broken gold wa tch, three huia feathers, and a pounamu tiki. They
represented the deal done between R ātana and Labour. Four years later, Mickey Savage
died. Since then no one has seen these taong a, these artefacts that supposedly bound the
Labour Party and R ātana together—or, I should  say, that supposedly bound M āori
together with the Labour Party in 1936. You would have thought that Labour would
keep hold of them. You would have thought that  they were so prec ious and they meant
so much to the Labour Party and to New Z ealand, in fact, that these taonga would be
kept on display for the rest of the nation to see.
So let us talk about relationships and where they go. Let us talk about Treaty
settlements and the 67 Treaty se ttlements since they were es tablished. Out of 67 Treaty
settlements, 41 were settled under National in the last 5 years. Billions of dollars were
created out of those just settlements, and the T ūhoe settlement is still to come. There
were 26 of those 67 settlements in the 9 years—9 years—of the Labour Government.
When I delivered the Muriwhe nua report as Minister of M āori Affairs, way back last
century, some bright spark on the other side said: “Er, mate, what we’re going to do is
wait for Labour, because they’ll give us more.” Well, they waited for Labour, and
Labour came and went. In those 9 years Muriwhenua still had not been settled. It is only
through the good grace of our Cabinet and of  our Minister for Treaty of Waitangi
Negotiations, the Hon Chris Finlayson, that  on the weekend a deal was signed with
Ngāti Kurī, part of the Muriwhenua conglomerate.
What have we done in terms of land use? Well, let us have a look at Te Ture Whenua
Maori Act / Maori Land Act. There is around $8 billion worth of land that actually sits
idle because nobody had thought of trying to un lock it. Who is out there now trying to
unlock that? Who is out there doing the business to review Te Ture Whenua Maori Act?
None other than National and the M āori Party. That is what we call “engagement”—
engagement. You know, I love to go to huis and listen to how Labour has a great
relationship with M āori. Labour members talk a good game, but who delivers on that
relationship? It is the National Party. Who funded k ōhanga reo first and foremost? Oh,
that is right, it was actua lly Muldoon who funded k ōhanga reo way back. But anybody
would have thought that it is this relationship between Māori and Labour that does all of
this. It is not. It is not. It is a lie.
The previous speaker, Moana Mackey, talked about housing. Well, here is something
that all New Zealand should know about. At R ātana there are houses—State houses,
even—that were in need of some work. A nd who was the Government member who sat
down in a relationship with R ātana about this? My colleague and my friend the former
Minister of Housing, the Hon Phil Heatley. All of those homes have been fixed, they
have been made warm, and they have been  made safe for that community. You would
have thought that over a 70-year period Labour would do something along the lines of a
real relationship, but oh no. Th e real relationship comes when there are people who are
interested not in talking a good game but in playing a good game. That is the difference
between Labour and National. National does not  just sit there and pontificate and talk a
good game; our Ministers get in and get their hands dirty and do that—$100 million has
been spent on the insulation project. Many of those homes that have been insulated are
Māori homes. There was nothing under Labour.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: 45 percent.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Forty-five percent of those homes are Māori homes.
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15775
I think that what we are seeing today is the realignment of where history should sit—
that is, that National has been good for the relationship with M āori. Have a look at
education, for goodness’ sake. In terms of early childhood education, there are more
Māori in early childhood educat ion than ever before. The uptake of early childhood
education for M āori families is hugely significant —hugely significant. There are more
Māori achieving now under national standard s and under the National Certificate of
Educational Achievement than ever before. They are staying at school longer. There are
more graduates from w ānanga, from universities, a nd from polytechs. Out of 9,000
places under the Youth Guarantee scheme, 4,000 are M āori students—4,000 are M āori
young people.
So when it comes to talking about relationships, the delivery of service to M āori
under a National Government is beyond repro ach. We have done our fair share. I
implore the community to think very seriously about where their vote goes. It is OK in
the individual vote. I mean, pe ople have their own individual  preferences. But, as my
colleague said, the most important vote is th e party vote, because th at is the party you
want to see in Government. Who do you th ink—no, not you, Mr Deputy Speaker; them
folks out there—should govern this country on behalf of the country? That is why I say
to those who have been duped over the last few years—M āori and others, and the
Pacific Island community as well—by this touchy-touchy-feely-feely way of handling
politics where members have empathy with the poor old Pacific Island community, they
have empathy with the poor old M āori community, and they even go to lengths like I
saw at Waitangi the other day, with David C unliffe trying his best to pull the waka on
board, trying to say—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Where were you?

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Where was I? Actually, I was planning my father’s unveiling
that day, Mr Goff.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: OK. We’ll let you off, then.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Oh, you will let me off. That is the attitude—

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: Sanctimonious.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: —the sanctimonious attitude, w ith something like that. When
somebody tells the truth, they go back into their little shell and—

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: “We’ll let you off.”

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Yes, “We’ll let you off.” Well, thanks very much. Thanks
very much, Phil. I am sure my father feels great at th is moment, 6 feet under or
wherever he is.
You know, the fact of the matte r is that we have deliver ed on our relationship with
tangata whenua and delivered so much that we will keep delivering because it is good
for the country—not because Māori want it and not because we think that M āori want it
but because it is good for the relationship between the Government and tangata whenua.
Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: It is
with great delight that I get to speak in suppor t of the Prime Minister’s statement to this
Parliament.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: This could go viral.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: This could go viral, yes.  What I can say to the
House is that given that it is an election year, I think it is worthwhile trying to nail down
here once and for all what it is that voters actually use to make their decision about how
they will vote. I think it is as simple as this —just two straight things. Is it: “Time for a
change.”, or “Do not change a winning formula.”? For nearly every election I have been
involved in over many, many years, and before that just working as a member of the
party, there were times when you could see th at it was time for a ch ange, that there was
15776 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 11 Feb 2014
a stale, old Government that needed to be  changed, and there were other times when
people said that the last thing this country could afford was to change to the alternative
and therefore create mayhem again.
So on that basis I am going to raise some issues along the way. The first one is for
the voters of this country to try to get to understand what the other side’s policies would
actually be, because, for the first time ever in  an MMP Government, if there was to be a
Labour-Green coalition it would not be one e normous big party with the vast bulk of
things and a couple of smaller support partie s of one or two or ma ybe four or five; it
would be Labour only fractionally bigger than the Greens, and the Greens having a huge
amount of say—a huge amount of say—in the coalition policy. Whether I agree with
some of Labour’s views on economic policy or not is irrelevant. The fact is that you
would not know whether you were getting that or not, because the Greens have an off-
the-planet view about what  the economy should look lik e and how it should be run.
Voters should be very afraid of putting at risk the fragile gains that have been made.
And they are fragile.
Let us go back to when we came into office. We came into office in 2008 with the
global financial crisis just beginning to break. I accept that on “Planet Labour” the
global financial crisis did not occur. T hose members quite regularly get up and say
“Look how much higher unemployment is unde r National than when we were in
office.”, or “Look at National having run de ficits when we ran surpluses.” Well, guess
what! In 2008 the financial world changed. Some countries went into bankruptcy. The
United States fell out of bed, as did its sharemarket. We were lucky that the Western
World’s economic structures stayed in place.  To then say “Well, look, you’ve got a
deficit and not a surplus like we used to.”, and “You’ve got higher unemployment.” is
not the question.
What is so good about the general voting publ ic of New Zealand is that they are not
stupid enough to fall for stup id rhetoric like “You’ve got  deficits now and we had
surpluses.” In fact, the vast bulk of the voter s whom I talk to now are terribly, terribly
positive in the fact that Bill English, as th e finance Minister, took us through some of
the roughest, toughest times that  you could ever possibly fa ce and did not do it with a
slash-and-burn mentality of throwing out ev erything that was trying to keep the ship
afloat. He did take up some big borrowings—and, yes, we have got a lot of debt on the
books—but he still was very careful and ve ry frugal about new spending and about
what we did in terms of trying to get some  economic growth back. So I think that the
public will judge the economic situation that we are in now as a real plus for the current
National-led Government. They will also know th at it is terribly fragile. Even if the
economic situation was very robust and guara nteed, some of the extreme lunacy that
would come from a Labour-Greens Government  would blow it out of the water. They
have got these absolutely crazy schemes. They have opposed just about every measure
we have taken—in fact, I put it that they have opposed every measure we have taken—
to try to settle the economy down.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: And so have Labour.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: Well, I am actually talking about both lots. They
have opposed the lot. I am talking about La bour, the Greens, and whatever other Uncle
Tom Cobbleigh they would have to pull togeth er to try to make the thing work. But
what I find really interesting—and we have got another example today with the Trans-
Pacific Partnership—is just how their institutional memory seems to have been wiped.
The public will not fall for that . The public will not have a ba r of it. They will not have
a bar of it, for example, in terms of the sale  of land to foreigners. Let us take that one—
it is a cracker. Phil Goff has even got a member’s bill because he is so opposed—he is
so opposed—to selling land to foreigners.
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15777
However, let us have a look at  the track record. In 9 years in office, Labour sold five
times as much land to foreigners as we have—five times.
I will give you the best year, the very best year—it was 2006. This is my personal
favourite. Winston Peters was foreign Minister  in the Government of the day, and he
cannot deny that. He was fore ign Minister in the Governme nt of the day. In that one
year alone, the Labour Government, with Mr Peters as foreign Minister in it, sold
300,000 hectares of land. We have not even broken 120,000 hectares in our whole time
in office, and yet Labour is coming along w ith what I think the general public would
say—and I cannot use the “h” word; I will go with so mething else—was a double
standard.
It is a double standard for a party that pres ided over the Government of this country
for 9 years and sold 666,000 hectares of land to foreigners to then say: “We’re opposed
to selling land to foreigners, and this dread ful National Government has sold just over
100,000, about 120,000.” They are not laughing, but  they should be. It should be so
embarrassing that that is Labour’s policy. Then you get some more, like David Cunliffe
saying: “John Key came back from Austra lia with nothing in his hand, and didn’t get
the rights for New Zealand residents over there—didn’t get them.” What he should have
said was that it was the former Labour lead er, the former Labour Prime Minister, who
signed away on that when she went over there. Oh no, not a mutter, not a murmur, not a
whisper on that one. What sort of a double standard is that?
If I had done something, and then some year s later claimed that it was wrong for the
person who did it, and it turned out it was me , I would be so red in the face it would not
be funny. Mr Goff is rabbiting on about so mething else. How about the free-trade
agreement negotiations with China? They we re kept under wraps, for very good reason,
until they were finalised. It is the same with the Trans-Pacific Partnership right now.
They were kept under wraps, for very, very good reason—because they are in
negotiation.

items.speaker: It is a little bit like asking
items.text: “How mu ch did you pay for your house?”. Well, I would
be happy to tell people what I paid for my house once I had signed the deal and the bank
stuff had gone through and the mortgage had been set up. But I would not be telling
anybody what I was currently negotiating with the seller of it, because I would be
hoping to get a little bit more here, or get them  to leave the chattels  in here, or put in
some furniture, and, of course, negotiations  are normally always confidential. But,
again, it is to do with double standards. If  everything Labour did when it was in office
was transparent, Labour members would have every right to come to this House today
and say: “That Government over there isn’t transparent, it doesn’t tell us, and we always
did.” But the bizarre reality of it is that they do not.
So here is my last bit of advice to Labour. I should not be giving Labour advice, but I
will. The voters of this country actually ma ke a decision based on the things they talk
about at the breakfast table—not the sideshows and the bizarre stuff about Kim Dotcom,
or who leaked what, or whatever. There is no t a single family that sits at the breakfast
table and says: “What do you think about the secrecy of the Trans-Pacific Partnership
document?”. They do not. What they do is they get up and say: “Will I still have a job?
Will our income pay the bills? Will my kids be getting a good standard of education?”.
In the case of every one of those headline elements that matters—in the case of every
one—this National Government has delivered fantastic outcomes, be it the lowest crime
rate in 30 years, be it a su rplus coming in the Budget, or be it a number of things, like
standards in education and th e national standards, which ar e giving parents some good
information. Every one of the things that pare nts talk about at the breakfast table with
their families, every one of the things that  matter to them, is heading in the right
15778 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 11 Feb 2014
direction. The general view of the public will be that we cannot afford to put this at risk
while we have got the lunatics wanting to take over running the asylum. That is it.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Can I take just a few moments of my first
speech in the House this year to deliver some pleasantries. I hope everyone had a good
break, and I wish everyone the best for election year.
There are two things on which I do agree with the previous speaker, Maurice
Williamson. The first is that people will make their decisions on how they vote around
things they talk about at the breakfast table or the dinner table, if they are lucky enough
to have dinner that night, and they will decide whether the formula for a party is a mood
for change or not. So let us talk about what people do talk about at  the breakfast table.
The power bill comes in. I want to talk sp ecifically in terms of the community I
represent, and that is the Pacific community.

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: It went up dramatically more under Labour than us.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: The power bill comes in, Mr Williamson, and a Pacific family will
be wondering how they can pay that power bill. If you look at the Salvation Army
report last year, it shows that in the peri od between 2007 a nd 2012, although the
average weekly income for every household in this country went up by $54 during that
period, for the same period a Pacific house hold’s income went up by $2 a week. So
when that family looks at how they are goi ng to pay the power bills, they will make a
decision about whether or not they feel better under this Government and the track
record, when someone else’s average hous ehold weekly income goes up by $54 a week
and a Pacific Island family’s average weekly income goes up by $2 a week. Twenty-
seven times more is the national average than  for a Pacific Island family. That is from
the Salvation Army report released last year.
They will also sit around the breakfast table wondering whether Johnny is going to
have a job. They will talk about  that, so let us look at the Pacific unemployment rate at
the moment. It is 13.7 percent, which is twi ce the national average at the moment. They
will do that maths in their head, Mr Williamson, as to whether they think they are
getting a fair deal and whether it is time for a change. You will see the Pacific
community mobilise this year, because they have felt the rough edges of the recession.
This Government has done nothing for them . Their average weekly income has pretty
much stayed the same for the last 6 year s under this National Government, and the
Pacific unemployment rate means their familie s are twice as worse off than any other
family in this country. So they will do that  maths, sitting around the breakfast table, and
they will make a very wise decision to turf this Government.
We are speaking to the Prime Minister’s statement. John Key, the Prime Minister,
the Rt Hon John Key, the National leader, call him what you like, but over the course of
this year you will find that he will have a nother title and that will be Nigel-no-mates.
Over the rest of the year he will realise—and he is already starting to realise—that his
friends around this House will soon disa ppear and he will not  have enough, when it
comes election time, to cross the threshold a nd have a majority in this House. He has
already started making signals around that to other parties that he would not
accommodate in the past because it goes ag ainst everything in his political judgment—
he would not go into co alition with these parties. But now, all of a sudden, Mr Key is
Nigel-no-mates and has to start thinking about who his mates might be post election.
Look at his mates who are propping up the G overnment at the moment. We have got
John Banks, who will spend most of this parliamentary year in the dock, facing electoral
fraud charges. That is a really good look. Th at is a really, real ly good look for this
Government. And who else have we got? O h, the United Future leader, Peter Dunne,
who was asked in this House today whether or not he has the integrity as a Minister who
is responsible for the security  of documentation and secur ity of information in this
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15779
country, whether he is the person who should be in charge, whether or not he leaked
sensitive documents, and he will not give a straight answer. Well, I think the people of
New Zealand will read behind the lines of that and realise that this Government is being
propped up by two MPs who are, I guess you coul d say, tricky or dodgy in that respect,
and as this year progresses old Nigel- no-mates over there will realise that his
parliamentary term will come to an end whenever he calls an election. This Government
is being propped up by two MPs whose time will soon come to an end.
Also, we are seeing this Government tr ying to gerrymander its way back into
Government, but not necessarily making the decisions around MMP that it should, and
trying to make sure it has got its mates back in this Government by making sure that the
coat-tail rule in MMP stays in. It is a pi ece of law that 70 percent of New Zealanders
say sucks. But, no, this Governme nt is so out of touch that it will keep it th ere, just to
make sure that in the faint hope that one of  those two get back in, National can still be
the Government.
Who are the other options? Colin Craig. Even Maurice Williamson cannot have a
straight face. I did not even say anything a bout Colin Craig. I just mentioned his name,
and Maurice Williamson cannot even keep a stra ight face. This is the man whom this
National Party wants to do a deal with in or der to stay in power. This Government will
do almost anything—almost anything—to stay in  power. That is not a Government that
we should be keeping.
We are looking forward to this election y ear, actually. As Mr Williamson said, there
is a mood for change out there. We are l ooking forward to going out there and telling
our story about how this Labour Party will bring in policies that will help Kiwi families.
We have already announced one piece of policy, and that is our Best Start policy, which
will look at investing in Kiwi ch ildren to make sure that we give them the best start in
life. We will, as Sue Moroney’s member’s bi ll is proposing, extend paid parental leave
for 26 weeks. I think you will find that most families out there in New Zealand who are
looking to start families, or to have another child, really support making sure that there
is a good period of time, when they do have young kids, when mums or dads can spend
time with them in that first 6 months. We will also look at making sure that those
families are getting $60 a week for the first year of the baby’s life to make sure they can
meet the needs of those kids and that those kids can get the best start in life.
In terms of early childhood education, th ere is something that Trevor Mallard
introduced, with 20 free hours early childhood education. That will be extended from 20
hours to 25 hours. When I visited the Discove ry kindergarten in Whitby about a week
ago, those parents to whom I spoke about that part of our Best Start policy were more
than happy to make sure that they could ha ve some more hours available to them, so
they could either get more work or look fo r more part-time work, as parents of young
children. The Best Start policy is about inves ting in our children and I am proud of it. I
am really proud that we have laid the platfo rm of what this campaign will be about for
the Labour Party. It is about investing in our children.
We have heard too many extreme storie s about children in New Zealand—horror
stories—to sit here in this Parliament a nd not take action. I think my colleague Poto
Williams spoke of one extreme case in her maiden speech, James Whakaruru, who was
beaten to death by one of hi s caregivers. We hear too many horror stories of children
living in poverty. I understand that the statistic is that roughly about one in four children
in New Zealand lives in poverty. In this House that is not good enough. So the Best
Start policy, which David Cun liffe introduced a fortnight ago, is one way that this
Labour Party is going to go out there and tell its story in an election year to garner
support.
15780 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 11 Feb 2014
That Best Start policy will help a lot of families locally in my community. Around
1,500 new babies are born in the Mana elec torate every year—roughly 1,000 in Porirua
and 500 in the K āpiti area. So that investment will be a good investment for children
locally. Every one dollar spent in those early years of a ch ild’s life results in $11 of
taxpayers’ money saved later on in their lives, in terms of education, health, and
keeping them out of the justice sector. That  is a good investment. If you told anyone on
the street that you would give them $110 if  they handed over $10, they would certainly
take those odds. What have we had from the Government on this policy? Well, it has
just been scaremongering and more out of touc h rhetoric from the National Party. It is
so out of touch that even in what you w ould call a relatively str ong National Party area
of my electorate in Whitby, they quite like that policy.
So, as you can see, this Government is full of rhetoric and is out of touch, and the
people of Mana know that, especially when you ask them their opinions on policies like
that one, and on policies like st opping asset sales. The Government tried to hide the last
referendum result but it was a resounding victory for those New Zealanders who did not
want this Government to sell assets. Around 70 percent of people in the Mana electorate
said no to asset sales. But what did this G overnment do? Did it li sten? No, it did not.
This is a Government that is out of touc h. We are looking forward to this election
campaign, when people will make their deci sions around what they discuss at the
breakfast table, as Mr Williamson said. Th is Government has a poor track record on
incomes and jobs.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: It is a huge pleasure to get up and take a call on the
Prime Minister’s statement. I cannot believe that the previous speaker, Kris Faafoi, who
is normally a man of some rectitude, and w ho has been known to contribute on the field
to the parliamentary rugby team, was talking about power bills. Mr Faafoi, power bills
went up 77 percent under your watch—77 percent. The people in your electorate will be
just giving thanks that there is a fine National Government there that is taking control of
this situation, which was out of control under your watch. They probably enjoy having
you there briefly from time to time visiting th em, but on these matters of power bills,
Mr Faafoi, they are very happy that there is a National-led Government.
This is a National-led Government that is producing results. These are results for our
most vulnerable, results for our newborn, results for our young people, results for our
families, results for our seniors, and results for M āori, Pasifika, and our recent
immigrants. These are results for all New Zeala nders. I will come back to this in more
detail because the Prime Minister’s stat ement reflects our deep understanding of the
global financial situation and our success in  navigating our way through it. It is a
statement that reflects our steadfast resolv e to cushion the most vulnerable from the
worst edges of the recession, and an apprecia tion that we as a na tion have to work
together in a smarter way and formulate intell igent and innovative poli cies to facilitate
this.
This is a Government that respects New Zealanders. What a contrast to the recent
announcement from the third Labour leader in  3 years, David Cunliffe. That was the
announcement of a scheme to pa y money to virtually any fer tile New Zealand family to
have a child. It is a poorly  targeted spray of dollars, loopy largesse, and unfocused,
loose thinking, and is giving money to thous ands of high-income families who have no
need of it. How would this be paid for? He re, the Prime Minister has pointed out that
the third Labour leader in 3 years has been very tricky. Has Mr Cunliffe been cunning?
Perhaps he thought he had been. Who doe s not like being given money? But New
Zealand voters are more insightful that th at. Has Mr Cunliffe been conning the
electorate with his explana tion of how this cadeau woul d be paid for? Cancelling
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15781
policies that are not in force saves nothing. Has he b een conning the electorate? Many
believe he has.
Labour is living in an economic Middle Ea rth and the voters of New Zealand are
underwhelmed and cynical at an opening sa lvo in the 2014 campaign that portrays the
author as both “Disingenuous David” and “Devious David”. Instead of a Best Start, it is
a stuttering misfire, which underlines the fact that Labour has learnt nothing in the last 5
years in Opposition—nothing, nada, nil—and ha s disregarded the global financial crisis
completely. It is firmly stuck in the same  old mind-set of tax more, spend more, and
hope. The 2014 parliamentary year is just a few weeks old and already the Labour
Opposition is promising $750 million in more spending—$750 million. That is three-
quarters of a billion dollars in money that it  does not have, and it has no idea where it is
going to get it from.
This speech by the third Labour leader in 3 years was an opening pirouette in a dance
of the desperate. It is only early February in an election  year and Labour is already
promising $750 million in the hope of buying voter support. But he was not done
there—he was not done there. The very next day he complained that the majority of
New Zealand meat exports were frozen carcas ses. That is wrong. Th e fact is that well
over 90 percent of our meat products are cut and prepared in New Zealand before
export. Anyone who has been overseas and se en our meat products on display will
know how well we do—how well we do and how well they have been presented.
Where else has the Labour Party been wrong, I hear you ask. Labour members would
have us believe that income inequality in New Zealand is getting worse. That is wrong,
wrong, wrong. The figures of long-term Ministry of Social Development research
statistician Bryan Perry are clear that over the last 10 years or so the numbers have
barely changed. Interestingl y, Australia is less equa l than New Zealand. Labour
members would have you believe that the wage gap between Australia and New
Zealand is widening. That is  wrong, wrong, and wrong again. Th e fact is that in real,
after-tax terms, the gap between wages in Australia and New Zealand is narrowing
under this National-led Government. Labour members constantly complain and claim
that more and more New Zealanders are goi ng to live in Australia. That is wrong,
wrong, wrong. We have got the Minister of Im migration saying it is definitely wrong,
right here in front of us. The fact is that according to Statistics New Zealand the number
of New Zealanders moving to Australia has been falling steadily since December 2012.
Labour members would have you believe that National ignores older people—wrong,
wrong, wrong. The fact is that, under Nationa l, superannuation for a married couple has
increased by well over 25 percent since 2008—25 percent since 2008—which is far
more than compensating for the increase in prices from inflation over the same period.
There have been well over 40,000 more elective surgerie s, improving the quality of
life for over-65-year-olds. Our older people are doing better under National.
So far, the third Labour leader in 3 years has been caught out in a web of inaccuracy,
a slew of untruths, and a comedy of erro rs. You can understand why the Labour caucus
is so ambivalent about supporting him. You know, if this is the Best Start possible, it is
going to be a long slide to virtual irreleva ncy by the time the election comes around—
and that is just the leader, “Devious Davi d Cunliffe”. What other innovative ideas has
the Labour Party developed as it enters its sixth year in Opposition? How many ideas?
Well, actually, not many. Its spokesman on revenue, Dr David Clark, normally a man of
sober thought and mien, obviously gave the ma tter a little bit of thought—a little bit of
thought. Possibly he was texting Kim Il S ung of South Korea for inspiration, because
Dr Clark has been on the record as proposing to ban multinational—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Kim Il Sung is North Korea.
15782 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 11 Feb 2014

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: —of North Korea—corporations like Facebook from the
internet. Closing down Facebook is certainly a left-field suggestion, even from a party
of the left, and certainly seemed to take his caucus colleagues by surprise. So Labour
members in their first days back after the rejuvenating summer break have proved
themselves bereft of new ideas, instead serving up ill-conceived, poorly costed, ill-
directed, middle-class welfare, and plainly risible fantasy—and that is just Labour.
The possibility of a Labour-Green coaliti on would pose a very real clear and present
danger. The Labor-Greens have left the econo my of Australia a vi rtual train wreck.
After years of Labor-Green misgovernment ther e, Australia is facing huge deficits and
rising unemployment. Globally, the recovery from the worst recession in decades is still
very gradual. I heard my erstwhile colleag ue here, the Hon Maurice Richardson, point
that out himself. The Greens would have a more dominant role in New Zealand with the
Labour Party than they do in Australia and th ey are philosophically opposed to farming,
to manufacturing, to exportation of oil a nd mineral resources—the major underpinnings
of our economy.
This is a Government of fresh ideas th at is willing, ready, and able to provide
principled and pragmatic leadership for New Zealand so that all can share in a brighter
future and seize the growing opportunity our burgeoning economy provides.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: In that extraordinary theatrical
performance, the member who has just resumed his seat, Dr Cam Calder, accused our
side of the House of being a bit loose with the facts. He then rapidly promoted Kim Il
Sung to be the leader of South Korea. That will come as a bit of a shock to many, many
people living in that co untry. Then, in a bit of a revival of the “mother of all Budgets”,
he referred to his colleague Maurice Williamson as “Maurice Richardson”. I think it is a
bit rich for that member to tell us we ar e a bit loose with the facts; he cannot even
remember his own colleagues’ names.
I am very pleased to be speaking in this debate in support of the amendment of David
Cunliffe to the Prime Minister’s statemen t, which reads “this House expresses no
confidence in this National led Government  because New Zealand has become more
and more divided, because those in the middl e are struggling, and because the poor are
going backwards.” The facts speak for themselves on that amendment. That amendment
is absolutely accurate and every member of the National Party knows it. They can come
into this House and spin their lines as often as they like, but the facts will, in the end,
get in the way of their story. The reason that  will happen is that outside this House
people are living their lives and they know how  their lives are. Th ey know when they
hear John Key speak that he is arrogant and that he is out of touch with the reality of
how hard they work and how little they earn comp ared with the effort that they put into
their jobs.
I remember Bill English saying at the time  he cut the tax for the highest income
earners in New Zealand that if people were not earning enough money they should work
harder. That is an example of the arrogance of the National Party members and how out
of touch they are with many, many New Z ealanders who work much harder, frankly,
than many people in this House and who cannot get enough money from their wage or
salary to give their families the opportunitie s that many of us have just taken for
granted, like the opportunity to get a higher e ducation and the opportun ity to get into a
job that is challenging and satisfying and give s people value in their wage packet that is
comparable to what they are putting into our economy.
Many people have had that opportunity take n away from them by the National-led
Government. Its members are out of touch with many, many New Zealanders and that is
where the truth will come to bite them, because those are the New Zealanders who
choose our Government. Later on this year , whether it is September, October, or
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15783
November, they will cast their ballot in favour  of the party that they know represents
their voice and understands their lives—and that certainly is not National. I know that it
is Labour.
Labour wants an economy that works for a ll New Zealanders. We do have growing
inequality in New Zealand fo r retired people, for middle-in come earners, and for young
families. It is now harder and harder for them to pay their bills and live a quality life.
They do not want to go to Hawaii for a holiday, necessarily. That would probably be the
icing on the cake, but what they would like is at least one layer of the cake, one slice of
it, to give their life some a dded value, to have some good ti mes, and to not have every
day with just enough to get by, or perhaps not even that much. At the same time, they
are seeing people on really high incomes getting massive pay increases and bonuses.
That does not equate to a fair or a just society.
In New Zealand we used to be so proud of  so many things. We used to be so proud
of being an egalitarian society where it did not matter where you were born or what
state your family was in at the time —you would have access to early childhood
education, you would have access to a high-qu ality local school, a public education
system, and you would be able to afford to go to a polytechnic or a university and have
a really good chance at a decent job in the futu re. For many people, that is just off their
menu now. This National-led Government ha s taken that chance away from so many
people—that opportunity for everyone to be the best they can possibly be because of the
collective services that we provide them with, whether it is th rough the education
system, whether it is through the health system, or whether it is through social housing.
Those supports give people the chance to give back to their country everything that they
are capable of, and that is the opportunity that is gone.
One of the other things that New Zealanders  feel very passionate and proud about is
our environment. I have been just appalled  at the lack of passion from the National
Party for anything in the environmental space.  We used to boast about our clean, green
image and John Key even dissed that. He said: “F orget about that. It’s not real; it’s just
a marketing slogan.” He told the world that we did not have a clean, green country, that
it was just a marketing slogan. A nd, actually, it is getting closer  and closer to the truth.
We have seen our water quality standards degraded. We have seen the lack of protection
of our national parks. We nearly had mining in our most precious parts of the country. If
it was not for 40,000 Aucklanders who cared pa ssionately about Great Barrier Island
and Coromandel, mining in the most preci ous parts of New Zeal and would have gone
ahead. Thank goodness that the Government listened—just that single time—to the
voices of New Zealanders.
We have also seen a complete undermini ng of the principles of the Resource
Management Act in some areas. We have seen  it in the exclusive economic zone, in the
lack of passion and commitment, and certainly in the lack of action from the fisheries
Minister and the Minister of C onservation for protection of the M āui’s dolphins. There
are 55 M āui’s dolphins left—not just only around New Zealand but on the planet—but
this Government has failed to take any decisi ve action in order to protect that species. I
think that is a disgrace. What will happen to  the New Zealand reputation that we have
been so proud of in the past if this Government oversees the extinction of that species?
It is a disgrace. It is so irresponsible, it is so arrogant, and it is so out of keeping with the
pride and passion that New Zealanders have in their society and in our environment.
Labour has been putting up some good alternat ives, and I was delighted to see David
Cunliffe’s first announcement—and it will be  the first of many this year—being a
strong commitment to New Zealanders who have young families. That is a very good
place to start, and it was very appropriately named Best Start, because that is what
Labour wants to give every child who is born in New Zealand—the best start. I am sure
15784 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 11 Feb 2014
that “Maurice Richardson” would agree with th at commitment. I am sure that he would
agree with the principle of giving every New Z ealand child the best start, so that is an
important package.
I just want to conclude by looking at the st ate that the National-led Government is in
now. I remember John Key boasting about how  he would provide New Zealand with a
stable Government. We have got the M āori Party, which has been  roundly criticised by
its own supporters for propping up a Govern ment that has done so much damage to
Māori around New Zealand. The part y itself is very torn about  that. It thinks it gets
more by being in coalition, but, actually, the pr ice of that support is  far too high, in my
view. The price of supporting damage to your own constituency is a price that I do not
think should ever be paid.
John Banks is up in court for forgetting he  got massive donations from Kim Dotcom,
who is a very big man. He lives in a ma ssive mansion—an extrao rdinary place—with
his wife. John Banks flew in a helicopter to have lunch with this very large German man
with a really unusual name, got the cheque, a nd then forgot it. Perhaps he does that
quite regularly. I actually do not go out to lunch at a mansion in North Auckland to get a
cheque from Kim Dotcom very often, but perhaps John Banks does it so often he forgot
about it. So that is anothe r coalition partner,  and now we have got John Key giving
Peter Dunne back his job.
Again, today the question and answer session at Parliament at 2 p.m. provided very
little relief about what Peter Dunne actually had as his invo lvement with the Kitteridge
report. John Key is now reneging on his pr evious criticism of Winston Peters and
offering him a lifeline. This is  not the stable Government that we were promised. It is
arrogant and out of touch.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: That speech by Ruth Dyson is not
worth commenting on, but we have got a cha nging world out there. It is especially
heartening to see the public of New Zealand understand the change that is going on in
New Zealand and around the world. They se e a Government that understands that
change, is part of that change, and is leading that change in a positive and constructive
way. They see a Government that  is getting its house in or der, that has got through the
worse recession in our generation, and that ha s started on the rebuild of Christchurch.
They see a Government that understands what needs to be done fo r its people and that
has a wide ambit of knowledge and unde rstanding of what can be done for New
Zealanders going forward. It is a positive, future-looking, and aspirational Government.
It is what the people of Ne w Zealand have demanded for y ears and they have finally
got.
On the other side, we have an Opposition that cannot get out of the trenches. The
members look behind themselves all the tim e. They have no vision, no understanding,
and no comprehension of the modern world. They live in an environment where they
think everything should be protected as it  was in 1950. They think that everybody
should have the same job that they had 20 years ago. They thi nk that everybody should
have the same income that they had 20 year s ago. They do not live in the modern world
and that will be the difference at this elec tion. The public will go out there and look at a
Government that will deliver and build a stronger future or an Opposition that will try to
attack and demean New Zealanders going fo rward, and the public will not accept the
approach of the Opposition.
Often we hear in our city, like other cities, about the loss of jobs, and people say that
it is terrible that th ere has been a loss of jobs. Well,  it is. Nobody wants to see anybody
lose their job. But there is the developm ent of the workplace and there is the
development of new jobs that come into e ach city, like Hamilton, for example, where
the number of people employed has increased  in the last few years and where the
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15785
participation rate in the workforce has increa sed over the last few years. There are more
people working, more people looking for work, and more people getting jobs. That does
not mean that there will not be any cha nge in employment in  the state of where
somebody has been working.

items.speaker: A great example was a few weeks ago
items.text: Kodak. Everyone remembers Kodak, that
great company that just filed for bankruptcy recently. It had 145,000 people working for
it in its heyday. It was huge. It was a world brand. Everybody knew Kodak. But it did
not understand the digital market. It did not pi ck where the market we nt in the products
that it provided, and it went under. Somethi ng like Instagram, which Facebook has just
recently bought for about a billion dollars, shows the development and change that you
see in a modern society and in a modern economy. We cannot all maintain those jobs
that were there in 1950. We have to look fo rward to a country that goes forward, is
competitive, and can take its place in the mo dern world. That is the change and the
direction that we need to l ook at. We need to be innovative , we need to work off our
strengths, and we need to look forward, not look backwards. Our public does not want
us to look backwards; they want us to give them that direction going forward.
When you see the policies of the Opposition, th ey are all negative policies. It wants
to tax those people who are earning income . It wants to increase the taxes on those
people earning income. We will see that later in the year when it comes up with its tax
policy. It wants to tax and tax and tax. Then it  says that it is bringing in this parental
policy, this Best Start policy. That is a polic y that is a trick for New Zealanders. Most
New Zealanders will not get it. We did not know the detail until 2 days later. Even Mr
Cunliffe did not know the details until 2 days later, which counted out basically half the
people who would be getting paid  parental leave. When you actually bring the taxes in
that will go on those middle-income earners to pay for these policies, there will be
nothing in it for them. They will actually be losing money to pay for more money to be
spent on the core vote that the Labour Party seeks to get. That is not a progressive
policy. That is not a future-forward policy th at looks at building a stronger economy or
country. That is a policy of going backwards and trying to keep people under the control
of the Government. That is where the Labour  Party stands, and it has always stood that
way.
You will hear things about the minimum wa ge, and even the Green Party will talk
about living wages and things like that. How the Government of the day will suddenly
be able to tell people what their income level should be and then make it work will be
great to see. I would like to see where it sits on that num ber, because the Green Party
has certainly got a higher number than the La bour Party in terms of what it sees the
minimum wage should be. Where that will actually go in the end is something that is yet
to be seen.
When you look at the other party on the other side th ere, you have got the New
Zealand First Party. That is an anti-immigration party that  is against the changing face
of New Zealand. It is a party that is stuck in the past. It does not understand the future of
this country going forward. It is disgraceful that we have  a party like that in this
Parliament that says the things it does and attacks those New Zealanders who come here
and build their future in this country. That party should be ashamed of what it says. It is
a disgrace to this Parliament that it says those things when we have a country that will
go forward. Those people who come here and mi grate here to build this country to be
stronger should be encouraged. We should be  encouraging those people. We should be
rewarding them for making the choice to come to New Zealand. We should be making it
easier for people to make that choice, and not  be listening to the 1950s rhetoric of a
party that has no understanding of the modern world going forward.
15786 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 11 Feb 2014
Then the Green Party is here—the Green Part y that used that mantra of the clean,
green image that it stands for. The Green Party does not stand for environmental
reasons. The Green Party is the far left of socialism in this Parliament. It seeks to have a
socialist agenda. “Communism” is too good a word for the Green Party. It is to the far
left of socialism, and it will not be succe ssful. Look at the countries around the world
that have gone left in recent years: Fran ce and Australia. How ar e those two economies
doing? They are in the mire because they ha ve listened to the people who are talking of
the past policies that you see from the La bour Party and the Greens. When you look at
countries that are going forw ard, they have been progre ssive right to centre-right
Governments. This Government is l ooking at building a stronger economy, giving
everybody the opportunity through th e education system, and ma king sure that we look
after all New Zealanders, regardless of their country of origin. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: I have spent the afternoon in the House
listening carefully to the speeches made by the Government members, and what actually
surprised me more than I thought it would was the sheer arroga nce and out-of-touch
nature of what they have been saying. You kno w, this is a Government that is so out of
touch that when two-thirds of New Zeala nders vote in a referendum to say that the
Government’s policy is wrong, the Prime Mini ster gives them a two-fingered salute.
That is how arrogant the Prime Minister is . He totally ignores the clearly expressed
views of New Zealanders on the question of a sset sales. New Zealanders do not want to
see their country asset-stripped. They do not wa nt to see the assets, the institutions, that
were owned by all of us as New Zealande rs now being owned by 1 percent of New
Zealanders and a whole lot of foreign investors, and that is what is happening.
Then they consider the Prime Minister on another set of recommendations, from the
Electoral Commission. The El ectoral Commission is an independent body. It made
recommendations that included that there s hould be no more coat-tailing—an MP who
wins an electorate seat being able to bring a whole lot of other MPs in with them even
though the MP’s party does not get to the th reshold level of 5 percent. It was the
Electoral Commission that made that recommen dation, yet this National Party relies on
two discredited members of Parliament, one facing electoral charges before the court;
the other who deliberately leak ed a document contrary to th e ministerial oath that he
took to preserve the confidentiality of the Executive Council. And National wants them
back. It wants them back, despite the fact that the public does not want them. That is
arrogance; that is out of touch.
But what is also out of touch is that I have not heard a word from the National
Government on the sorts of issues that I hear my kids, my family, my electorate, and my
friends talking about and that  actually worry them. You know, when you consider it, I
come—and you come, Mr Assistant Speak er—from a very lucky generation. Our
fathers went to war. They went through a De pression. They did not get a chance for an
education, but, by God, they worked hard to  give their kids a chance. They really
worked hard to do that. Their goal, with the helping hand of the State, was to enable
their kids to achieve the Kiwi dream. What  was the Kiwi dream? The Kiwi dream was
that everyone had opportunity—not just a lucky few but everyone  had opportunity. I
and my benchmate here, David Shearer, we nt to a school called Papatoetoe High
School, a public school just down the road from King’s Co llege. We got an education
that was the equal of a privat e school education. It gave us kids from a working-class
background a chance to go forward.
We had a health system that meant that when we were young, my parents never took
out health insurance for us, because the hea lth system was there when we needed it.
You could get a prescription. You could get in to the doctor. You could afford that. You
could get into hospital. Of course, we had the aspiration that we wanted to own our own
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15787
homes. That is part of the Kiwi dream. At 23 or 24 I was able to buy my own home. It
was fantastic. When I look at my kids, two of them—the two boys—have now got a
home of their own. They could not buy in M ount Roskill. Why not Mount Roskill? It is
a working-class suburb. Yeah, like hell it is! The median price of a property is
$650,000. You know, they are on good wages. They are tradesmen. They work hard for
their living. They got their skills, they do their overtime, and they were looking at
paying seven or eight times their annual inco me for a house. For my generation—I paid
two and a half times my annual income; I could realise the Kiwi dream.
In each of these cases the State was there to  give us a helping hand. We did not rely
on it. It was not dependency, but, if you wanted to get into your own home, your parents
might get a loan from the State Advances Corporation at 3 percent, or they could
capitalise their family benefit. You could realise that dream. Eighty percent of
Aucklanders could realise that dream; now it is barely touching 60 percent. More people
are being locked into renting because the Government does not care about those who are
struggling to get ahead and who are working hard to get ahead. In  fact, it is going
backwards.
We have heard all the fine words fr om the Government and from Maurice
Williamson. We did not hear anything about the fact that in the last 5 years New
Zealand educational standards, compared wi th other countries in  the world, have gone
backwards. What is this Government’s answer ? It is to give char ter schools five times
the payment per student that it gives public  schools—the charter sc hools. It is not
interested in public education an d strengthening it; it is not in terested in the majority of
New Zealand kids, but it will  give the big handouts to th e private schools and to the
charter schools. That is not the answer.
I worry about my kids. I worry about their generation because they are going to have
to meet the cost of us baby boomers going in to retirement, and there are a whole lot of
us. When dad came back from the war, you know, he wanted what he had missed out on
for 5 years. He decided to have his fam ily and to expand his family—and good luck to
him—and thousands of other New Zealand men did the same thing. But we are all
retiring at the same time. My kids, who will not be able to retire at 65, will be
supporting me for a very long time. My dad turns 93 the week after next. He has been
retired for 33 years. He knows, and my ki ds know, that that sort of policy is
unsustainable and that we have no intergenerational equity.
What I think Labour did that was a really  good idea was to give  a helping hand to
those having families. None of my kids have  kids yet. How can they have babies of
their own when both incomes are going to  pay off the mortgage? So Labour comes
along in a family-friendly way and says that, OK, instead of the mum having to go back
to work and put the kid in a creche when the baby is only a few weeks old, she will have
the opportunity to have paid  parental leave for 6 mont hs. What a great idea—help
thousands of New Zealanders and encourage our  kids to have kids of their own because
they can afford it and it can give them th e chance and the opportunity that they need.
What is wrong with giving that benefit of  $60 a week to the families that are middle
income as well as to low-income families for the first year, and then targeting the lower-
income families to help them with those ba sic costs—the napkins and the food? It just
gives them a helping hand. Mum and Dad got six bucks a week from the Government
way back in the 1950s. That is at least $60 now. This is not gene rous; this is just
acknowledging that having kids is expensive, so you give people a helping hand. That is
what the community is about. That is what the State is about.
Those are the positive things. We can cr eate a really good New Zealand. You know,
I am in this place because New Zealand gave me  a chance. I want to see our kids in the
15788 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 11 Feb 2014
next generation get the same chances that you and I did. That is what we should be here
for, but it is not happening.
I just want to finish by talking about the Pr ime Minister’s trip to Australia last week.
There were two big issues on the agenda . One was that the monopoly supermarket
system in Australia of Coles and Woolworths , which together control 80 percent of the
retail trade, are not selling New Zealand products as part of their home brand, simply
because they are made in New Zealand. They are banning New Zealand - made
products. You know, Mr Assistant Speaker, yo u and I can remember that 30 years ago
we brought in Closer Economic Relations. Wh at does Closer Economic Relations say?
Well, I have got the agreement here in my hand. It says that it is about eliminating
“barriers to trade between Australia and New Z ealand”. That is articl e 1(c). It is about
developing trade between New Zealand and Australia under conditions “of fair
competition”.
The Aussie supermarkets have done what our Government wanted the opposite of.
They have put up new barriers—not tariff ba rriers, not quota barriers, but behind-the-
border barriers—that stop our producers selling their goods in Australian supermarkets.
John Key said that he does not think that that  is against CER. Of course it is against
CER. CER was explicitly about gaining entr y and about fair competition. I wanted to
see my Prime Minister go across to Aust ralia and stand up for the rights of New
Zealanders. Instead I saw on television that Tony Abbott stroked him like a cat—
stroked him like a cat. He flat tered him, and in return the Prime Minister behaved like a
pussy, a wimp. He did not stand up for New Z ealanders. He forgot one thing: the only
thing the cat gets is to swallow dead rats. That is what New Zealand has had to swallow
because John Key did not stand up for the rights of New Zealanders.
There is another set of New Zealanders. It is the 300,000 that he has chased to
Australia because they could not get opportunities here. The Australian Government last
year passed the National Disability Insurance Scheme, and every New Zealander paying
tax in Australia is levied specifically to  pay for the National Disability Insurance
Scheme. That is fair enough. There is one thing wrong. They pay the levy but they are
not entitled to the benefits. It is like you, Mr Assistant Speaker, paying your premium to
an insurance company but not being able to claim when you need help. How can that be
fair, and why did John Key not  stand up for the rights of New Zealanders? That is not
too much to expect from our Prime Minister. He failed, and he has failed to do the right
thing by this country here and abroad.

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: I am going to speak today in the debate on
the Prime Minister’s statement and focus on the things that do matter to New Zealand. I
am not going to resort to the sorts of co mments and offensive remarks made by the
speaker who just resumed his seat, Mr Phil Goff. I am really su rprised at the Labour
women sitting in the House, who did not violently object to the phrase that Mr Goff just
used about the Prime Minister.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: What phrase?

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: I am not repeating it, Mr Goff, because it does not honour this
House. No, no, I refuse to use that word, and I am just shocked that  none of the Labour
women did anything about using such offensive language in this House.
Anyway, this side of the House, this Government, under John Key’s leadership, is
creating a New Zealand that is  better today and better tomo rrow, a stronger place for
today’s families and tomorrow’s families. If you think about the things the Prime
Minister covered in his addres s at the opening of Parliament, they are the issues that
matter to Kiwis up and down this country: a stronger economy, more jobs, better front-
line health and education services, a safe r New Zealand, and, of course, rebuilding
Christchurch and Canterbury.
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15789
But, actually, all of this stuff comes from having a stronge r economy. We have
Labour members who instead spea k about the need or desire to interfere with a private
company’s business and think that that is going to solve the problems of the New
Zealand economy. Well, we have spent 5 y ears—this is our sixth year—focusing on
what does make a difference in the economy, a nd we are reaping those rewards. We do
not reap those rewards for our benefit; they are for the benefit of every single New
Zealander. In the first week in the Hous e the Opposition was instead already talking
about spending three-quarters of a billion dolla rs that is not even sitting there. So we
have an Opposition that just wants to go back to the old ways of the past, thinking that
just because we are getting the books balanced this year, we then go off on a lolly
scramble, we go out and spend when we still have a fragile economy. Yes, it is growing,
and, yes, things are looking up, but, actually, we should not go out and spend all of the
benefits of what has been a very tough period of time.
One thing I am really encouraged by, though, is visiting the different towns, the
smaller towns in the Taup ō electorate, whether it is Cambridge, T īrau, or T ūrangi. It is
really, really encouraging to see the nu mber of new businesses that are opening,
whether it is in retail, ma nufacturing, or tourism. Th ere are new businesses opening
every week, which is really fantastic. That  comes from the confidence of an economy
that is growing, because no one in their right mind would go out there and start a
business, start employing staff, and take on t hose sorts of commitments if they did not
think that the economic environment was one that could sustain th at opportunity. So I
want to say congratulations to those small businesses in the Taup ō community that are
out there doing it and taking risks to employ people in this environment that is growing.
Business confidence is clearly up.
So what we are seeing is that the signs are there and it is looking positive, but we
should not basically be putting that at risk. We have still got to be cautious. We have
still got to be careful and not basically just  go out and spend everyt hing that we have in
the strength of position we have got to. If you look at business confidence, it is the
highest it has been since 1999. That is  a phenomenal result. We often have

2.8 percent in the last year, a nd that is compared with an inflation rate of 1.6 percent.
So, yes, the gap is small, but it means that in  terms of wages we are heading in the right
direction.
One example, Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch, that I wanted to sp eak about today, and
one that you will be very familiar with, is the Cambridge section of the Waikato
Expressway. One of the platforms of the Government’s Business Growth Agenda is
infrastructure and its role in helping to fu el this economic growth  and opportunity. We
