yesterday. It is really fantastic to see the number of people who are employed as a result
of that project. But, more important, the re al benefit that I am immensely proud of is
that, as a result, out of that project’ s 300 jobs, 20 are done by people who were on
benefits in the local Work and Income offi ce and who now have jobs. That is 20 people
who, before this project, did not have j obs, and now do. Not only do they now have a
job and a pay packet to take home each week; they are getting ski lls, they are getting
certifications, and they are passing the rigours of  the work environment that is in place
on that project, which is fantastic.
So it was fantastic to see that this is anot her section of the Waikato Expressway that,
when finished, will carve something like 20 or 25 minutes off a trip from T īrau to
Auckland, which is great. I know that the Gree ns will always talk about the fact that
they do not want more roads and they do not  want roads of national significance, but
people in my electorate still drive cars on ro ads, trucks are used to get their export
15790 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 11 Feb 2014
goods to market and to the ports, and, although it  is great to see the increase in cycling,
good luck if you wanted to try to cycle from one end of my electorate to the other any
day soon.
In terms of other opport unities or other things that th is Government is focused on,
one of the other aspects of the Business Gr owth Agenda is, of course, around education
and skills. This is an area that members on the other side of the House absolutely get
wound up about because we are getting results in areas where they did not when they

Waitangi. I am enormously proud when he stan ds up and speaks to audiences and gives
the results that this Government is achieving in M āori education. We often hear that
Māori are disadvantaged, that they turn up in all the statistics we do not want them in,
but, actually, education is one of the main areas wher e we get to improve those
statistics. We are getting hi gher levels of participation in early childhood education,

numbers in trade training opportunities and apprenticeships. They are the things that
count. They are the things that count in terms of getting results, getting achievement,

One of the highlights for the start of this year was the Prime Minister’s
announcement about the opportunities for high-q uality teaching and principals, because
it is an issue, particularly in some of the rural areas. We do sometimes have difficulty
attracting teachers and principals into the sm all rural areas, and that  has been an issue
that some of the schools and the boards of tr ustees have raised w ith me over and over
again. Well, this way we get to have the teaching excellence shared amongst a group of

So I am very proud that the Prime Minister’s  statement to the Hous e this year talked

items.speaker: MEKA WHAITIRI
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker.
Tēnā koutou katoa. E ngā mema o te Whare nei, ngā mihi o te Tau Hou.
[To the members of this House, greetings of the New Year.]
I join with others on this side in wishi ng warm greetings to you and all members of
the House and of this complex for the new year of 2014, and I hope you have all had a
good rest. I join members on this side of th e House in support of David Cunliffe, the
Leader of the Opposition, and his motion that this House express no confidence in this
National-led Government because New Zeal and has become more and more divided,
because those in the middle are struggling, and because the poor are going backwards.
I stand as the proud member for Ikaroa-R āwhiti, an electorate that has raised and
nurtured many fine people, some  famous and some infamous, all of whom in their time
have etched their mark on the uni que canvas that makes up Ikaroa-R āwhiti. It is an
electorate of fertile lands, prime coastline,  and majestic rivers, where an honest day’s
work for an honest day’s pay is the norm, where having fruit trees and vege gardens and
the ability to go to the river or to the beach  to gather food is a normal way of life. For
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15791
many, the prospect of an honest job for hone st wages and for gathering food from our
beaches and our waterways is no longer the nor m. In fact, it is under serious threat. I
may be a new member to this House, but you can rest assured that I come with some 25
years of serving our people, creating empl oyment opportunities, and creating platforms
to grow capacity at the local, regional, and national levels, for supporting initiatives that
work, and for calling out those that clearly do not.
This National-led Government is failing the people of Ikaroa-R āwhiti. I have sat on
this side of the House fo r some 6 months—hopefully, not on this side for too much
longer, come the general election—and I have heard what this National-led Government
has done for the people of New Zeal and and for the people of Ikaroa-R āwhiti. Well, I
am here to put the story right. I am here to give you the real low-down on my electorate.
I am here to do what the people of Ikaroa-Rāwhiti have asked me to do, and that is to be
their voice in this House. This National-led Government is arroga nt. This National-led
Government is out of touch. This National-led Government is in it only for its mates.
One of my first questions in this H ouse was to the Minister for Economic
Development, Mr Steven Joyce. When I as ked what he was doing about the high rates
of unemployment in Gisborne and Hawke’s Bay, did I hear “more apprenticeships”?
Did I hear “a greater focus on transition from schools to jobs  to further training”? Did I
hear “enterprise development support”? And did I hear “unlocking potential
opportunities in partnership with  iwi”? No, I did not. The reason why I did not is that
those are Labour policies. What I heard from  Mr Joyce, in term s of his addressing
unemployment in Hawke’s Bay and Gisborne, was three things: cycleways, mining and
drilling, and—wait for it—a dam. That is righ t—a dam. I can report to this House, as I
stand in front of you, that there have been no jobs created in Hawke’s Bay and Gisborne
in those areas. Again, that is a legacy of this National-led Government.
But do not listen to me. Let us look at the statistics. Let us look at the unemployment
statistics. The household labour force survey statistics for December 2013 say that since
National has been in office, the number of unemployed 20 to 24-year-olds has increased
by 11,300. A total of 27,600 20 to 24-year-olds are without jobs in the Hawke’s Bay
and Gisborne region. That is not a record to be proud of. It is not a record to be laughed
at or to be jeered at or to  be flicked aside. Youth not in  employment or training or
education—since National took office, the nu mber of 15 to 24-year-old “neets” has
increased by 5,000 to a total of 72,000. That is  an indictment on this country when we
have 15 to 24-year-olds, 72,000 of them, with no hope, with no platform, and with no
opportunities to seek what they have every right to have as citizens of this country, be it
employment or education or traini ng—72,000 have been forgotten. Long-term
unemployment is 44,600—an increase of 29,800 since National came into Government
in December 2008. In my region specifically —the unemployment figures in Hawke’s
Bay and Gisborne—when Labour was last in  Government there were 6,900 people who
were unemployed. By December 2013 that number had grown to 8,100. Again, on these
statistics you cannot argue that many more  of our people in my region are not
suffering—and the jobs are simply not there.
One of the burning topics in my region has been the management of our fresh water.
It is to that area that I tu rn the House’s attention, to talk  about the Tukituki catchment
proposal, which has been undergoing a board  of inquiry for some 28 days. I was
fortunate, before I joined the House of Repr esentatives, to be the chief executive of
Ngāti Kahungunu Iwi Incorporated, which took a very strong stance on water quality
issues and water management, not only in the catchment of Ng āti Kahungunu but also
throughout the country. So before coming to this House I was well aware of what was
happening in our particular area.
15792 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 11 Feb 2014
Coming here to this place a nd hearing the National Policy Statement for Freshwater
Management from the Minister for the Envi ronment, Amy Adams, I have been really
quite interested in some of the responses to  what clearly are very complex issues: water
quality, water use, and water management across the nation. I want to acknowledge,
first and foremost, the work of all the stakeholders in the Land and Water Forum, who

items.text: Who set up the Land and Water Forum?

items.text: Yes, I know. I know who set it up, but I am also aware that
there were some very significant recommendati ons that the forum put to the Minister,
and it is very upsetting to see the Minist er cherry-pick—cherry-pick—some of those

absolutely need better processes, but , unfortunately, under this National-led
Government we have not got them.
So, in closing, I want to say, with reference to the Prime Minister’s speech, that there
was only one line that actually got me listeni ng, and that, actually, was the last line,
where he said: “We are going to say to New Z ealanders that they can trust what we say,
and they can trust us to deliver what we do.” I can assure you that when I go around all
the communities in Ikaroa-R āwhiti, “trust” is not a word they align with the National-
led Government and its coalition partners. So  I look forward to what the year presents.
Tēnā tātou katoa.

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.role: Minis ter of Pacific Island Affairs
items.text: It is a
privilege to speak on this, the Prime Minister’s statement to this House, and to speak for
the first time as the Minister of Pacific Island Affairs. I am honoured and humbled to be
entrusted with that particular title, as well as that of Associate Minister of Local
Government. I am honoured that the Prime Mini ster placed his trust and his faith in me
to deliver for those portfolios. I am honoured  to have a Prime Minister who has led a
Government that has stabilised the economy, that has grown this economy, and that has
grown jobs in this nation of Aotearoa New Zealand. It ha s also provided an
infrastructure, educational services, and health services that all New Zealanders should
be proud of.
Just on education, last Friday I attended  an opening ceremony for a unique school in
my original home community of M āngere. The Rise UP Trus t is a not-for-profit
community organisation that provides e ducational services for Pasifika and M āori
whānau. This was the first—but it will not be the last—partnership school with Pacific
leadership, with Pacific governance, with t eachers teaching Pacific values within the
New Zealand Curriculum. Those programme s were designed by teachers who have
grown up and worked in South Auckland schools for many years. This school started in
a M āngere garage, culminating last week in the opening of this second partnership
school. I consider this school to mark a small but significant milestone for this country’s
youngest and fastest-growing population in and around M āngere. It represents a
promising new approach to teaching Pasifika children, and I am proud that this National
Government has poured resources into Paci fic people, into Pacific communities, and
into the communities of South Auckland so th at they can have opportunities, they can
have hope, and, ultimately, they can have financial freedom and self-reliance. The
11 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15793
Pacific community, which makes up 64 percent of M āngere, has mobilised itself and is
taking charge of its own children’s futures. It is going to be a bright one.
In the last 5 years we have seen big results based on the commitments and the
promises that the National Pa rty electioneered on—the platfo rm that we came in on in
2008, which we are delivering on. It is about  building a faster-growing economy with
more jobs, raising incomes, and supporting New Zealanders and their families. It is also
about being fiscally prudent so that a Budget surplus is forecast for the next financial
year, 2014-15. Why would New Z ealanders risk that with a Labour-Greens coalition,
which is prepared to tax and spend at exor bitant and reckless rates? Our economy has
grown 3.5 percent, and it has been picked  up by leaders around the world as a role
model for developed nations. Our wages ha ve outpaced inflation, as Mr Simpson
knows.

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: Tell that to all the people who haven’t had a pay increase.

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: Ms Beaumont might scoff, but here are the facts.
We have had a 16.1 percent rise in wage s since 2008, and inflation has gone up only
10.8 percent.

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: Forty percent didn’t get a pay increase last year.

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: I suggest, ma’am, that you do your homework and
find out—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Was that the median wage, Sam, or is that just rich people
getting richer? Sam, is that the median wage, or is it the rich people getting richer?

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: —that wages have increased faster than inflation.
This morning—and Mr Lees-Galloway knows this—66,000 more people went to work
in New Zealand than this time last ye ar. There are 66,000 more New Zealanders
currently employed than this time last ye ar. As the last 5 years have shown, this
National-led Government has delivered stable  leadership and put New Zealanders back
on the right track.
The future success and prosperity of Pacific people will influence the outcomes for
New Zealand as a whole. We know that they currently represent 8 percent of the
population. It is estimated that by 2026 they will represent 10 percent of the population.
They predict that by 2050 M āori and Pacific people and other ethnic groups will form
approximately 50 percent of the population. So we need to ha ve our next generation of
Pacific people in prominent positions, not just  as doctors, lawyers, teachers, scientists,
and accountants but also in trades. The most  important thing, which this Government
has stated, is that they are employed and that they have better skills to meet the demands
for the 21st century—a century in which we are comp eting with nations in not just Asia
and Europe but also the Americas. Our Gove rnment is working hard to prepare young
people for the future, giving them the educational foundation to succeed in life.
Last year I attended the Prime Minister’s  Pacific Youth Awards scholarships right
here in Parliament. I was proud to see seve n young people given awards for leadership,
creativity, technological flair, and educationa l promise. Each of them was a tertiary
student, and I would offer the view that each will go on to great success. A common
theme was the tribute that each of these students paid to their families and the support
given to them by their whānau and families in their educational endeavours. It is not just
about education, programmes, buildings, sports fields, and the like; it really is about the
support that whānau can give. It is about the support that their families can give outside
of school. It is about the s upport and encouragement and love  that they can give to
whānau in order that they can succeed, not just at school but in the workplace and in our
communities. Without exception, they credited education as fundamental to that
success. That is why our Government is focused very much on standards in education. It
15794 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 11 Feb 2014
is focused very much on achievement levels . It is focused very much on our kids
gaining the skills that they need to succeed in the future.
In 2012 Minister Parata released the Pasi fika Education Plan 2013-2017. It is an
overarching plan to increase Pasifika achieve ment and participation in education, from
early childhood education right up to tertiary-level educati on. One of the goals is to
raise National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) level 2 pass rates in
ways that are connected with entering empl oyment or further training. Already I can
report to this House and to our country that  Pacific achievement in NCEA level 2 has
improved from 56.5 percent in 2009 to 64.8 percent in 2012.
Last Friday I attended a breakfast for P acific students at Rosmini College on the
North Shore. These Pacific students achieved a 100 percent pass rate at NCEA levels 1
and 3 and a 91 percent pass rate at level 2. So  we have got some stars out there. We
have got young kids who are really performing and achieving. Although we accept that
these achievement levels are going up, there is still more to be done out there.
We have introduced programmes like Pasifi ka Power UP, with Minister Parata
leading the charge to help Pacific student s prepare and study for exams. It takes a
whole-of-family approach. Pasifika Power UP is a 12-month engagement programme
with an intensive 8-week challenge deliver ed through eight Pacifi c community - based
study hubs, predominantly in South Auck land. The young people receive support and
advice around their studies. Parents are info rmed about the struct ure of NCEA and its
significance. The hubs provide advice aroun d family support for their children’s
success. These Pasifika Power UP programmes help give effect to the energy and the
desire in Pacific communities for young peopl e to do better in NCEA levels 1, 2, and 3.
We had over 1,600 Pasifika students, parent s, and families attend these programmes
right across the country—as I said, predomin antly in South Auckland. That is a great
sign that Pacific people are passionate about education and eager to be part of the
skilled workforce.
Just on employment, I have said that there are currently just under 2.3 million people
employed across our country. Forecasts show that these trends will continue this year as
the Government’s Business Growth Agenda leads to expanded export markets, more
innovation, better infrastructure , greater skills developmen t, and improved resources.
Our Pacific community is sharing in the em ployment gains. The unemployment rate for
Pasifika is down 2.3 percent from a year  ago. Since 2011 Pacific Employment Support
Services has assisted providers to help raise NCEA level 2 su ccess in 25 schools
throughout Auckland.
I just want to sum up by saying that we  are approaching a general election where
New Zealanders will have a clear choice.

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: That’s true. That’s very true.

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: Through difficult times, this Government—and Ms
Beaumont knows this—has put New Zeala nd on a strong financial footing. The
economy is growing, we are crea ting jobs, and we are havi ng higher incomes. That is
for all New Zealanders. This Government will  continue to deliver  those results going
forward.
