items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: It gives me great pleasure to speak in
support of the Subantarctic Is lands Marine Reserves Bill at  its third reading. We have
supported this bill all the way through. I gue ss part of the reason it gives me great
pleasure to do so is that this bill—and bette r protection of our marine areas—is a real
reflection of some of the str ongest values that New Zeala nders have. These values are
pride in our environment, a passion fo r the great outdoors, and recognising the
responsibility that the current generation has to ensure th at protections are enhanced so
that future generations can benefit from the be autiful surrounds that we have. This bill
really is a bit of a step towards a recognition of that passion, and I want to acknowledge
and thank the Minister of Conservation, the H on Dr Nick Smith, for his work in this. I
believe that he is a person who has a personal commitment and passion for the
conservation portfolio and also for the great outdoors more generally. I am sure that it
has given him great pleasure to be able to progress this bill to this stage.
What this bill does is better protect three of the Subantarctic Islands marine areas
around the Antipodes Islands, the Bounty Islands , and Campbell Islan d. I have had the
pleasure of visiting Campbell Island and I can say that it—and the whole of the
Subantarctic Islands area—is a part of th e world that more members of Parliament
should visit. Some perhaps need not hasten on their return from such  a visit, but it is
certainly very worthwhile to  see such an amazing area. We should consider ourselves
very fortunate that we live in New Zealand and are able to access such beauty.
The bill also provides for an independent review of the Campbell Island Marine
Reserve in 5 years, because there is part of the surrounding area of Campbell Island that
is not included in the marine  reserve area. The review woul d look at whether or not the
reserve should be extended to include that part in the marine reserve.
The third part of the bill is making the commanding officers of the New Zealand
Defence Force rangers so that they are ab le to enforce the protections that this
legislation gives to those three islands. I think that it is a very good piece of legislation
and I am very pleased to be part of the La bour team, which totally supports this. As I
15814 Subantarctic Islands Mari ne Reserves Bill 11 Feb 2014
said, one of the reasons it is so important is that it is a reflection of the values that so
many New Zealanders have: our passion for th e great outdoors, our love for the natural
environment, and our understa nding of the responsibility that we have for future
generations. The record of th e National Government has not  been great in all those
areas, though. There have been what I would regard as broken promises, and I think that
is deeply disappointing in an area that is so important to the average New Zealander.
One of the two areas that I just want to to uch on in comparison with what I think is a
great bill that gives us this enhanced marine  protection is the total lack of a sense of
urgency, of a sense of res ponsibility, and of any strong  action to protect the M āui’s
dolphins. In the world there are 55 adult M āui’s dolphins left. That  is fewer than the
members of this Parliament. But yet when the opportunity arose for the Minister of
Conservation and the Minister for Primar y Industries to say that we have the
responsibility to ensure the future survival of this species, the Mi nisters said: “No, that
is a little bit hard for us. It is a big call. We are not going to do it. We are going to back
away and take the easy option.”  They tinkered with the pr otections and it was a total
lose-lose. The biggest loss, of course, is the future of the M āui’s dolphins. It will be an
unforgivable act if those Mi nisters end up being responsib le for the demise of the
species. It will be an unforgivable act when they have had such an opportunity to adopt
the precautionary principle, which would be to  take all possible ac tion to protect those
dolphins. They are critically  endangered. I do not know what part of “critically
endangered” Ministers Nick Smith and Nath an Guy do not understand,  but they clearly
do not.
It is also an opportunity for a win-wi n in regard to the fishing industry.
Internationally now scientists and lovers of the marine environment are calling for a
boycott on New Zealand fish because it is the bycatch of our fishing industry that is
endangering the Māui’s dolphins. So our fishing industry is also under threat, as well as
the Māui’s dolphins. How can that be of bene fit to anyone? The Ministers had a chance
to say that they want to move our fishi ng industry forward in a sustainable manner by
putting some money in to back that transiti on. It does not need to be much. The people
in the fishing industry are up to it. They are bright peop le. They can see the benefits for
them and for the country. They know the benefits for M āui’s dolphins. They do not
want the bycatch. They do not want to be ta rred with the brush of the extinction of a
species. So we could have had, with a bit of  vision from the Ministers, the sort of
reflection, again, of the values of New Zeal anders that would make us all proud.
Instead, we got a wishy-washy, half-h earted approach. Nobody was happy. We now
have a critically endangered species when the potential for saving it was much higher.
The other area in which I want to express extreme disappointment is the involvement
of the Minister of Conservation in the process and the submissions from the Department
of Conservation in the proposal on the Tukituki River—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is not part of this bill.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: The Minister of Conservation, unl ike his actions in regard to
this legislation establishing three marine reserves, did exactly the opposite in the case of
the Ruataniwha Dam, where he meddled to the point of the department being silenced.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! We are on the third reading,
and the third reading relates to the contents of the bill as reported back from the Local
Government and Environment Committee. If  you look at Speakers’ rulings 122/4-7 and
123/1, it is very clear that third readings relate to the report back from the committee.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: I am absolutely confident that the Minister of Conservation
exercised the correct approach in regard to the Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserve, and
did not exercise the correct approach in re gard to either the Ruataniwha Dam or the
Māui’s dolphins. It actually s hows a bit of arrogance from  the Minister that such
11 Feb 2014 Subantarctic Islands  Marine Reserves Bill 15815
important issues with such strong community and, in fact, international concern could
be so disregarded. That is not the sort of leadership that I want to see from our Minister
of Conservation.
Just going back, in my fina l comments, to the Subantarct ic Islands Marine Reserves
Bill, as I said at the beginning of my contribution, this has been legislation that Labour
has supported since it was introduced. We suppor ted it at the select committee and I am
certainly very pleased to support it in the thir d reading. It is the sort  of opportunity that
this Parliament does not have very often. Well, I cannot speak for the Hon John Banks.
Heaven only knows what he might do in regard to his party vote on this bill. But I am
pretty sure that all other parties are going to say: “This is a responsibility that we have.
This is an opportunity that we have as legi slators, and we are very pleased that the
Minister of Conservation has taken this opportunity and enhanced our marine reserves.”
I have seen a poll that the Government is  undertaking at the moment to see whether
New Zealanders support the establishment of a further marine reserve in the Kermadec
Islands. I guess the Government is waiting for the poll results to come back to see which
way the wind blows. It is not an approach th at I would consider principled or visionary;
it is a poll driven by fruitcakes, actually. That is what a former Prime Minister said. It is
definitely not evidence-based or driven by any ambition for New Zealand. I hope that a
Kermadec Islands reserves bill is introduced. I actually hope that it is introduced by
Gareth Hughes, because he has got a member’s  bill in his name. He is well ahead of the
Government in that regard. I know that if the polling come s out right, Steven Joyce will
say: “That looks like a winner for us. Let’s get on to it. It won’t cause any controversy.”
That is not the sort of appro ach that I like to see running  our country. But leaving that
concern aside, if that bill came to Parlia ment, I would certainly support it in the same
way that I support the Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill.

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I too want to support this
Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill at its third reading. The Subantarctic Islands
are a unique and spectacular natural environm ent. The land in that area is already
protected under the national nature reserves status, but this legislation will protect the
ocean around that land. The whole area is so  spectacular that it  has World Heritage
status. This legislation will make sure that these three island groups—the Antipodes
Islands, the Bounty Islands, and Campbell Isla nd—are able to join  with the Auckland
Islands in having marine reserve protecti on. The Auckland Islands were protected in
These new reserves cover an enormous area  of about 435,000 hectar es. It is a great
step forward in protecting our oceans. It is absolutely in lin e with National’s long-
established interest in mari ne protection. It was the Natio nal Government back in 1971
that passed the first Marine Reserves Act. That led to establishing the first marine
reserve at Leigh, just north of Auckland, in  1975. In those days that was absolutely
groundbreaking legislation and new to the worl d. That reserve in Leigh has gone on to
entertain, to educate, and to inspire New Zealanders and people w ho visit our country,
from that day to this.
Currently, New Zealand has 48 marine protected areas. That covers about 8.2 percent
of our territorial seas. These new reserves ar e so big that when they are gazetted that
will increase to 9.5 percent of our territorial seas. Under our present legislation we can
create marine reserves only in  our territorial seas. There are more reserves to come.
Since National has been in Government we  have announced nine new marine reserves,
and there are further areas that are beginning stakeholder talks.
Creating marine reserves can be quite difficult for communities. New Zealanders are
absolutely passionate about the sea. They love  to recreate there, to swim, and to fish.
But sometimes there is a bit of a differen ce of opinion as to where marine protected
15816 Subantarctic Islands Mari ne Reserves Bill 11 Feb 2014
reserves could be. Of course we all want to protect the ocean, but maybe the community
does not want it happening qui te in their own backyard. We  have come up with a new
collaborative stakeholder process that seems to make decisions about marine reserves
much more palatable and easily done. That  was based on the first collaborative
approach taken by the Guardians of Fiordland’s Fisheries and Marine Environment. It is
similar to the collaborative approach that we are seeing nationally in terms of things like
the Land and Water Forum, and we are also s eeing it locally in terms of things like Te
Korowai o Te Tai o Marokura in Kaik ōura, which is another marine protection
mechanism.
Basically, the strengths of these models is  that they allow everybody to have a say
and allow them to work together to create a compromise that works for all stakeholders.
Indeed, this bill was written as a result of a collaborative stakeholder forum with input
from iwi, industry representa tives, scientific and conservation groups, and the general
public. This bill was based directly on thei r decisions. There is even a compromise
written into the bill, as there had been iden tified the possibility of a commercial deep-
water crab-fishing industry around Campbell Island. This bill gives a window of time to
explore that option. If the evidence shows that a viable, sustainable fishery with
minimal impact on the marine environmen t and ecosystems is possible, then the
boundaries will remain as stated in this bill. But if not, the reserve will be expanded to
take in the whole of the territorial s ea around Campbell Island. The Local Government
and Environment Committee has ensured that th is will happen in a timely fashion and
that the review must be completed within 5 years of the bill being passed.
Finally, I would like to say that the whole of the Local Government and Environment
Committee supported this bill. We enjoyed wo rking on it. It was extremely interesting.
We believe that we have pa ssed good legislation. We believe that it was based on a fair
and effective process and that it will have a valuable outcome for our oceans. My only
regret is that we as a committee did not manage to have a site visit.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: It gives me great pleasure to also
support this bill, the Subantarctic Islands Ma rine Reserves Bill, and to commend to the
House the work of both the Minister of Conservation and the Local Government and
Environment Committee in getting this bill through. It was actually  started back in
Labour’s time, and it has been good to see th at this has been continued and processed
through so that we do actually have a piece of legislation, as many of the speakers have
said up to now, that we can be rightfully proud of.
New Zealanders do care about th eir environment. They do very much feel a distinct
link to our environment. It is something that you feel a certain longing for when you are
on the other side of the world and you se e a New Zealand environment or a New
Zealand landscape. I recall just a few years ago an advertising agency that was looking
into what stimulates New Zealanders, what sells goods, found that the environment was
one of the most important thi ngs that it could us e to help sell pr oducts. When it asked
New Zealanders what they thought about the environment or how to describe it, they
talked about recreation in and around it, caring for it, being part of it, and looking after
it—those were the main values. It did the sa me thing in Australia and the response was
totally different. The response in Australia was that it was a harsh environment, you
needed to tame it, you needed to control it, you dug it up, and, basically, you dominated
it. New Zealanders had a very  different approach and an approach that I think comes
through in this piece of legislation, the Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill.
We have wanted—and I think there is a real appetite in New Zealand—to protect our
broad areas, our natural areas,  and this goes to the hearts of many New Zealanders. It
will mean now that in addition to the Au ckland Islands, the Antipodes Islands group,
the Bounty Islands, and Campbell Island wi ll be protected. We have already had
11 Feb 2014 Subantarctic Islands  Marine Reserves Bill 15817
protection on the terrestrial part of the island s, but this now extends to the marine areas
around those islands and expands, as was just said, the area  up to about 450,000
hectares. A novel part of this is that the rangers who are going to be looking after this
are actually going to be from the Defence Force. Because they frequent these areas
more frequently than others, they will be able to do that.
The process by which this has gone through has been a very collaborative one, and
that is very good. There has been wide-rangi ng exploration of various people’s feelings
about it. There were no real issues around mining. There wa s little interest in petroleum
that might be there. And Ng āi Tahu, the iwi of the South Island, was very comfortable
with the progression of  this bill, as well. So in many ways it ticks a lot of boxes. In
return for that, in terms of economic benefit, there is actually a significant tourism
benefit to New Zealand from the tourist boats that do go down there. It is a niche type of
industry but nevertheless one th at looks at natural environments and sees them in their
most natural and most pristine state. But it also, of course, e nhances New Zealand’s
overall reputation, a reputati on of looking after our environment, even though in some
cases this is not exactly what I would call warranted.
I want to just pick up on two points in this regard. One is the absolute shambles
around trying to bring New Zealand into the Convention on the Conservation of
Antarctic Marine Living Re sources. We were offered a partnership with the United
States, which we refused and then belatedly took up. The shambles that resulted meant
that that convention flopped when it could have actually co me to pass and we could
have had greater protection over the Ross Sea.
In addition to that I also want to pick up what my colleague Ruth Dyson was talking
about in terms of M āui’s and Hector’s dolphin s, but particularly M āui’s dolphins. I
mentioned in the second reading of this bill that I was out surfing one day when a
couple of surfers around me called out “Sha rk! Shark!”, disappeared off a wave, and
paddled frantically to shore. I was a bit sl ower to get off the mark, but what I did
manage to see were two M āui’s dolphins—only very, very small but with a beautiful,
rounded fin—swimming around my board and disa ppearing out to sea. There are only
55 of these left in existence, and I saw tw o in one go while sitti ng on the back of a
board. I have to say, I came in feeling absolu tely enthralled that I had actually seen
these two wonderful animals while out on a surfboard all alone.
We have got an absolute responsibility to protect those dolphins. They are the most
endangered in the world. There are only 55 of  them. They live only to the age of 23.
The females do not breed until the age of 9 and then they have a calf only between
every 2 and 4 years. Therefore, they are incr edibly endangered in te rms of their ability
to fight back, and we have to make absolu tely sure that we do. Unfortunately, I do not
believe that Nick Smith—perhaps his Cabi net colleagues rolled him on this one—has
done enough in order to actually protect them.
The other issue that I wanted to just point  out as we are pushing through this special
piece of legislation—this good pi ece of legislation, which we do have quite widespread
agreement on—is that the 1971 Marine Reserv es Act, which my colleague across the
House, Nicky Wagner, was just talking about, was brought in in 1971. It was world
leading in its time, but that was a long time ago. We now need to  look at updating that
legislation so that we do not have to go th rough the same procedure every time we want
to make a particular area like the Subantarctic  Islands a marine reserve. We want to be
able to have an efficient piece of legislation that looks at, and facilitates the creation of,
marine reserves within our territorial waters and beyond into our economic zone in
addition to that.
I would like to see many more marine rese rves enacted and brought into place. They
do have a real role in the ability to rege nerate fisheries. A nybody who has gone up to
15818 Subantarctic Islands Mari ne Reserves Bill 11 Feb 2014
Goat Island or any of the other marine reserves or the Poor Knights Islands and who has
seen the proliferation of fish and marine life in those areas knows that these areas are
valuable not only in terms of the informa tion, the education, and the wonder they can
provide us with when we are in those area s but also in terms of helping those areas
regenerate and the fish stocks regenerate as well.
I am not going to continue any further on this. I just wanted to say once again that the
Labour Party has been behind this bill and supported th e Government on it. It was
something that we felt str ongly about during our time in office. This Government is
taking it on further. The work of the Lo cal Government and Environment Committee
has been very good. I commend once again th e Minister of Conservation for pushing
this through. I think it is a ve ry good point for this Parliament to be agreeing to the
protection of a particularly important part of our ecosystem around New Zealand
through the Subantarctic Marine Reserves Bill. So with that  I commend this bill to the
House.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker. Ng ā mihi nui ki a
koutou. Kia ora. It is a great pleasure to rise in support of  the Subantarctic Islands
Marine Reserves Bill tonight. Like the last  speaker, David Shearer , I think probably
every member in this House and, I believe , everyone in our country has a similar
example where they had a spiritual, a visc eral, a human connection with the oceans or
the incredible animals that live within them. It  is something that is , I believe, unique to
our country. We are a maritime nation. We ha ve got waters 15 times larger than our
land masses.
I grew up in Gisborne. Every summer we used to go camping at Pouawa Beach. My
dad had a lifestyle block up at Whangar ā. No doubt Hekia Parata knows that location
well. For 18 years we used to camp at the same campsite. I learnt to swim there. I used
to go out on the dinghy with my dad and put  the crayfish pots out. Reflecting on the
debate tonight reminded me of when I learnt to scuba-dive just before the last election
in 2011. That was at the Taputeranga Marine Reserve, a new marine reserve we have
created in Wellington—an absolutely spec tacular place. I th ink that when New
Zealanders get to experience these beau tiful marine reserves we have around the
country, they are committed and they want to see more of them.
That is the science that informs the debate —that we need more marine reserves. Our
oceans are under threat, despite having these amazing dolphin sightings, shark
sightings, and experiences with our oceans. We  love them but we also know that they
are threatened. We see it when we go down to the beach and we see the waste washing
up. We see it when those dying, starving turt les wash up in Northland. We see it when
the finned sharks wash ashore. We all know  that our oceans are sick and they are
unhealthy, and we need to do something about it. This is why it is  good to see this
Parliament coming together to do something ab out it. But this bill is not enough. It is
not going to save our oceans. It is not even  going to protect the full waters around these
World Heritage listed islands. It is going to be protecting only 39 percent of Campbell
Island’s waters and 58 percent of the Bount y Islands’ waters. But it is good to be doing
something about marine reserves. They are so mething we all love and we all want to
protect.
We see when we watch the news and read the science reports that there is rising
acidification, the great garbage Gaia—the grea t giant Pacific garbage patch, as it is also
known—and overfishing in the oceans. We ar e literally replacing keystone species in
the marine ecosystem with jellyfish. I am your stereotypical green ie vegetarian who
does not eat fish, but you know what? I think many people in New Zealand—and,
perhaps more relevantly, around the world—wil l have to get used to having jellyfish
and chips instead of their fish and chips. The jellies are literally taking over our oceans
11 Feb 2014 Subantarctic Islands  Marine Reserves Bill 15819
because of overfishing. The question is not wh ere the fish went, because the answer is
clear: we have literally eaten all the fis h. Using our industrial fishing fleets and the
might of our industrial civilisa tion, we have gone out to ha rvest the world’s fisheries,
and we are seeing them collapse. Our large shark species have seen a population decline
of 90 percent since 1950 because we are using the advanced technological fishing
techniques we now have to hunt, target, and—unfortunately, for 73 million of them
every year—fin them and dump them overboard.
We all know the risks, the threats, and the dangers facing our oceans, and we all
know the answer. Marine reserves are a simple, effective, and cheap way we can protect
our oceans. That is why it is good to be going some way towards that tonight. It is clear
we need more marine reserves in New Z ealand. Sure, you know, th ese reserves cover
435,000 hectares. It sounds like a large num ber when you have the National members
trumpeting about it, but these marine reserv es take the percentage of New Zealand
waters in marine reserves only from 0.31 to  0.41 percent. That is still less than 0.5
percent.
Here we see the Minister of Conser vation trumpeting these announcements and
saying that he wants to gazette a record  number of marine reserves. Nick Smith
thunders about eight new marine reserves in his kayak as he does his media stunts. He
says we are going to set a record. Never mind that the eight marine reserves he is talking
about were started under the last Government . Never mind that all his marine reserves
are still taking us to less than 0.5 percent of our waters protected. Never mind that a
single year’s oil block offer is greater than al l of these marine reserves we are creating
tonight. Let us put it in contrast. We need more progress. Kiwis know it, they support it,
and that is what they told Colmar Brunt on—96 percent of New Zealanders want to see
more marine reserves. That is why in a recent Andrea Vance column recent polling
showed that, in fact, most New Zealanders thought we already had 30 percent coverage.
No, we will have only 0.41 percent, if this bill passes.
I have talked before about the irony of needing a law from Parliament to create
marine reserves. It shows how out of date and out of touch our legislation from 1971
has become. What we need to do is modern ise that law. Under National it languished
for the second-longest period of any legislation in our c ountry’s history. Remember, we
are the fourth-oldest democracy in the world, and the second-oldest bill ever to languish
and die in a select committ ee happened over marine rese rves, and we still cannot
produce them in the exclusive economic zone.
Remember, we saw this Government dec line the Akaroa marine reserve. The
Government members are trumpeting as if  they are environmental champions or
something, yet let us not forget that they declined the Akaroa marine reserve. It was not
until they were taken to court and had a judi cial review go in the Akaroa community’s
favour that they did something a bout it. Let us not forget that  this is a Government that
is quite happy to have oil wells in the middle of those M āui’s dolphins sanctuaries. It is
not providing a sanctuary.
The Government is quite happy for the iron sands and Chatham Rock phosphate
miners to literally vacuum up the seabed be tween 5 and 20 metres. On the West Coast,
for example, 50 million tonnes of sediment is going to get vacuumed up, but the
Government is quite happy for that to happen in benthic protected areas. These are areas
where fishers cannot go, 100 metres above the seabed. This Government is quite happy
to have industrial fleets literally vac uuming up the seabed and is not providing
protection in these benthic protected areas.
This is my last call in this debate, and I want to reiterate the support for this
legislation. It is good to be doing something about it. The Greens would go further. We
would protect 100 percent of these World He ritage listed islands and the waters
15820 Subantarctic Islands Mari ne Reserves Bill 11 Feb 2014
surrounding them. But I want to touch on the po litics, because, after all, this is a house
of politics. This is a year of politics, being an election year. I want to question what the
rationale is. What are National’s focus groups showing? Why do National suddenly feel
compelled, after 5 years of doi ng nothing—in fact, taking a t oxic “wreck it, destroy it”
approach to the environm ent—to be rushing through legislation lik e this? Why,
finally—5 years in and after allowing innumer able sharks to be finned and thrown
overboard, dead—does National have to do something about it?
What we know—and I think what the data the National Party strategists are looking
at shows—is that this is an issue National is incredibly weak on. It is an issue where
some of its voters are potentially leaving it . We know that female voters in particular
have historically had a problem with the National Party. The National Party has got a
problem. The problem is that it does not care about the environment. It is not protecting
the environment. It is actively destroying it. It is not a problem that is going to be
remediated through spin or through public relations. It is a problem that can be
addressed only by taking action, by actually pr oducing more marine reserves. We have
talked about expanding the Kermadec Islands  Marine Reserve, which I am advocating
for and trying to build parliamentary suppor t for. That would see 15 percent of our
waters protected overnight. We need to upgrade our laws. We need an integrated oceans
policy. We need to stop the deep-sea drilling that is risking our marine environment. We
need to stop the seabed mining. We need to protect our Māui’s dolphins.
These are the solutions Kiwis support. These are the solutions the prosperity of our
country is going to be built on. We know that the $1.5 billion aquaculture and fisheries
sector depends on our brand. International consumers do not want to be buying crabs
from a World Heritage area that is not protected. They do not want to buy our fish when
they know that our M āui’s dolphins and Hector’s dolphins  or those sea lions we heard
about last year are becoming extinct,. If Na tional has identified it has a problem when it
comes to New Zealanders’ perceptions of its environmentalism, the answer is not more
spin. The answer is not more gloss or more media stunts fo r Nick Smith. The answer is
to do something about it. But I guess I am not holding out in hope or holding my breath,
because what we have seen under the 5 years of this Government is a callous disregard
for the environment and the prosperity that the New Zealand economy relies on that is
based on that environment.
So it is quite good that New Zealanders will get a choice this election. They will get
to choose between protecting the M āui’s dolphins or slaughtering them indiscriminately
in those unsustainable fishing nets. They will get a choice between more marine
reserves—protecting the Kermadec Islands  and other marine reserves around New
Zealand—or the spin. They will get a choice between clean energy or deep-sea drilling.
That is the challenge we are giving to the Na tional Party, and that is the challenge and
the option we are giving New Zealand voters at this election. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: As I said before, National has got
a proud history of marine protection. We did pass the original Mari ne Reserves Act in
1971 and at that time, leading up to that, the Labour Party had talked about it for many,
many years, as is its habit. The Green me mber who has taken his seat, Gareth Hughes,
discussed the fact that the Labour Party had proposals for eight marine reserves on the
books for the 9 years while it was in Govern ment, and that is quite true. The Labour
Party did do that, and talked about them fo r a year, then it talked about them for a
second year, then it consulted on them for a th ird and fourth year, and then talked about
them again for a fifth year. Labour wrung its hands, for a sixth year, and then talked
around and around in circles again for anothe r 2 years, making it 9 years of talking
about marine reserves and how wonderful th ey are, but not actua lly establishing this
marine reserve or others that National has put in since being in Government.
11 Feb 2014 Subantarctic Islands  Marine Reserves Bill 15821
It is great to hear that Gareth Hughes,  before the 2011 election, took the opportunity
to do some diving in a marine reserve—ag ain, one that the National Government had
decided to put in place. A lthough the Labour Party and the Green Party talk big about
marine protection, they are so busy consulting, so busy arguing, so busy going around in
circles that they do not actual ly do anything. I think this coun try’s fear is that although
the Labour Party and the Green Party are very good at talking, consulting, holding
hands, and hugging, actual action and decision making are not their strong suit. As we
have come out of the recession and we are starting this rebuild of the economy, which is
a delicate thing, and of our environment, I do not think that we really need a bunch of
hand-wringers in charge. Anyway, this is another solid run on the board for the National
Government.
Here we are looking at this particular ma rine protected area, in the Subantarctic
Islands Marine Reserves Bill. I recall myself as Minister of Fisheries and Kate
Wilkinson as conservation Minister at the time pushing through the consultation on this
marine reserve. We eventually landed on a decision that we made about 18 months or 2
years ago. Further submissions to the Lo cal Government and Environment Committee
have resulted in this particular proposal and we are very proud of it. Although the three
island groups have a protecte d area status, the territorial  waters around them are not
currently protected but they w ill be under this bill. It rec ognises great opportunities for
tourism, research, and fishing. There is very little current extractive use in the islands
surrounding our waters. Some of that will co ntinue with the deep-w ater crab fisheries
around Campbell Island.
I must reiterate too how important it is that the fishing indus try and recreational
fishers are able to fish su stainably outside these marine  reserves. Although the Green
member Gareth Hughes talks about marine reserves actually improving the fisheries
environment outside the reserve, that is not generally the case, because most fish species
are territorial. Although you ge t wonderful growth and development of fish species
within a marine reserve, outside a marine reserve it does not tend to flow over. We have
to manage those fisheries well as well, within the quota management system.
I gladly commend this legislation to the H ouse. It is another substantial run on the
board, one that is measurable and that Na tional has done. It is  something Labour did
talk about for 9 years. Again, we have ac tually achieved it. I am very proud of the
result.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I take a call on behalf of New Zealand First,
and in my address I hope to take  the politics out of it and get back to the basis of this
debate, which is all about the environment and about these very special islands in the
subantarctic.
This bill, the Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill, represents a 400,000 hectare
area that will be protected unde r law as a result of this  bill going through the House
tonight and when it is signed off by the Governor-General. These three sets of islands—
the Antipodes Islands, the Bounty Islands , and Campbell Island—off the south-east
coast of the New Zealand mainland are a ve ry special part of New Zealand. The
Antipodes Islands, some 860 kilometres south-east of Stewart Island, were first
discovered in 1800 by Captain Henry Waterhouse on the HMS Reliance. So we are
talking about one of the very early discoveries several hundred years ago in terms of the
island mass of New Zealand.
It is also now one of three World Herita ge status areas in New Zealand. We have
Fiordland as one of our Worl d Heritage status areas, we have Tongariro National Park
up in the North Island, and then  this third one, the Subant arctic Islands, which in 1998
were accorded World Heritage status. So it is  a very important third part of our World
Heritage collection. In having World Heritage status we are effectively the guardians on
15822 Subantarctic Islands Mari ne Reserves Bill 11 Feb 2014
behalf of the citizens of the world for this  particular location. Therefore, it is very
special and it is incumbent on us as New Zealanders to ensure that this area is protected.
The sea around the Bounty Islands is the deep est in New Zealand’s territorial waters.
It is some 3,000 metres deep. So it is an extraordinary piece of ocean in New Zealand’s
territorial waters. Eighty percent of e ndemic protected species in New Zealand—
meaning that they exist only in New Zeal and—are found out in the oceans around New
Zealand. Over a dozen species in these Subant arctic Islands are endangered, such as the
southern royal albatross.
We are very fortunate that New Zealand now  has 34 marine reserves and that this
will become the latest marine reserve. It is very special when you do visit some of them,
such as the original one at  Goat Island up near Leigh, wh ich now has wonderful fish
life. It is wonderful for schools and universit ies and the public to go and to visit to see
what has happened as a result of that marine reserve, and to go to the likes of the
Akaroa marine reserve that has now been pr ovided, and other marine reserves around
the coast, where fish species, fish life, and marine life have been preserved as a result of
making areas protected.
The Local Government and Environment Committee considered a great deal of
evidence on this bill. It was one of the more  pleasing bills, in that the whole committee
was in agreement with what was required to put this through in to legislation. The
committee agreed on a shorter review time in  terms of what was originally in the
legislation. Again, we felt that it was appropr iate that the review period be reduced
because of the special nature of these is lands. It was a very good, cordial agreement by
the Local Government and Environment Co mmittee to achieve a good outcome for this
bill.
It is pleasing to see that this week the HMNZS Wellington set sail from Devonport
naval base yesterday, heading to the Subantarctic Islands. It will be picking up the
Minister of Conservation, Nick Smith, some where on the way as it travels south. The
Minister will be on there. So by the time th is bill is enacted and perhaps signed off by
the Governor-General in the next couple of days and is in force, the Minister will
actually be arriving in these islands to ma ke the appropriate a nnouncement. I am sure
the National Party will make sure that that is heard loud and clear in all available media.
More especially, on board the HMNZS Wellington there are 12 Sir Peter Blake Trust
young leaders. They left from Auckland. They have been selected as some of the top
young leaders that this country has. They are going down there to the Subantarctic
Islands. In the spirit of Sir Peter Blake and all the great work that he has done out on the
oceans around the world and in the ma rine environment, those 12 young New
Zealanders are going for a 13-day expedition to  look at the Subantarctic Islands with
representatives from the Department of C onservation, from the National Institute of
Water and Atmospheric Research, from Otago University, and from a number of other
organisations and hosted, of course, by the Royal New Zealand Navy.
The group, while they are ther e looking at the islands, wi ll be drafting a feasibility
plan for a world-leading subantarctic resear ch station, which is hoped to be completed
by 2015. The station will allow New Zealand scientists and worldwide agencies to study
the effects of ocean and climate change  and also the effects on many of those
endangered species, wildlife, marine life, and the southern oceans around the islands.
This has, again, huge potential for the outreach of New Zealand into a special part of the
oceans that surround New Zealand. We certa inly commend those young people for the
good work they will be doing over the next 13 days on board that naval ship—with the
naval officers and the many other Government  support people and scientists who are in
support of them—to come up with some good r ecommendations as to how that station
will be established.
11 Feb 2014 Subantarctic Islands  Marine Reserves Bill 15823
In closing, it is not often that we have una nimous support in this House, but this is
one of those occasions. This is a special occasion because this will be our most far-
reaching outpost in terms of a marine reserv e for New Zealand as a nation. It is very
special and it shows that New Zealanders, as a whole, place a high priority on the
environment and conservation and on ensuring that we do our very best for the natural
environment. So New Zealand First is very happy to support and commend this bill.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: It is amazing how jealous we all are of the
Hon Nick Smith’s trip down to the Subantar ctic Islands. It speaks volumes, I think, for
New Zealand’s regard for those islands, and so I proudly stand to support the
Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill at its third reading.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: The previous speaker, Jacqui Dean, is earning her
salary tonight! I am very happy to stand and take a call—

items.speaker: Hon Judith Collins
items.text: Well, you know, at least she does earn her salary, not like that
member.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Oh, calm down! Calm down! It was just a joke, Mrs Collins.
Have a sense of humour. Anyway, I am ve ry happy to stand and take a call on the
Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill. It is a very interesting bill and it was a very
enjoyable experience having th is bill at the Local G overnment and Environment
Committee. I wish we had more pieces of environmental legislation coming to the Local
Government and Environment Committee that  we could all agree on and that are
actually doing good things fo r the environment, as opp osed to undermining and
destroying the environment, which is usually the tenor of environm ental legislation we
deal with at that select committee. But, in  this instance, it wa s a very good piece of
legislation.
I think it is important to note that nearly  all the submitters who came along did say
that they did not think it went far enough. They  were very supportive of the protections
that were being put in place, but they did fe el that the areas being protected were not
sufficient. We responded by amending the review period in this legislation from 5 years
down to 2 years in order to reflect the fact th at they did not feel that we needed to wait
that long period of time in order to make those decisions and determinations.

items.speaker: This bill will create three marine reserv es
items.text: the Antipodes Island Marine Reserve, or
Moutere Mahue; the Bounty Islands Marine Reserve, or Moutere Hauriri; and the
Campbell Island Marine Reserve, or Mout ere Ihupuku. These are in credibly important
parts of our subantarctic ocean. They have been recognised as World Heritage sites, and
in that respect we welcome this piece of legislation.
Marine reserves have had a bit of a bumpy ri de in New Zealand in general. I think it
is fair to say that in terms of marine polic y right across the board we are kind of playing
catch-up. We do not really know a lot of what is out there in our marine environment,
particularly around the various ecosystems, around the make-up of the sea floor. In fact,
the Australians have a lot more information than us because when they did a lot of their
oil and gas development in the 1970s they re quired the companies to do that work and
to provide that spatial information about the marine environment to the Government.
They have been able to base a lot of th eir policies and decisions on information that
they required as a bottom line and as a condi tion of that activity going ahead. We have
not had the benefit of that, so what has happened is that right throughout the decades we
have sometimes had a rather piecemeal approach to how we deal with marine policy. As
previous speakers have said, it would be very, very desirabl e to see a far more coherent
approach to marine policy in New Zealand a nd to have a strategy for how we want to
use, to enjoy, and to extract resources from  our marine environment, but to have a
strategy instead of siloed debates around each of those issues without connecting them
up. That, unfortunately, is what has been missing in New Zealand.
15824 Subantarctic Islands Mari ne Reserves Bill 11 Feb 2014
Again, comments were made around the fact that we have benthic protected areas but
then we have issued mining permits in those benthic protected areas, and for a lot of the
general public that does not make a lot of sense. Why would you cr eate these protected
areas and then allow mining to go ahead? These are conversations where we have
enormous numbers of layered pieces of le gislation all sitting on top of each other,
different strategies, and diffe rent approaches, but it is difficult to find a coherent
strategy for the use and enjoyment and protection of our marine environment.
Marine reserves have had a long history in New Zealand, but we have not actually
gone that far in terms of the pe rcentage of our marine environment that is put into these
protected areas. They are important because th ey are very effective. We have a marine
reserve up near where I live—from Pouawa , just north of Gisborne, up to Whangar ā—
and it was very controversial when it went in. When you are dealing with marine policy,
because that work has not been done, there are a lot of existing interests there. There are
a lot of people who make thei r livelihood out of that environment, so when you start to
talk about changing the way in which they ma y have to operate in  that environment,
sometimes they do not like it. There was real concern that we were locking up the
ocean, I think they call it—cutting off large parts of areas that had previously been open
to fishing and shutting those down. Of course , the idea of locking up an ocean is not
very real. Fish are not going to magically stay within a marine reserve or go outside—

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: Passports.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: They do not need passports; thank you, Mr Prasad. But what
in fact happened was that within a very short period of time we saw an incredible
resurgence of the fish stocks within the ma rine reserve. We saw species coming back
that we had not seen for a long time in our waters, and this was in a relatively short
period of time. I think Chris Carter was the Minister of Conservation at the time when
we went up there, and it was only 4 years after the marine reserve had been created.
They had a PhD student who was doing her PhD work on that particular marine reserve.
What she was doing was she was measuring th e amount of legal size crayfish that she
was getting outside of the ma rine reserve and comparing th at with inside the marine
reserve. Bear in mind that, of course, crayfi sh do not know where th e marine reserve is.
I do not know, maybe they do, but it would seem unlikely. And yet outside of the
marine reserve, after 4 years—and we have a real issue with our crayfish stock on the
East Coast; it is really heavily depleted—she was getting half a kilogram of legal size
crayfish per pot, and inside the marine reserve she was getting over 30 kilograms of
legal size crayfish per pot. So that was an extraordinary resurgence of our crayfish
stock, which was in serious trouble. What happened was that the fishermen actually
quite liked the marine reserve because the be st fishing was suddenly on the border of
the marine reserve. Everyone would ask how  the fishermen were going to know where
the marine reserve was. Well, anyone w ho did not know where the marine reserve
boundary was just had to look at where all th e fishing boats were. It was pretty clear
where the boundary was.
What happened was that there is a reef at Whangar ā that was not actually included in
the marine reserve initially at the time. They actually ended up with an unofficial
agreement to extend the marine reserve out over that reef in order to protect the crayfish
stock. It was fantastic because kids would come down and go out to Whangar ā. They
would go walking on the reef. The crayfish were walking around in the day with their
antennae sticking out of the water, which is highly unusual because they are meant to be
nocturnal. But they were walking around. Kids were getting to see crayfish in their
natural environment. The Department of Cons ervation said to us that when it sends
people down to actually just check on the st ocks and do some of the chipping that it
does and the tracing, people actually ring the police to say that someone is fishing in the
11 Feb 2014 Subantarctic Islands  Marine Reserves Bill 15825
marine reserve and that they are taking crayfish out of the marine reserve. So then, of
course, the police say that, no, that is a Depa rtment of Conservation worker and he is
just there making sure that everything is OK.
So we have had an incredibly positive experience of that particular marine reserve on
the East Coast, and that is why Labour would like to see more of these marine reserves
created. The subantarctic ones do raise an interesting difference,  which is that it is one
thing to police marine reserves that are just off the coast of New Zealand like this one,
but policing them in areas that are far away from New Zealand is a completely different
matter. There are clauses in this bill to allow rangers to be appointed from the New
Zealand Defence Force, but I know that ther e have been concerns around fishing boats
that have been seen around the Kermadec Islands Marine Reserve, and from time to
time other concerns are raised about fishing boats that just seem to be kind of hanging
out there. Foreign fishing vessels—there is really no reason why they would be there.
These people do email us and say that they  have contacted the Ministry for Primary
Industries and it really does not seem that fu ssed about it. Unless these marine reserves
that are far offshore are goi ng to be policed or checke d—however that is done—then
you can pass all the marine reserve law in the world, but if people can just breach it and
there are no consequences, then it does undermine that particular piece of legislation.
We are very happy to support this legisla tion. I would say to members on the other
side of the House that I would not get t oo carried away. We are not solving climate
change here. It is a good piece of legislati on, but there is an awful lot more to do. As
previous members have said, wh en we look at our marine ecos ystem, it is tied in to our
rivers and our waterways in New Zealand. The entire health of that marine ecosystem is
linked with the health of our land and with the health of our fresh waterways, and we
cannot just divorce them from each other a nd pat ourselves on the back for doing this
whilst we turn the Tukituki River toxic in Ruataniwha, which is going to spill out into
the marine environment. You cannot just sepa rate everything out and pretend that they
do not all join up, because that  is not how these ecological systems work. We need to
look after our environment on land, at sea, in our freshwater waterways, and in the air,
and until we have a change of  Government, unfortunately we  are not going to get that
kind of strategic approach.

items.speaker: CLAUDETTE HAUITI
items.text: Ka tū ake ahau ki te mihi i a koe.
[I rise to acknowledge you.]
I stand to commend the Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill to the House. Kia
ora.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: That was—even by Claudette Hauiti’s
standards—a very short and enig matic speech. There is plenty to say about this bill, the
Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill. Marine reserves, I think, are increasingly an
important part of the conservation agenda . I want to start by noting that marine
conservation has been, I suppose, the poor c ousin in the conservation field. As New
Zealanders, I think we were probably late to the game. For at least a couple of decades,
much of the conservation energy was really  devoted to protecting our forests and our
terrestrial biodiversity.
I think it has been heartening to see that New Zealanders increasingly see the
importance of not only our coastal and ma rine environment but also our inland
waterways. The degradation of our streams and our rivers from intensive dairying and
the other uses that are putting those waterw ays at threat has become a major public
focus. Our marine environment has also beco me a major public focus, particularly in
areas where you have got large populations, urbanisation, and indus trial development,
and where even just recreational use depletes  fish stocks and she llfish populations. So
this is something that is increasingly coming up on the agenda.
15826 Subantarctic Islands Mari ne Reserves Bill 11 Feb 2014
As a number of colleagues have pointed ou t, there has been a little too much self-
congratulation on the Government benches over this bill, considering that these marine
reserves have been sitting around for a number of years and were, in  fact, started during
the fifth Labour Government. Also, I think that although it is undoubtedly a positive thing
that these marine reserves are being created, they are, you would have to say, low-hanging
fruit. There is very little in the way of commercial fishing where these zones are, down in
the Subantarctic Islands. There are not big vested commercial interests that are wanting to
protect their right to fish in the area, although I know that earlier in the debate a number
of speakers pointed out that one of the zones was somewhat truncated in order to allow
the possibility that the industry might develop some commercial fishing in that area.
These reserves are low-hanging fruit, and it would be great to see the Minister of
Conservation show the same kind of enthus iasm and resolve for establishing marine
reserves in the Hauraki Gulf. That would be a fine thing. It is an altogether more
complicated proposition to establish marine reserves close to a large population base, but
that is exactly what I think we should be doing.
I recently spent a few days ka yaking around the Waitemat ā Harbour and spent time
with many of the marine biologists, scien tists, and environmental activists who are
working in the Hauraki Gulf and working to restore those waters. They make the case that
in terms of repairing the damaged marine habitats, marine reserves are probably the most
powerful tool that we have. The particular problem in the Haurak i Gulf is that the
depletion of crayfish and snapper stocks has been so severe that it has allowed for an
explosion in the population of kina, believe it or not. What the kina do when they reach a
certain level is that they wipe out the kelp forests, which are an endemic habitat there in
the gulf, and they create these things called kina barrens. Basically, a kina barren is a
completely bare ocean floor, devoid of a ny kind of vegetation and devoid of any life
except for kina. If you really love kina, you might think that that is a fine thing, but it is
very much a degraded habitat.
The only way that we know of to restore th at habitat and to restore the biodiversity,
like the snapper and the crayfish, is through ha ving marine reserves. Reserves at places
like H āhei and up at Goat Island have demonstrated how successful that is. I do not
suppose that the problems are the same down in the Subantarctic Islands, but nevertheless
we do support the creation of these reserves, and we want to see many more of them.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Eugenie Sage—5 minutes.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speak er. I am pleased to be
speaking at the third reading of the Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill, but I think
we need a bit of a lesson in history here. One of the earlier National speakers, the Hon
Phil Heatley, a former Minister of Fisherie s, was almost claimi ng that National was
responsible for marine conservation in New Zealand because it had passed the initial
legislation in 1971. But the hone sty around the history is the fact that that member and
other National speakers need to acknowledge that the substantive work to establish these
marine reserves was actually done under the previous Labour Government. It was in 2006
that the Department of Conservation produced this background resource document. It
described the immense conservation and scientific values of the land and sea communities
of the Subantarctic Islands. It was this document that recognised the strong international
interest in better protecting the marine envi ronment in the Subantarctic Islands. It was
also an initiative of the previous Labour  Government—not the National Government—
that established the Subantarctic Islands Ma rine Protection Planning Forum in 2008 to
actually go and investigate and consult on th e options for marine protection around the
islands. So National is reaping the reward of this work, but it cannot claim all of the credit
for it.
11 Feb 2014 Subantarctic Islands  Marine Reserves Bill 15827
In relation to the work of the subantarc tic forum, the bill is very much a missed
opportunity because it implements the opti on for protection that  was recommended by
commercial fishers, not the op tion that was recommended by Ng āi Tahu, by
environmental organisations like the Envir onment and Conservation Organisations of
New Zealand and Forest and Bi rd, by the National Institute  of Water and Atmospheric
Research representative, and by the scientif ic representatives on th e forum. They were
recommending that there be full protection of the territorial sea around the Bounty Islands
and around Campbell Island. It would have been world leading if National had done that
in developing the bill and if it had listened to the submitters to the Local Government and
Environment Committee who supported that fu ll extent of the territorial sea being
protected. So what we have is  a much-truncated couple of reserves coming through this
bill. Nearly a third of the territorial sea around the Bounty Islands will be outside the
marine reserve, and that is so a longline fishery for ling can continue—a fishery that
results in about half a million dollars a year of revenue, so it is hardly a valuable fishery.
The bill should have included the full extent of the territorial sea, because the Bounty
Islands have got hundreds of thousands of seabirds using the land mass and using the seas
around the islands. We have got the biggest breeding colony in the world of New Zealand
fur seals. If we had had a decent reserve there, it would have gone right out to the extent
of the territorial sea. That is critical because on the Bounty Islands you have got very little
vegetation and very little soil, and the seabirds and the other species depend absolutely on
the oceans. Yet we have failed to recognise the full extent of that interdependence by
failing to protect the full extent of the territorial sea.
It is also a missed opportunity because around Campbell Island 61 percent of the
territorial sea is going to be open to fishi ng, subject to a prohib ition on Danish seining,
and it is not going to be part of the marine reserve. One of the good things that the select
committee did was to ensure that there was a review of that and of  the potential for a
deep-water crab fishery within 3 years of the bill going into law, rather than 5 years, as
was proposed in the bill as introduced. But th e far greater worth of an intact ecosystem
would have been much better recognised if we had had a proper, full marine reserve there.
The Greens obviously would support that 100 percent protection, but we do support
this bill because something is always better than nothing. The United Nations
Environment Programme described the islands as the most diverse and extensive of all the
subantarctic archipelago, so this bill, with  some protection, is definitely better than
nothing. But the fact that we are establishing the marine reserves under special legislation
and that Parliament’s time is being taken to pass it shows again the fact that National has
failed to introduce the marine reserves bill that it has long promised. Thank you.
