TUESDAY, 11 FEBRUARY 2014 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
VISITORS 
Viet Nam—Delegation, National Assembly 
Mr SPEAKER: I have much pleasure in informing the House that a parliamentary 
delegation from Viet Nam, led by Her Excellency Madam Truong Thi Mai, member of 
the Standing Committee of the National Assembly and chairman of the Committee for 
Social Affairs of the National Assembly, is  present in the gallery. I am sure that 
members would wish the delegation be welcomed. 
VISITORS 
Switzerland—Thomas Aeschi, National Council 
Mr SPEAKER : I have much pleasure in informing the House that Mr Thomas 
Aeschi, member of the National Council of Switzerland and chair of the Parliamentary 
Association—Switzerland, Australia, and New Zealand group—is present in the gallery. 
I am sure members would like him to be welcomed. 
POINTS OF ORDER 
Trans-Pacific Partnership—Leave to Move Motion Without Notice 
Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Lead er of the Opposition) : I raise a point of order, Mr 
Speaker. I seek leave to move a motion w ithout notice that the House call on the New 
Zealand Government to publish the text of the Trans-Pacific Partnership agreement— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! [Interruption] Order! I now just need to put the leave. Leave 
is sought for the member to move that mo tion. Is there is any objection? There is 
objection. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Trans-Pacific Partnership—Release of Information and Ratification Process 
1. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First)  to the Prime Minister: Does 
he stand by his statement that “personally I’ve  been of the view that transparency is a 
good thing. As Prime Minister I’ve tried to lead that charge…”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : Yes, I stand by that statement, which was 
made in the context of discussing reform of  MPs’ remuneration and travel privileges 
and transparency around expenses. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Could he explain to the count ry and the House how he is 
leading the charge on transparency in respect of the Trans-Pacific Partnership 
negotiations when, in his words— 
Hon Dr Nick Smith: It’s the same as China. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : —exactly; that’s a communist  country, a one-party State, 
thank you very much—“we do not know what is actually on the table and what is off.”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: We are following the same process that has been followed for 
all other free-trade agreements, including the China free-trade agreement. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Why is he trying to keep  the New Zealand public in 
ignorance of Trans-Pacific Partnership negotiating terms and details when the European 
Commission, in a similar deal with the Un ited States, the Tran satlantic Trade and 
15744 Questions for Oral Answer 11 Feb 2014 
Investment Partnership, is releasing bot h the proposed investment chapter and a 
layperson’s explanation for public consultation?  
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: For a start-off, all members of the Trans-Pacific Partnership—
all 12 countries—have agreed to keep ne gotiating text confidential. Secondly, our 
negotiators are negoti ating in the best in terests of New Zeala nd. You would not think, 
actually, that we would go out  there and want to give an advantage to the other 
countries we are negotiating with.  
Hon David Cunliffe: Is the Prime Minister aware of the likely date of the text being 
tabled in the United States C ongress, and can he confirm that  that will be before the 
mid-term elections and well before it has the opportunity for ratification? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: No one knows that date, because the Trans-Pacific Partnership 
itself has not been concluded yet. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Why is the Prime Minist er arguing for secrecy in 
negotiations when it is co mmon practice in the World Tr ade Organization to release 
negotiating texts? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : It is not common practice wi th the way that free-trade 
agreements have been negotiated in this c ountry. The member is quite aware, actually, 
that we have a very thorough parliamentary pr ocess. At the point at which a text has 
been agreed, then it will go through the full process, including going off to the Foreign 
Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee, for input from the public. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Does ratification by Parliament represent transparency 
when by that time the public would have had,  and will continue to  have, no say in the 
negotiations; and what is in the negotiations and the discussions—[ Interruption] Struck 
a nerve, obviously. What is in the negotiati ons and the discussions that is of such—
[Interruption] Mr Speaker, I would like to try to get this question out. It is rather 
serious. 
Mr SPEAKER: The member has already got the fi rst question out. He is actually 
asking a second supplementary question within it, but it would assist the order of the 
House if the member could complete his question without interjections. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Thank you, Mr Speaker. Does ratification by Parliament 
represent transparency when by that time th e public would have had, and will continue 
to have, no say in the negotia tions; and what is in the ne gotiations and the discussions 
that is of such concern to him and his Government that they presently want to keep it all 
secret from the New Zealand people? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : A few things. Firstly, my advice is that the Trans-Pacific 
Partnership will require legislation, so, ul timately, once it has gone through the select 
committee and the public have had their chance to have input, and it has gone through 
all of those various stages, the Government of the day will require a parliamentary 
mandate, so by definition people would have ha d a lot of input. The second thing is that 
the consultation process undert aken by the Trans-Pacific Partnership is amongst the 
most extensive that a New Zealand G overnment has undertaken for any trade 
negotiations. Public comment on the Trans-Pacific Partnership was first sought in 2008, 
and has been invited since. Negotiators have conducted a proactive consultation process 
that has included regular meetings with business groups, local c ouncils, the health 
sector and other representatives, unions  and other NGOs, and ot her individuals and 
academics. Opposition parties have also been  briefed on the negotiations as we go 
along. I think we all know that Mr Peters is opp osed to free trade. This is the man who 
voted against the China free-trade agreement. Well, good luck, but they happen to be 
our second-largest trading partner and almost certainly will one day be our largest. 
Brendan Horan: Would the Prime Minister think th ere would be transparency in an 
entity submitting multiple Official Information Act requests in a made-up name, such 
11 Feb 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 15745 
as, for example, Bruce Bayliss, and does he think such a practice would be transparent 
enough for a political party research unit? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I have no evidence to support th at Mr Bayliss is putting in 
Official Information Act requests under a pseudonym or false name, but I am aware that 
Mr Bayliss is associated with, and works for, New Zealand First. [Interruption] 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! [Interruption] Order! A point of order has been called.  
Rt Hon Winston Peters : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. There is emerging of 
late a tendency to get up and ask a supplem entary question that has nothing to do with 
the primary question or any supplementary question or any answ er that the Prime 
Minister might give that would give that member liberty to exte nd his question. I have 
got no idea who Mr Bayliss is. 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! The essence of the question was around transparency and 
related to the original primary question. 
Prime Minister—Statements 
2. Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Lea der of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister: 
Does he stand by all his statements? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes. 
Hon David Cunliffe : Does he stand by his 2007 stat ement in relation to trans-
Tasman regulatory harmonisation, that “We al ways have to make sure what we are 
doing is in the best interests of New Zeal and.”; if so, why did he come home empty-
handed from Australia in relation to the supermarket boycott of New Zealand products? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Far from coming home empt y-handed from Australia, we 
came home with a trans-Tasman visa for the Cricket World Cup; we came home with an 
invitation for New Zealand businesses to be part of the G20 and be part of 400 global 
chief executive officers; we came home unpicking the terrible deal that Helen Clark and 
Phil Goff and David Cunliffe signed New Zealanders up to, by making sure that student 
loans actually will be accessible to New Zealanders who are special class visa holders— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! That answer is quite long enough, thank you. 
Hon David Cunliffe : Has the Prime Minister sought any advice as to how many 
Kiwi jobs will be lost as a result of this boyc ott; if so, what was the number, and, if not, 
why has he not asked? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I do not have that number but I do have the number of people 
who have lost their job in the Labour Pa rty today. It is one—the Leader of the 
Opposition’s chief of staff has quit. 
Hon David Cunliffe: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I am trying to assist the member who is raising a point of 
order. 
Hon David Cunliffe : The question was a simple and straightforward one: “Has he 
asked for any advice?”. He has not turned himself to that question. 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! There were two parts to the supplementary question. The 
Prime Minister addressed one part in saying how many—he said “None.” 
Hon Annette King: He said he didn’t have the number. 
Mr SPEAKER: That is true. He said he didn’t have the number, which answers the 
question. 
Hon David Cunliffe: Does the Prime Minister agree w ith his soul mate that the only 
appeal available to New Zealand exporters, who could be facing a loss of up to $700 
million per annum, is an appeal to the Australian Competition and Consumer 
Commission; if so, why? 
15746 Questions for Oral Answer 11 Feb 2014 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : First, and quite fundamentall y, I think the Le ader of the 
Opposition is probably inven ting numbers from somewhere. They are not from a 
reliable source. More important— 
Hon David Cunliffe: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! I apologise to the Prime Mi nister but we have a point of 
order. 
Hon David Cunliffe : The Prime Minister has called my veracity into question. The 
number came from the National Business Review, a renowned— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Order! That is not a point of order. That is a matter of debate 
within the answer, and the—[Interruption] Order! The member has the opportunity with 
further supplementary questions, if he wishes  to tease out that information. Does the 
Prime Minister wish to complete his answer? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : What is clear is that this is a commercial matter, and that in 
fact the Government does not support a buy Australian-made campaign, any more that it 
actually supports the supermarkets in New Zealand that actually run buy New Zealand - 
made campaigns. What is clear is that the Australian Government is actually running a 
full investigation into competition policy in Australia. There is an opportunity for New 
Zealand companies to submit to that. But these are actions by a commercial company, 
so if the member is telling us that he is going to intervene with them, that is a very 
interesting thing to hear. 
Hon David Cunliffe: Does the Prime Minister consider cups of tea and shady deals 
with extreme minor parties to be gerrymandering the MMP electoral system? 
Hon Gerry Brownlee: How does that relate to the Prime Minister? 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The Prime Minister is quite capable of answering it.  
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I think if the member wants to talk about some of those issues, 
he should go and look in the mirror and also talk to Dr Norman. 
Hon David Cunliffe : Does the Prime Minister stand by his statement that “People 
want greater transparency.”; if so, why will his Government not release the text of the 
Trans-Pacific Partnership agreement before any final agreement is signed? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : As I said earlier, firstly, th e Government has been involving 
all of the interested stakeholders. My understa nding is that the trade Minister has been 
talking to both Mr Goff and Mr Shearer. If they feel they want more information and 
they are prepared potentially even to answer  confidentiality arrangements, I am sure we 
could go another step forward. We are following— 
Hon David Cunliffe: Point of order, Mr Speaker— 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: No, no, sit down, sunshine, I have not finished. 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Both members—[Interruption] Order! I am on my feet. Both 
members will resume their seats. Is there a point of order? 
Hon David Cunliffe : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. As the question went to 
the matter of the text of the Trans-Pacifi c Partnership agreement, I thought it might 
assist the Prime Minister to clarify— 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! Again—[ Interruption] Order! That is not a valid point of 
order. The question related to transparency, and the Prime Minister was addressing that. 
Does the Prime Minister wish to add further to his answer? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I do, Mr Speaker. The process that is being followed here is 
the identical process that was followed with  the China free-trade agreement. We are 
more than happy to try to keep parties up to date once texts are complete and we are in a 
position to be able to do that through a proper process. This is the same process that was 
followed for China. 
11 Feb 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 15747 
Hon David Cunliffe: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Quite clearly the question 
concerned the Trans-Pacific Partnership ag reement. The Prime Minister is obviously 
new to foreign policy— 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! Again, for the third occasion, that is not a valid point of 
order. What the member is attempting to do is to use the point of order process to debate 
an answer that has been given. The process would be better accomplished by using 
further supplementary questions. 
Hon David Cunliffe: Given that the Prime Minister routinely refuses to comment on 
intelligence and security matters, why did he make statements in relation to operational 
intelligence regarding New Zealanders in Syria? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : From time to time I do offer answers where I believe it is the 
right thing to do. I have done that on othe r occasions in the past. Actually, the 
interesting thing yesterday was that it wa s a great example of how the Government 
Communications Security Bureau actually assi sts the Security Intelligence Service to 
protect New Zealanders. Interestingly enough, I remember in this House about 6 months 
ago the strongest opposition coming from the Labour Party, yet last night David 
Cunliffe was once again on TV telling New Z ealanders he wanted to go further than 
that. He wanted more information and more  laws. Fortunately, Mr Goff straightened 
him up on the radio this morning.  
Hon David Cunliffe: Point of order—[Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER: Order! This is a point of order and it will be heard in silence. 
Hon David Cunliffe : I seek leave to table an arti cle on Australian supermarkets 
locking out New Zealand exports— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The source— 
Hon David Cunliffe: —tabled in the National Business Review— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I am not prepared even to put the leave. I am not tabling the 
National Business Review. 
Question No. 1 to Minister 
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First): I seek to table a list of the New 
Zealand First parliamentary staff showing no Mr Bayliss. 
Mr SPEAKER: The easiest way is for the House to determine this. Leave is sought 
to table a list of New Zealand First staff. Is there any objection to that being tabled? 
There appears to be no objection. It can be so tabled. 
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House. 
Job Creation and Unemployment—Statistics 
3. Hon KATE WILKINSON (National—Waimakariri)  to the Minister of 
Finance: How is the stronger New Zealand econ omy supporting more jobs and higher 
incomes? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associat e Minister of Finance) on behalf of the Minister 
of Finance: There are a number of indicators c onfirming that the stronger economy is 
translating into more jobs and higher inco mes. They range from business confidence 
and employment intentions running at the highest levels for ar ound 20 years, and the 
number of job ads on the SEEK website increasing 13 percent to almost 24,000 in 
January. Just last week Statistics New Z ealand issued the labour market data, which 
confirmed further growth in job numbers and real wages, and a decline in the 
unemployment rate from 6.2 percent to 6 per cent in the December qua rter. They are all 
further signs that the Government’s ec onomic programme, including the Business 
15748 Questions for Oral Answer 11 Feb 2014 
Growth Agenda to help businesses invest, grow, and employ more people, is working 
successfully as we recover from the global financial crisis. 
Hon Kate Wilkinson : What did the official labour ma rket statistics say last week 
about the growth in jobs during the period to December 2013? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : The household labour force survey confirmed that 
employment increased by 1.1 percent in the December quarter. That means 24,000 more 
New Zealanders were in jobs in that quarter alone. For the year to December the news 
was also positive. Between the December quarters of 2012 and 2013 employment 
increased 3 percent, meaning another 66,000 Ne w Zealanders were in work compared 
with a year earlier. That is the stronge st annual increase since June 2006, again 
confirming that the Government’s economic programme is heading in the right direction 
for the benefit of New Zealand families. 
Hon Kate Wilkinson : What other indicators in the labour market statistics issued 
last week provided further evidence that th e improving labour market is helping more 
New Zealanders to get ahead? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : Apart from the lower unemployment rate and the strong 
increase in new jobs, another positive indica tor is the continuing growth in wages. The 
quarterly employment survey is the best sour ce of wage movements, and that is why it 
has been used by successive Governments as the basis for setting, for example, paid 
parental leave and New Zealand superannuatio n. Using this measure, average weekly 
earnings rose by 2.8 percent over the year to December, while inflation was only 1.6 
percent. So, on average, wages ar e continuing to rise faster than inflation. The gains are 
even more significant when measured on an  after-tax basis. The average weekly 
earnings after tax—[Interruption]; they do not want to hear it—have gone up 25 percent 
since September 2008, compared with inflation of just 10 percent over the same period. 
Hon Kate Wilkinson : How has the growth in new jobs over the past 4 years, as 
reported by Statistics New Zealand, compared w ith Treasury forecasts issued as part of 
Budget 2010? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : In Budget 2010, Treasury fore cast that there would be 
174,000 more jobs in the economy over the 4½ years to June 2014. 
Hon David Parker: That’s not what you promised, though—170,000 extra jobs over 
3 years, not 4. 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : I am pleased to report we a tracking pretty close to that 
forecast, which I remember Opposition partie s dismissing at the time as being way too 
optimistic for New Zealand. Actual employment growth in the 4 years to December 
2013 was 139,000 jobs, Mr Parker. To meet that full 4½-year Treasury forecast, another 
35,000 jobs need to be created over the next 6 months, which is not unrealistic, given 
that 52,000 new jobs were created in the 6 months to December. This is further 
evidence that the Government’s economic programme is working. 
Wage Growth—Measurement and Comparison with Inflation 
4. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Minister for Tertiary 
Education, Skills and Employment : By how much did wages and salaries increase 
between December 2008 and December 2013 acco rding to the Labour Cost Index and 
how does this compare to inflation accordi ng to the Consumer Price Index over the 
same period? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for T ertiary Education, Skills and 
Employment): I will give the member the informa tion he has asked for, but the House 
also needs to know that the labour cost inde x he refers to is not a measure of actual 
wage and salary increases in the workforce. Wage and salary increases in the workforce 
are captured by the quarterly employment su rvey and, in particular, the measure of 
11 Feb 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 15749 
average weekly earnings. That has increased 16.1 percent since December 2008. The 
labour cost index, on the other hand, is a st atistical construct de signed to measure 
inflation in the labour market. It ignores pay increases that are due to increased 
performance or productivity, for promotion, fo r taking on extra responsibilities, or for 
changing jobs. The labour cost index increased 9.3 percent since December 2008, 
which, not surprisingly, is similar to the othe r measure we have of inflation, which is 
the CPI, which increased 10.8 over the same period.  
Dr Russel Norman: Can the Minister confirm that th e labour cost index went up by 
9.3 percent under the National Government over this period, while inflation increased 
by 10.5 percent over the same period, meaning that people’ s pay packets have gotten 
smaller in real terms under the current Government? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: No. With the greatest respect to the member, he is being a 
bit tricky here, because the labour cost i ndex does not measure changes in wages, 
salaries, and earnings over the period. It mentions the pure inflation in the labour market 
for somebody who does not get any pay in creases from improved productivity or 
anything like that. The quarterly  employment survey is actually the method via which 
changes in employment, total weekly gross earnings, total weekly paid hours, and 
average hourly and average weekly earnings are reflected. I th ink the member does 
know that because he has asked questions  on the quarterly employment survey 
previously. Today, interestingly, he is asking only about the labour cost index. 
Dr Russel Norman : Is the Minister aware of Statistics New Zealand’s User guide 
for Statistics New Zealand’ s wage and income measures , the third edition, which says 
that “if you are interested in changes in earnings acro ss time, the Labour Cost Index 
(LCI) is a better measure than the QES.”? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: I have not got that particular  example in front  of me, but I 
can tell the member that on page 15 of the quarterly employment survey, which has just 
been released last week—helpfully, on the same day as the labour cost index, which 
may be why the member has confused it— it says: “The unadjusted LCI measures 
changes in salary and ordinary-time wage rates for a fixed quantity of labour.”— 
Grant Robertson: Arrogant man. 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: —no, just correct, Mr Robertson, in this case—“It fixes the 
relative importance of industries and occupati ons,” but does not fix the market rates, 
and so on, in terms of the quarterly  employment survey. Again, successive 
Governments have used the quarterly employme nt survey for calculating things such as 
superannuation and paid parental leave because  that measures the change in actual 
earnings of New Zealanders, and if the member  was not being tricky,  that is what he 
would use. 
Dr Russel Norman : Does the Minister not understa nd what Statistics New Zealand 
is saying in the quote from its own documents wh ere it says that the labour cost index is 
the official measure of the change in earni ngs over time, not the quarterly employment 
survey—which is why it puts it in its documents—because the quarterly employment 
survey will produce misleading results, such as showing an increase in the average 
wage when lots of low-wage jobs are lost, as has happened under this Government? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : I disagree with the member on a couple of points here. 
Firstly, if he has noticed in the previous ques tion, we were able to show the increase in 
jobs over the period that this Government ha s been in office—certainly, in recent times 
and since Budget 2010. But, again, I think the member is, I am sorry, being deliberately 
disingenuous here, because the labour cost inde x is about a measure of pure inflation in 
the labour market for a fixed and equal quan tity of labour that does not change. In 
reality, people’s income goes up because th ey are more productive, it goes up because 
they have been given a promotion, it goes up because they have changed jobs. That is 
15750 Questions for Oral Answer 11 Feb 2014 
captured in the quarterly empl oyment survey, and that is the actual measure of wages 
for New Zealanders and of how they have changed over time. 
Dr Russel Norman: Who is right: Statistics New Zealand, which produces both the 
labour cost index and the quarterly employment  survey, and says, as I quote again, that 
if you are interested in change s in earnings over time, the labour cost index is a better 
measure than the quarterly employment surv ey—is Statistics New Zealand right about

11 Feb 2014 Smoke-free Environments (P lain Packaging) Amdt Bill 15795 
SMOKE-FREE ENVIRONMENTS (TOBACCO PLAIN PACKAGING) 
AMENDMENT BILL 
First Reading 
Hon TARIANA TURIA (Associat e Minister of Health) : I move, That the Smoke-
free Environments (Tobacco Plain Packaging) Amendment Bill be now read a first time. 
I nominate the Health Committee to consider  the bill. As a gr eat-grandmother and 
grandmother of close to 50 mokopuna, I am  acutely aware of the importance of 
branding upon the psyche of the young person. What really matters is not so much 
about being neat and tidy but more that your socks have the tick strategically placed, the 
shirt is emblazoned with the latest label, and the cap is the right colour and the right 
look. So when I read the research reveal ing that consumers buy branded products as 
much for their symbolic value as for their utility, it made perfect sense.  
In essence, the decision to introduce plain packaging for tobacco products in New 
Zealand is all about the brandi ng. It takes away the last m eans of promoting tobacco as 
a desirable product. When tobacco manufact urers push tobacco, they are not simply 
selling a stick of nicotine; they are selling status, social acceptance, and adventure. The 
design and appearance of tobacco products and, in particular, the way they are packaged 
influence people’s perceptions about these products and the desi rability of smoking. 
Brand imagery demonstrably increases the ap peal of tobacco brands, particularly to 
youth and young adults, helping to attract ne w smokers and also implying wider social 
approval for tobacco use.  
The Smoke-free Environments Act 1990 in troduced extensive restrictions on 
traditional forms of advertising for tobacco  products. A quarter of a century later 
tobacco companies have deliberately used packaging design and appearance to make 
their products appear more desirable and to promote their use. The objectives of this bill 
are very clear: to reduce the appeal of tobacco products and smoking, particularly for 
young people; to further reduce any wider social acceptance and approval of smoking 
and tobacco products; to increase the noticeabi lity and effectiveness of mandated health 
warning messages and images; and to reduc e the likelihood that consumers might 
acquire false perceptions about the harms caused by tobacco products.  
For too long tobacco companies have been creating brands in advertising to persuade 
us to think that smoking is glamorous, fun, cool, sophisticated, and a part of life, 
knowing that they had to sell only the myth and the nicotine addiction would take over. 
I want to commend those parties across this House that have been consistently 
committed to this goal of being smoke-free. When Parliament moves together in one 
direction, we can make significant progress a nd improve the health of New Zealanders. 
That is surely what should be uppermost in the minds of every politician—protecting 
the health of future generations while at th e same time taking prudent responsibility for 
the use of taxpayer funds. We have been able to take a courageous approach to tobacco 
control measures, and I strongl y recommend we continue to do so. In this way we will 
create better health outcomes for all New Zealanders.  
Plain packaging will be most effective in  building on other legislation to improve 
tobacco control, such as the annual 10 percent tobacco tax increases through to 1 
January 2016, and the ban on displaying tobacc o products at the poi nt of sale, which 
this House overwhelmingly supported in 2011. No one measure will make the 
difference in isolation. Each of these m easures addresses specific elements in 
establishing a comprehensive tobacco contro l regime. Tax increases are a particularly 
effective policy tool to re duce tobacco consumption. We also know that reducing the 
visibility of tobacco products contributes to this objective. Having removed the display 
15796 Smoke-free Environments (Plain Packaging) Amdt Bill 11 Feb 2014 
of tobacco products in shops, we are now tackling how these products look by greatly 
reducing their appeal, especially to young people—our children and our grandchildren.  
I am determined that we must denormalis e smoking and build on the progress that 
we have seen to date. This bill is about  sending a very clear message to tobacco 
companies that this Government is serious  about ending unnece ssary deaths and poor 
health outcomes related to tobacco use. The intent of the legislation is to prevent the 
design and appearance of packaging and of pr oducts themselves from having any visual 
or other effect that could se rve to promote the attractivene ss of the product or increase 
the social appeal of smoking.  
The plain packaging regime will tightly control the design and appearance of tobacco 
product packaging and of the products th emselves by allowing the brand name and 
certain other manufacturer information to be printed on the pack, but with tight 
controls—for example, on the font used, its size, its colour, and its position on the pack. 
It will standardise all other design elements of tobacco product packaging, such as the 
materials, colours, and type faces or fonts that may be used. It will require the 
packaging to carry larger, mo re prominent, and more pe rtinent warning messages and 
graphic images, controlling the design and appearance of individual cigarettes and other 
products.  
The colouring and wording used on tobacco packaging has been shown to create 
misconceptions that tobacco products are less harmful and that it is easier to quit than is 
in fact the case. Internationally, smoking remains the largest cause of preventable death. 
It also contributes to profound health a nd social inequalities and outcomes for M āori 
and Pasifika peoples. There is no other consumer product that is so widely used and that 
directly poses such a high level of health ri sk to users, particularly long-term users. 
Quitting smoking or, even better, never smoki ng is the key to enjoying a longer and 
healthier life with loved ones.  
As a nation, the burden of disease and the national he alth costs caused by smoking 
are massive. The introduction of plain packag ing will do much to turn this situation 
round. It will discourage people from taking up smoking or using tobacco products, and 
encourage people to be smoke-free and health ier. It will also reduce people’s exposure 
to second-hand smoke from tobacco products. I want to signal that I am still of the view 
that we can do a lot more on this front, particularly on the goal of increasing the 
numbers of parents and careg ivers who do not allow smoking in their car at any time, 
fully cognisant of the threat that it imposes on their children.  
Finally, this bill w ill support New Zealand in meeti ng its international obligations 
and commitments under the World Health Organization’s Framew ork Convention on 
Tobacco Control, and it will align the tobacco  plain packaging legislation in Australia 
consistent with the Trans-Tasman Mutual Recognition Agreement. I am confident that 
this bill is consistent with all New Zealand’s international obligations. We are 
convinced that plain packaging is a really important step on our path to being a smoke-
free country by 2025, and that it will stack up against our World Trade Organization 
obligations. That is why we are pushing forward to take  the legislation through the 
parliamentary processes without delay.  
New Zealand takes all of its international obligations seriously. Our plain packaging 
regime has been developed to be consistent with our trade obligations, and our approach 
to negotiating new trade agreements continues to protect our ability to take public health 
measures such as plain packaging. The ag reements and treaties can, and should, work 
together to boost both international trade a nd public health, and this is a good example 
of where we can achieve both objectives.  
Although the tobacco industry may have laid down a threat if this legislation is 
passed, my message to it is th at our country has a sovereig n right and a legal right to 
11 Feb 2014 Smoke-free Environments (P lain Packaging) Amdt Bill 15797 
protect its citizens. I am firmly  of the opinion that it is not for any tobacco company to 
be telling us what we should be doing in  our own land. Five thousand New Zealanders 
die from smoking a year, and that death toll places a responsibility on every politician to 
pass legislation in our land that will help save lives and increase well-being—legislation 
that makes a tangible, enduring impact on th e lives of the people of this country. I 
commend this bill to the House for its first reading.

Akaroa marine reserve that has now been pr ovided, and other marine reserves around 
the coast, where fish species, fish life, and marine life have been preserved as a result of 
making areas protected.  
The Local Government and Environment Committee considered a great deal of 
evidence on this bill. It was one of the more  pleasing bills, in that the whole committee 
was in agreement with what was required to put this through in to legislation. The 
committee agreed on a shorter review time in  terms of what was originally in the 
legislation. Again, we felt that it was appropr iate that the review period be reduced 
because of the special nature of these is lands. It was a very good, cordial agreement by 
the Local Government and Environment Co mmittee to achieve a good outcome for this 
bill.  
It is pleasing to see that this week the HMNZS Wellington set sail from Devonport 
naval base yesterday, heading to the Subantarctic Islands. It will be picking up the 
Minister of Conservation, Nick Smith, some where on the way as it travels south. The 
Minister will be on there. So by the time th is bill is enacted and perhaps signed off by 
the Governor-General in the next couple of days and is in force, the Minister will 
actually be arriving in these islands to ma ke the appropriate a nnouncement. I am sure 
the National Party will make sure that that is heard loud and clear in all available media.  
More especially, on board the HMNZS Wellington there are 12 Sir Peter Blake Trust 
young leaders. They left from Auckland. They have been selected as some of the top 
young leaders that this country has. They are going down there to the Subantarctic 
Islands. In the spirit of Sir Peter Blake and all the great work that he has done out on the 
oceans around the world and in the ma rine environment, those 12 young New 
Zealanders are going for a 13-day expedition to  look at the Subantarctic Islands with 
representatives from the Department of C onservation, from the National Institute of 
Water and Atmospheric Research, from Otago University, and from a number of other 
organisations and hosted, of course, by the Royal New Zealand Navy. 
The group, while they are ther e looking at the islands, wi ll be drafting a feasibility 
plan for a world-leading subantarctic resear ch station, which is hoped to be completed 
by 2015. The station will allow New Zealand scientists and worldwide agencies to study 
the effects of ocean and climate change  and also the effects on many of those 
endangered species, wildlife, marine life, and the southern oceans around the islands. 
This has, again, huge potential for the outreach of New Zealand into a special part of the 
oceans that surround New Zealand. We certa inly commend those young people for the 
good work they will be doing over the next 13 days on board that naval ship—with the 
naval officers and the many other Government  support people and scientists who are in 
support of them—to come up with some good r ecommendations as to how that station 
will be established.  
11 Feb 2014 Subantarctic Islands  Marine Reserves Bill 15823 
In closing, it is not often that we have una nimous support in this House, but this is 
one of those occasions. This is a special occasion because this will be our most far-
reaching outpost in terms of a marine reserv e for New Zealand as a nation. It is very 
special and it shows that New Zealanders, as a whole, place a high priority on the 
environment and conservation and on ensuring that we do our very best for the natural 
environment. So New Zealand First is very happy to support and commend this bill. 
JACQUI DEAN (National—Waitaki) : It is amazing how jealous we all are of the 
Hon Nick Smith’s trip down to the Subantar ctic Islands. It speaks volumes, I think, for

MOANA MACKEY (Labour) : The previous speaker, Jacqui Dean, is earning her 
salary tonight! I am very happy to stand and take a call— 
Hon Judith Collins: Well, you know, at least she does earn her salary, not like that 
member. 
MOANA MACKEY: Oh, calm down! Calm down! It was just a joke, Mrs Collins. 
Have a sense of humour. Anyway, I am ve ry happy to stand and take a call on the 
Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill. It is a very interesting bill and it was a very 
enjoyable experience having th is bill at the Local G overnment and Environment 
Committee. I wish we had more pieces of environmental legislation coming to the Local 
Government and Environment Committee that  we could all agree on and that are 
actually doing good things fo r the environment, as opp osed to undermining and 
destroying the environment, which is usually the tenor of environm ental legislation we 
deal with at that select committee. But, in  this instance, it wa s a very good piece of 
legislation.  
I think it is important to note that nearly  all the submitters who came along did say 
that they did not think it went far enough. They  were very supportive of the protections 
that were being put in place, but they did fe el that the areas being protected were not 
sufficient. We responded by amending the review period in this legislation from 5 years 
down to 2 years in order to reflect the fact th at they did not feel that we needed to wait 
that long period of time in order to make those decisions and determinations.  
This bill will create three marine reserv es: the Antipodes Island Marine Reserve, or 
Moutere Mahue; the Bounty Islands Marine Reserve, or Moutere Hauriri; and the 
Campbell Island Marine Reserve, or Mout ere Ihupuku. These are in credibly important 
parts of our subantarctic ocean. They have been recognised as World Heritage sites, and 
in that respect we welcome this piece of legislation.  
Marine reserves have had a bit of a bumpy ri de in New Zealand in general. I think it 
is fair to say that in terms of marine polic y right across the board we are kind of playing 
catch-up. We do not really know a lot of what is out there in our marine environment, 
particularly around the various ecosystems, around the make-up of the sea floor. In fact, 
the Australians have a lot more information than us because when they did a lot of their 
oil and gas development in the 1970s they re quired the companies to do that work and 
to provide that spatial information about the marine environment to the Government. 
They have been able to base a lot of th eir policies and decisions on information that 
they required as a bottom line and as a condi tion of that activity going ahead. We have 
not had the benefit of that, so what has happened is that right throughout the decades we 
have sometimes had a rather piecemeal approach to how we deal with marine policy. As 
previous speakers have said, it would be very, very desirabl e to see a far more coherent 
approach to marine policy in New Zealand a nd to have a strategy for how we want to 
use, to enjoy, and to extract resources from  our marine environment, but to have a 
strategy instead of siloed debates around each of those issues without connecting them 
up. That, unfortunately, is what has been missing in New Zealand.  
15824 Subantarctic Islands Mari ne Reserves Bill 11 Feb 2014 
Again, comments were made around the fact that we have benthic protected areas but 
then we have issued mining permits in those benthic protected areas, and for a lot of the 
general public that does not make a lot of sense. Why would you cr eate these protected 
areas and then allow mining to go ahead? These are conversations where we have 
enormous numbers of layered pieces of le gislation all sitting on top of each other, 
different strategies, and diffe rent approaches, but it is difficult to find a coherent 
strategy for the use and enjoyment and protection of our marine environment.  
Marine reserves have had a long history in New Zealand, but we have not actually 
gone that far in terms of the pe rcentage of our marine environment that is put into these 
protected areas. They are important because th ey are very effective. We have a marine 
reserve up near where I live—from Pouawa , just north of Gisborne, up to Whangar ā—
and it was very controversial when it went in. When you are dealing with marine policy, 
because that work has not been done, there are a lot of existing interests there. There are 
a lot of people who make thei r livelihood out of that environment, so when you start to 
talk about changing the way in which they ma y have to operate in  that environment, 
sometimes they do not like it. There was real concern that we were locking up the 
ocean, I think they call it—cutting off large parts of areas that had previously been open 
to fishing and shutting those down. Of course , the idea of locking up an ocean is not 
very real. Fish are not going to magically stay within a marine reserve or go outside— 
Dr Rajen Prasad: Passports. 
MOANA MACKEY: They do not need passports; thank you, Mr Prasad. But what 
in fact happened was that within a very short period of time we saw an incredible 
resurgence of the fish stocks within the ma rine reserve. We saw species coming back 
that we had not seen for a long time in our waters, and this was in a relatively short 
period of time. I think Chris Carter was the Minister of Conservation at the time when 
we went up there, and it was only 4 years after the marine reserve had been created. 
They had a PhD student who was doing her PhD work on that particular marine reserve. 
What she was doing was she was measuring th e amount of legal size crayfish that she 
was getting outside of the ma rine reserve and comparing th at with inside the marine 
reserve. Bear in mind that, of course, crayfi sh do not know where th e marine reserve is. 
I do not know, maybe they do, but it would seem unlikely. And yet outside of the 
marine reserve, after 4 years—and we have a real issue with our crayfish stock on the 
East Coast; it is really heavily depleted—she was getting half a kilogram of legal size 
crayfish per pot, and inside the marine reserve she was getting over 30 kilograms of 
legal size crayfish per pot. So that was an extraordinary resurgence of our crayfish 
stock, which was in serious trouble. What happened was that the fishermen actually 
quite liked the marine reserve because the be st fishing was suddenly on the border of 
the marine reserve. Everyone would ask how  the fishermen were going to know where 
the marine reserve was. Well, anyone w ho did not know where the marine reserve 
boundary was just had to look at where all th e fishing boats were. It was pretty clear 
where the boundary was.  
What happened was that there is a reef at Whangar ā that was not actually included in 
the marine reserve initially at the time. They actually ended up with an unofficial 
agreement to extend the marine reserve out over that reef in order to protect the crayfish 
stock. It was fantastic because kids would come down and go out to Whangar ā. They 
would go walking on the reef. The crayfish were walking around in the day with their 
antennae sticking out of the water, which is highly unusual because they are meant to be 
nocturnal. But they were walking around. Kids were getting to see crayfish in their 
natural environment. The Department of Cons ervation said to us that when it sends 
people down to actually just check on the st ocks and do some of the chipping that it 
does and the tracing, people actually ring the police to say that someone is fishing in the 
11 Feb 2014 Subantarctic Islands  Marine Reserves Bill 15825 
marine reserve and that they are taking crayfish out of the marine reserve. So then, of 
course, the police say that, no, that is a Depa rtment of Conservation worker and he is 
just there making sure that everything is OK.  
So we have had an incredibly positive experience of that particular marine reserve on 
the East Coast, and that is why Labour would like to see more of these marine reserves 
created. The subantarctic ones do raise an interesting difference,  which is that it is one 
thing to police marine reserves that are just off the coast of New Zealand like this one, 
but policing them in areas that are far away from New Zealand is a completely different 
matter. There are clauses in this bill to allow rangers to be appointed from the New 
Zealand Defence Force, but I know that ther e have been concerns around fishing boats 
that have been seen around the Kermadec Islands Marine Reserve, and from time to 
time other concerns are raised about fishing boats that just seem to be kind of hanging 
out there. Foreign fishing vessels—there is really no reason why they would be there. 
These people do email us and say that they  have contacted the Ministry for Primary 
Industries and it really does not seem that fu ssed about it. Unless these marine reserves 
that are far offshore are goi ng to be policed or checke d—however that is done—then 
you can pass all the marine reserve law in the world, but if people can just breach it and 
there are no consequences, then it does undermine that particular piece of legislation.  
We are very happy to support this legisla tion. I would say to members on the other 
side of the House that I would not get t oo carried away. We are not solving climate 
change here. It is a good piece of legislati on, but there is an awful lot more to do. As 
previous members have said, wh en we look at our marine ecos ystem, it is tied in to our 
rivers and our waterways in New Zealand. The entire health of that marine ecosystem is 
linked with the health of our land and with the health of our fresh waterways, and we 
cannot just divorce them from each other a nd pat ourselves on the back for doing this 
whilst we turn the Tukituki River toxic in Ruataniwha, which is going to spill out into 
the marine environment. You cannot just sepa rate everything out and pretend that they 
do not all join up, because that  is not how these ecological systems work. We need to 
look after our environment on land, at sea, in our freshwater waterways, and in the air, 
and until we have a change of  Government, unfortunately we  are not going to get that 
kind of strategic approach.

PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atat ū): That was—even by Claudette Hauiti’s 
standards—a very short and enig matic speech. There is plenty to say about this bill, the 
Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill. Marine reserves, I think, are increasingly an 
important part of the conservation agenda . I want to start by noting that marine 
conservation has been, I suppose, the poor c ousin in the conservation field. As New 
Zealanders, I think we were probably late to the game. For at least a couple of decades, 
much of the conservation energy was really  devoted to protecting our forests and our 
terrestrial biodiversity.  
I think it has been heartening to see that New Zealanders increasingly see the 
importance of not only our coastal and ma rine environment but also our inland 
waterways. The degradation of our streams and our rivers from intensive dairying and 
the other uses that are putting those waterw ays at threat has become a major public 
focus. Our marine environment has also beco me a major public focus, particularly in 
areas where you have got large populations, urbanisation, and indus trial development, 
and where even just recreational use depletes  fish stocks and she llfish populations. So 
this is something that is increasingly coming up on the agenda.  
15826 Subantarctic Islands Mari ne Reserves Bill 11 Feb 2014 
As a number of colleagues have pointed ou t, there has been a little too much self-
congratulation on the Government benches over this bill, considering that these marine 
reserves have been sitting around for a number of years and were, in  fact, started during 
the fifth Labour Government. Also, I think that although it is undoubtedly a positive thing 
that these marine reserves are being created, they are, you would have to say, low-hanging 
fruit. There is very little in the way of commercial fishing where these zones are, down in 
the Subantarctic Islands. There are not big vested commercial interests that are wanting to 
protect their right to fish in the area, although I know that earlier in the debate a number 
of speakers pointed out that one of the zones was somewhat truncated in order to allow 
the possibility that the industry might develop some commercial fishing in that area.  
These reserves are low-hanging fruit, and it would be great to see the Minister of 
Conservation show the same kind of enthus iasm and resolve for establishing marine 
reserves in the Hauraki Gulf. That would be a fine thing. It is an altogether more 
complicated proposition to establish marine reserves close to a large population base, but 
that is exactly what I think we should be doing.  
I recently spent a few days ka yaking around the Waitemat ā Harbour and spent time 
with many of the marine biologists, scien tists, and environmental activists who are 
working in the Hauraki Gulf and working to restore those waters. They make the case that 
in terms of repairing the damaged marine habitats, marine reserves are probably the most 
powerful tool that we have. The particular problem in the Haurak i Gulf is that the 
depletion of crayfish and snapper stocks has been so severe that it has allowed for an 
explosion in the population of kina, believe it or not. What the kina do when they reach a 
certain level is that they wipe out the kelp forests, which are an endemic habitat there in 
the gulf, and they create these things called kina barrens. Basically, a kina barren is a 
completely bare ocean floor, devoid of a ny kind of vegetation and devoid of any life 
except for kina. If you really love kina, you might think that that is a fine thing, but it is 
very much a degraded habitat.  
The only way that we know of to restore th at habitat and to restore the biodiversity, 
like the snapper and the crayfish, is through ha ving marine reserves. Reserves at places 
like H āhei and up at Goat Island have demonstrated how successful that is. I do not 
suppose that the problems are the same down in the Subantarctic Islands, but nevertheless 
we do support the creation of these reserves, and we want to see many more of them. 
The ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Lindsay Tisch): I call Eugenie Sage—5 minutes. 
EUGENIE SAGE (Green) : T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speak er. I am pleased to be 
speaking at the third reading of the Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill, but I think 
we need a bit of a lesson in history here. One of the earlier National speakers, the Hon 
Phil Heatley, a former Minister of Fisherie s, was almost claimi ng that National was 
responsible for marine conservation in New Zealand because it had passed the initial 
legislation in 1971. But the hone sty around the history is the fact that that member and 
other National speakers need to acknowledge that the substantive work to establish these 
marine reserves was actually done under the previous Labour Government. It was in 2006 
that the Department of Conservation produced this background resource document. It 
described the immense conservation and scientific values of the land and sea communities 
of the Subantarctic Islands. It was this document that recognised the strong international 
interest in better protecting the marine envi ronment in the Subantarctic Islands. It was 
also an initiative of the previous Labour  Government—not the National Government—
that established the Subantarctic Islands Ma rine Protection Planning Forum in 2008 to 
actually go and investigate and consult on th e options for marine protection around the 
islands. So National is reaping the reward of this work, but it cannot claim all of the credit 
for it.  
11 Feb 2014 Subantarctic Islands  Marine Reserves Bill 15827 
In relation to the work of the subantarc tic forum, the bill is very much a missed 
opportunity because it implements the opti on for protection that  was recommended by 
commercial fishers, not the op tion that was recommended by Ng āi Tahu, by 
environmental organisations like the Envir onment and Conservation Organisations of 
New Zealand and Forest and Bi rd, by the National Institute  of Water and Atmospheric 
Research representative, and by the scientif ic representatives on th e forum. They were 
recommending that there be full protection of the territorial sea around the Bounty Islands 
and around Campbell Island. It would have been world leading if National had done that 
in developing the bill and if it had listened to the submitters to the Local Government and 
Environment Committee who supported that fu ll extent of the territorial sea being 
protected. So what we have is  a much-truncated couple of reserves coming through this 
bill. Nearly a third of the territorial sea around the Bounty Islands will be outside the 
marine reserve, and that is so a longline fishery for ling can continue—a fishery that 
results in about half a million dollars a year of revenue, so it is hardly a valuable fishery.  
The bill should have included the full extent of the territorial sea, because the Bounty 
Islands have got hundreds of thousands of seabirds using the land mass and using the seas 
around the islands. We have got the biggest breeding colony in the world of New Zealand 
fur seals. If we had had a decent reserve there, it would have gone right out to the extent 
of the territorial sea. That is critical because on the Bounty Islands you have got very little 
vegetation and very little soil, and the seabirds and the other species depend absolutely on 
the oceans. Yet we have failed to recognise the full extent of that interdependence by 
failing to protect the full extent of the territorial sea.  
It is also a missed opportunity because around Campbell Island 61 percent of the 
territorial sea is going to be open to fishi ng, subject to a prohib ition on Danish seining, 
and it is not going to be part of the marine reserve. One of the good things that the select 
committee did was to ensure that there was a review of that and of  the potential for a 
deep-water crab fishery within 3 years of the bill going into law, rather than 5 years, as 
was proposed in the bill as introduced. But th e far greater worth of an intact ecosystem 
would have been much better recognised if we had had a proper, full marine reserve there.  
The Greens obviously would support that 100 percent protection, but we do support 
this bill because something is always better than nothing. The United Nations 
Environment Programme described the islands as the most diverse and extensive of all the 
subantarctic archipelago, so this bill, with  some protection, is definitely better than 
nothing. But the fact that we are establishing the marine reserves under special legislation 
and that Parliament’s time is being taken to pass it shows again the fact that National has 
failed to introduce the marine reserves bill that it has long promised. Thank you.
